articles.title: Is it a missile? Is it a drone? What’s the Pelican used by Ukraine?
articles.body:
Is it a missile? Is it a drone? What’s the Pelican used by Ukraine?
The use of the Pelican has sparked interest among military analysts about whether it was a tactical ballistic missile or a drone.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday’s large-scale strike on Russia involved several weapons, including a “Pelican” for the first time.
In a post on X on Sunday morning, Zelenskyy wrote that long-range attacks on Moscow’s region had a “very significant impact”.

- list 3 of 3Russia’s elections are more than political theatre
“One of Russia’s key oil industry facilities and the aggressor’s logistics facility were hit. These are billions of dollars that sustain the war machine. The systems used included FP-1, RZ-100, MICH-2000, Palianytsia, Vendetta, Liutyi, Bars, Flamingo, Sichen and Pelican,” he said.
The attack on the final day of voting in Russia’s parliamentary elections killed at least three people. Moscow’s Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said more than 1,600 drones were intercepted, 450 of them heading for the capital.
However, the use of the Pelican has interested military analysts about whether it is a tactical ballistic missile or a drone.
Here’s what we know:
What is a Pelican missile and why is there confusion?
Speaking at the 34th International Defence Industry Exhibition in Poland last week, the CEO of Ukrainian defence firm Fire Point said Ukraine could start deploying its FP-7 tactical ballistic missile to target Russia in weeks, reported The Kyiv Post.
Iryna Terekh explained that the new weapons could strike targets 200km (125 miles) away and carry a warhead weighing up to 150kg.
The FP-7 system is ground-launched and has a maximum projectile speed of 1,500 metres per second. Fire Point founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman told Ukrainian media back in March that the system is cheaper than the US-made Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) surface-to-surface ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy also said last month that they expected to use their first domestically produced ballistic missile as early as in the autumn.
So far, there is no official confirmation that the FP-7 tactical ballistic missile is the Pelican, but Ukrainian media, such as The Kyiv Post, has linked the two together.
The New Voice of Ukraine reported on Sunday that Fire Point, the Ukrainian company that also produces the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile, had earlier this year applied to register the Pelican trademark.
However, the RBC-Ukraine news agency, citing unnamed sources, reported on Sunday without elaborating that the Pelican was an aircraft-type drone.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the Ukrainian media reports.
What is Ukraine’s weapons production like?
In February, Ukraine’s defence ministry said that the domestic weapons industry had demonstrated “unprecedented growth”, with production capacity increasing 50-fold to $50bn.
“As a result, domestic manufacturers now meet over half of the Defence Forces’ needs for weapons and military equipment,” the ministry said.
On Saturday, Zelenskyy posted on X that the military counterintelligence unit at the Security Service of Ukraine has developed a new interceptor drone that had been “successfully deployed” against Iranian-made Shahed drones used by Russia throughout the war to target Ukraine.
“Step by step, we are moving forward to give Ukraine greater protection. I thank all the developers and manufacturers who work every day to scale up the weapons we need,” he said.
In March, Oleksandr Syrskyi, the former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, said more than 70 per cent of Shahed-type attack drones were destroyed using interceptor drones in February.
The success of Ukraine’s drone interceptors also led to interest from Gulf states targeted by Iranian drones and missiles during the US-Israeli war.
How have attacks on Russia changed recently?
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified attacks on each other’s infrastructure, targeting oil facilities and logistics hubs.
Ukraine has also repeatedly struck warehouses belonging to Russia’s Wildberries e-commerce giant since July, in what has been described as an attack on Moscow’s supply chains and to hurt the Russian economy.
On Monday, the Financial Times reported that US President Donald Trump spoke to Zelenskyy on Sunday, urging him to stop attacking Russian refineries over concerns that it was worsening the global shortage of diesel and causing fuel prices to increase.

articles.title: Russia’s ‘Partial Mobilization’ Turns 4: Is Another Draft Coming?
articles.body:
On Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, exactly four years after Russian President Vladimir Putin announced “partial mobilization,” Moscow continues to insist that it can sustain its war against Ukraine without another mass call-up.
However, an examination of Russia’s legal framework, official recruitment figures, Ukrainian intelligence disclosures, assessments by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), and independent reporting shows that Russia is not relying solely on conventional voluntary recruitment. Instead, it has replaced one highly visible mobilization campaign with a permanent system combining contracts, large financial incentives, digital surveillance, and varying degrees of administrative pressure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
How Russia’s 2022 mobilization began
Putin announced the mobilization on Sept. 21, 2022, shortly after a Ukrainian counteroffensive forced Russian troops to retreat from large parts of the Kharkiv region.
Then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said 300,000 reservists would be called up. The campaign quickly became chaotic, with reports of summonses being sent to men who were medically unfit, too old, or lacked the military experience the Kremlin claimed it was seeking.
Members of ethnic minorities and residents of poorer regions were disproportionately affected. The uncertainty also triggered one of Russia’s largest wartime population movements. A EU Agency for Asylum estimate cited in an August 2026 UK government report said around 900,000 men left Russia after the announcement, although other estimates are lower.
Russia Hits 2 Gas Stations on Kyiv-Lviv M06 Highway
Shoigu declared the mobilization complete on Oct. 28, 2022, after the stated quota had been filled. Putin, however, never formally revoked the mobilization decree.
The decree does not mean that Russia has continuously conducted mass call-ups since 2022, but it allows mobilized troops to remain in service until the mobilization period is formally terminated. Many of those called up four years ago therefore remain in the military unless discharged for narrowly defined reasons.
Is Russia relying only on contract soldiers?
No. Contract recruitment is now the Kremlin’s main public method of bringing new personnel into the military, but it represents only one part of Russia’s manpower system.
The three main legal categories are different:
- Russia conducts routine compulsory military service for men aged 18-30. Around 300,000 are drafted annually for one year, according to the UK government’s military-service assessment.
- Mobilization applies primarily to reservists called into service during wartime.
- Contract service is officially voluntary and can include both first-time recruits and conscripts who agree to remain in the military.
In practice, the lines have become increasingly blurred.
The UK government report, which compiled evidence from European agencies, independent Russian media, and human rights groups, documented cases in which conscripts and other vulnerable men were deceived, threatened, or physically pressured into signing contracts. It stressed that this does not mean every Russian contract soldier was coerced, but it found that such practices were recurring.
Russian legislation also allows people facing criminal prosecution or serving prison sentences to sign military contracts. Regional authorities have targeted debtors, unemployed men, migrants, and people living in poverty, while companies have faced pressure to help meet recruitment targets.
A unified electronic military register now combines data from tax authorities, police, medical institutions, and other government systems. Electronic summonses can lead to restrictions on leaving Russia, receiving loans, conducting real-estate transactions, or holding a driver’s license.
Therefore, Russia can increase military intake without announcing a repeat of the nationally televised 2022 mobilization. It can raise enlistment bonuses, assign recruitment quotas to regions and employers, pressure conscripts to sign contracts, expand prison recruitment, and selectively summon reservists.
Is Russia’s recruitment system still working?
It continues to recruit hundreds of thousands of people, but at a rising financial and political cost.
Russian officials claimed that around 450,000 people signed military contracts in 2024. Deputy Security Council Chair Dmitry Medvedev said more than 422,000 did so in 2025, alongside around 32,000 recruits for volunteer formations, according to Reuters.
Medvedev subsequently claimed that about 200,000 contract soldiers and 16,000 volunteers joined during the first half of 2026. These figures cannot be independently verified and may include categories that overlap.
Russia’s reported 2026 target is approximately 409,000 contract recruits. In July, ISW assessed that Moscow was not on track to meet it.
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine offered an even more pessimistic assessment. It said Russia recruited approximately 232,000 contract personnel between January and July while suffering about 240,000 casualties, including at least 140,000 “irreversible” losses.
Total casualty figures also include wounded soldiers, some of whom may return to duty, so they cannot be directly compared with recruitment totals.
The broader trend is clear: Russia is still finding recruits at scale, but recruitment is becoming more expensive and may no longer provide enough personnel to replace losses and expand the military.
Some regional enlistment packages reached approximately 4.1 million rubles (around $49,000) in 2026. Continued increases in payments suggest that the pool of people willing to sign at previous rates is shrinking.
Is the Kremlin preparing another mobilization?
Ukrainian intelligence says it is preparing the option, but there is no evidence that Putin has issued a final order.
In August, Ukraine’s military and foreign intelligence agencies said the Russian General Staff had developed a plan to mobilize an additional 600,000 people – 300,000 during 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027. Kyiv Post previously reported that the plan would prioritize replenishing units already fighting in Ukraine and staffing newly formed units.
The intelligence briefing cited several preparatory measures: tighter military-registration controls, expanded prison recruitment, possible quotas for law-enforcement agencies, and additional coercive penalties for ignoring electronic summonses.
It also said more than 2,500 job advertisements for employees responsible for military registration and mobilization work had appeared at Russian enterprises by late July.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had prepared the infrastructure to recruit at least 300,000 more people, either through an open call-up or a less visible campaign. He predicted that Moscow would deny such plans until the State Duma election was over.
Putin denied the reports before the vote.
“As of today, there is no scenario that would require a mobilization,” Putin said on Sept. 3, according to Le Monde. Medvedev later supported his claim saying Russia had “absolutely no need for mobilization.”
Why the State Duma election matters
Russia held its parliamentary election from Sept. 18-20, the first State Duma vote since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
According to Reuters, with more than 95% of ballots counted, the Kremlin-backed United Russia party received 57.83% of the vote and was projected to take 355 of the Duma’s 450 seats, preserving its constitutional majority.
AP also reported that the result should not be treated as reliable evidence of popular support for a new mobilization. The election was conducted in a tightly controlled political system, with genuine opposition suppressed, anti-war candidates excluded or marginalized, and voting also staged in occupied Ukrainian territories.
United Russia already controlled parliament, while the nominal opposition parties normally support the Kremlin on major military legislation. The vote therefore did not give Putin a power he previously lacked.
Another mass call-up before voting could have revived memories of the panic and exodus of 2022. With the election over, that immediate political constraint has disappeared. The Kremlin can also portray the official result as public approval of its wartime course, regardless of whether the vote accurately reflects Russian opinion.
Ukrainian intelligence said the most likely time for a decision would be after the election. That was an assessment, not confirmation that a mobilization order had already been signed.
Analysts interviewed by Novaya Gazeta Europe argued that selective regional call-ups and increased recruitment quotas may be more likely initially than another simultaneous nationwide campaign.
As the 2022 decree remains formally in force, Russian legal experts cited by the publication said the Kremlin might not require an identical new decree to broaden call-ups. Moscow could instead use regional administrations, employers, military commissariats, and the digital register to mobilize people gradually.
What would another 300,000 troops change?
A call-up of 300,000 people would not place 300,000 combat-ready soldiers on the battlefield immediately.
New personnel would have to be processed, trained, equipped, organized into units, and transported. Ukrainian intelligence estimates that Russia could provide only 15-60 days of training to many mobilized recruits. Larger numbers could also strain training grounds, commanders, equipment stocks, and logistics.
The additional manpower could still allow Russia to replace casualties, rotate exhausted formations, fill assault units, and release more experienced soldiers from rear-area duties.
It could also support longer-term offensive planning. According to Ukrainian official Pavlo Palisa, in August Russian commanders had been instructed to prepare possible operational plans toward Kyiv and Chernihiv. He stressed that Ukraine had not observed a strike force forming in those directions and that military planning did not mean an attack was imminent.
Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky has also warned against assuming that more Russian troops would automatically produce major territorial gains.
“More infantry means more losses,” he said, arguing that drones, sensors, and rapid strike systems now shape battlefield effectiveness. Nevertheless, Biletsky acknowledged another mobilization would create additional pressure on Ukraine.
Would mobilization mean Russia is preparing to attack NATO?
Not necessarily. European officials have issued increasingly serious warnings about Russian provocations. Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka told The Guardian that Moscow could test NATO within “months, not years” through drones, missiles, a limited incursion, or a false-flag operation.
Other Baltic officials offered a more cautious assessment. Latvian State Security Service chief Normunds Mežviets said there were no indications of an imminent conventional attack and noted that Russian resources remained stretched by the war in Ukraine.
Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs similarly predicted that Russia could increase mobilization after the election and use the winter to intensify pressure on Ukraine and its supporters. However, he said he would rule out a conventional Russian incursion for now, while warning about sabotage, cyberattacks, and drone or missile incidents.
French OSINT analyst Clément Molin argued that Russia currently lacks the forces for a conventional war with Europe because most of its military resources remain committed in Ukraine and its force posture around Kaliningrad is insufficient. In his assessment, another mobilization would more likely replenish forces fighting Ukraine, while hybrid attacks against Europe remain a more realistic near-term scenario.
Earlier, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said intelligence assessments indicate Russia’s plans in its war against Ukraine include “hybrid” drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Kyiv, including Poland.
He warned there was a “real risk” that drones or other missiles could enter the territory of one or several NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank and cause damage.
A new mobilization would primarily strengthen Russia’s ability to continue or expand its war in Ukraine. Over time, however, it could also help Moscow rebuild forces available for pressure against NATO, particularly if fighting in Ukraine decreases.
How mobilization currently works in Ukraine
Ukraine remains under a formally declared general mobilization and martial law, both extended through Oct. 31, 2026. Unlike Russia’s preference for avoiding the politically sensitive word, Ukraine’s mobilization is publicly acknowledged as a continuous national process rather than a sequence of separate “waves.”
In general, medically fit men liable for military service between the ages of 25 and 60 may be mobilized if they do not have a legal deferment or official reservation.
Men aged 18-24 who have not previously served and are not in the reserve generally join voluntarily under military contracts. Those who already have military experience, officer status or another legal status making them liable for service, can be mobilized before turning 25, according to a review of the current rules.
No new Ukrainian mobilization “wave” or general reduction of the mobilization age has been announced.
What is most likely to happen next?
The available evidence supports three conclusions.
First, Russia’s contract system is still producing large numbers of troops. Claims that Moscow has already exhausted its human resources are not supported by the available data.
Second, the system is becoming more expensive, coercive, and less effective at creating additional forces beyond replacing battlefield losses.
Third, Russia has created the administrative and digital infrastructure required for another call-up, but preparation does not prove that Putin has decided to order one.
The most plausible immediate scenario is an expansion of hidden or selective mobilization: higher regional quotas, intensified pressure on conscripts, broader prison recruitment, electronic summonses, and targeted reserve call-ups. A public nationwide campaign becomes more likely if those methods fail to satisfy battlefield requirements.

articles.title: CNN, MS Now and Politico to sue Trump administration over White House ban – live
articles.body:
JD Vance says Trump’s White House media ban is ‘totally appropriate’ as networks halt TV pool coverage in response – live
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News, the fourth other networks that make up the White House TV pool, decided they would cease coverage in solidarity with banned CNN
'I think it's totally appropriate,' says JD Vance on Trump's White House media bans
JD Vance defended Trump’s ban of three news outlets from the White House while speaking to reporters en route to a campaign event in North Carolina.
“He’s not banning media outlets,” Vance said on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. (Trump, in his social media post announcing the move, referred to his actions as a ban.)
Vance continued: “What he’s doing is saying we’re not going to give you special access to the White House if you engage in what is effectively propaganda.”
He criticized the outlets for coverage that he said was overly negative of the Trump administration.
“That’s not representative of the American people. It’s not representative of public opinion. So if you’re going to engage in what is effectively far left propaganda, why would a Republican White House give you special access?”
But, he said, Trump’s actions didn’t violate the outlets’ rights, because “they can still report on the Trump White House, they can still get the public reports” and “they can still, of course, talk to people in the administration and outside the administration”.
“It’s about basic fairness. They can still report. They still have access to free speech. They’re just not going to get an office in the White House anymore. And I think it’s totally appropriate, unless, of course, they start to behave like real news organizations.”
It appears the media boycott of President Trump in response to his banning of several news outlets from the White House has expanded from video coverage to include still images.
On Monday afternoon, The Washington Post said in a statement posted to social media that it would not publish any photos of Trump until midnight.
“The Washington Post will not publish any photographs of today’s presidential events – including Trump’s departure from the White House and his events at the United Nations in New York – until midnight Eastern Time, joining a collective effort with photographers in other newsrooms covering the White House in a show of support of the banned outlets.”
It was unclear which other outlets, if any, had joined the Post’s roughly 8-hour moratorium on sharing images of the president.
Here's a quick breakdown of what's happened today:
Three news outlets sued after Trump blocked them from the White House. If you missed it, Trump on Friday announced a surprise decision to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House, citing unfavorable coverage of his administration. On Monday, the three outlets, as anticipated, filed a lawsuit to restore their access.
The other White House TV pool members paused coverage of Trump in solidarity. The pool, for the uninitiated, is a rotation of five major networks (ABC, NBC, CBS, Fox News, and the recently axed CNN) who take turns following the president day-to-day and sharing their collected footage with other outlets. After Trump’s decision to nix CNN, the other four outlets agreed to cease covering the president as per usual, so far leaving Trump bereft of his usual tag-along camera crew.
Some key Republicans are pressing their president hard on war-inflated diesel prices. As the war in Iran continues to jack up the price of diesel — the fuel that runs America’s semi trucks, tractors, and heavy machinery — some influential Republicans are coming out publicly to pressure the president to take more drastic action. Republican senator Chuck Grassley called for an embargo on diesel exports. And Republican congresswoman and Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson called for measures to tamp prices and bring an “immediate” end to the war in Iran.
Trump is beginning a busy week of diplomacy. Trump is heading to New York to attend the United Nations’ annual convening of world leaders. While there, he’s expected to meet with a number of key heads of state, including the US-backed interim president of Venezuela, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and possibly the leaders of Iran. But first, Trump will be meeting with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a political opposite with whom he’s so far maintained a strange rapport.

At UN, Trump looks to lean on Zelenskyy to agree to energy ceasefire with Russia
Andrew Roth
Donald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people.
On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine.
“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.”
“This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!”
Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities.
Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”.
“Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.”
The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with secretary of state Marco Rubio.
During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”.
“Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said.
Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”.
Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November.
Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez.
In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.”
Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued.
After a ribbon cutting ceremony not covered by the standard White House TV press pool, Trump boarded Marine One, en route to New York City for a planned meeting with Mayor Zohran Mamdani and, later, French President Emmanuel Macron.
The White House streamed video of Trump’s remarks. However, the audio was too distorted to make out what he said.
Iowa GOP Senate candidate calls for "immediate end" to Iran war
Ashley Hinson, a Republican member of the House of Representatives campaigning for a valuable Senate seat in Iowa, publicly called for an end to the war with Iran in a social media post on Monday.
“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote. “We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices.”
After listing some potential policy measures to mitigate the costs of diesel fuel, she added: “These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”
While Hinson didn’t name Trump outright, her comments diverge from the oft-repeated stance of a president who has said the high prices are a worthwhile setback to bring Iran’s leadership to heel.
Hinson, once a steady ally of Trump, has drifted further from the president in recent weeks. When JD Vance, a key surrogate for Trump on the 2026 campaign trail, headlined a rally in her state last week, Hinson was notably absent. Her comment also comes as Republicans worry that the unpopular conflict will hamstring the party in the midterm elections and help secure control of one or both chambers of Congress for the Democrats.

Key ally urges Trump to back US farmers amid anger over rising prices
Ariana Baio
Donald Trump is facing growing calls, including from within his own party, to boost support for US farmers as his administration faces mounting anger over its treatment of the agricultural sector.
Republican senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa called on the US president to place an embargo on diesel exports this weekend and help farmers grapple with high prices.
Grassley, who is largely aligned with Trump, suggested the embargo in multiple social media posts, calling on the president to issue a 1970s-style embargo on diesel and agricultural products to help farmers.
“If our [government] can embargo chips to China it can embargo diesel to help American farmers & truckers,” Grassley wrote on Sunday. “We need our family farmers who feed&fuel the world [to be] on the strongest footing possible no matter what’s happening across the globe.”
For months, farmers – traditionally a reliable Republican voting base – have been angry with the Trump administration because they believe some of its policies adversely affect them.
That includes tariffs, which have driven up the cost of fertilizer, machine parts, seed and more; increasing beef imports to lower prices for Americans, which undermines domestic producers; and the Iran war, which has made it more expensive for farmers to operate machinery and transport products.
The national average cost of diesel was $6.51 as of Sunday, according to AAA. In Iowa, it was slightly lower at $6.31 – still nearly $3 more than the cost one year ago.
Gas prices are not the only rising cost Americans are facing as a result of the Iran war. Groceries have also become more expensive, and the Trump administration has sought to lower some of those prices, particularly beef, by allowing 300,000 metric tons of overseas beef trimmings to enter the US at a reduced tariff rate.
But domestic farmers in the US, who are already struggling with smaller herds, say the decision will increase competition and make it more difficult to sell their own.
“It takes something big to change long-established voting patterns, but I think there’s a possibility that the Trump administration has done things that are big enough and bad enough from the standpoint of rural America to make some of the voters who shifted a decade ago reconsider their choice,” William Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told the Washington Sun.
US strikes on alleged drug boats may constitute ‘crimes against humanity’, UN finds
Tiago Rogero
South America correspondent
A special rapporteur for the UN human rights council has concluded that there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that the United States attacks on boats allegedly carrying drugs in the Pacific and Caribbean “constituted crimes against humanity”.
The boat strikes, carried out since September 2025 on the stated grounds of stopping drugs being trafficked by sea to the US, have killed more than 230 people. The latest, on Saturday, killed four people in the Caribbean.
The UN itself, along with several human rights organisations, lawyers and international law experts, had already described the bombings as “extrajudicial killings”, but special rapporteur Ben Saul went further.
In a briefing note posted by Saul on social media on Sunday night and first reported by the BBC, Saul wrote that, in addition to “serial extrajudicial killings”, the attacks were “in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law”.
He added: “There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law.”
The report cites 68 US attacks that killed 223 people. It is unclear how recently the figures were updated – tallies by organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America put the death toll at 234 people in 66 attacks.
US Southern Command, which has coordinated the attacks, posted on Saturday, alongside a grainy video, that it had “executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean. Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists”.
As has become standard in announcements of such attacks, the US did not identify the victims or provide any details about the alleged intelligence that supposedly confirmed their involvement in drug trafficking.
Saul’s report rejects the claim made by Donald Trump before Congress that the strikes amounted to “self-defence” against “designated terrorist organizations”.
The special rapporteur wrote that the crews were not “militarily armed and possessed the intent and capacity to launch military attacks” against the US.
“Even assuming that the vessels and crew attacked were members of the criminal groups listed as terrorist, such organizations have not mounted any ‘armed attack’ on the United States so as to trigger a right of self-defence,” he added.
The US Department of State has not yet responded to a request for comment.
Lauren Boebert slams ethics complaint alleging sexual relationships with three staffers as 'politically motivated'
Richard Luscombe
Lauren Boebert, the firebrand Colorado Republican congresswoman, is the subject of a House ethics complaint that she had sex with three staff members, and paid one to keep quiet. She said the allegations are untrue, and part of a “politically motivated” campaign against her.
Boebert’s denials came through a formal statement from her office, which said “the congresswoman rejects the claims as utterly false”, and a verbose video rant on social media in which she accused the person who filed the document as a “sloppy, desperate, obsessive hack”, and journalists who reported the story as falling victim to a “scam”.
According to the complaint, filed last week by David Wheeler, an independent journalist, activist, and founder of the American Muckrakers political action committee, Boebert committed at least seven violations of House ethics rules.
Among the most prominent allegations are that Boebert conducted a four-year “romantic and sexual relationship” with a senior female staffer, named as Clarice Navarro Ratzlaff, then paid her $200,000 when Ratzlaff broke off the affair and threatened to file an ethics complaint of her own.
Additionally, Wheeler alleges, Boebert had a sexual relationships around the same time with Raven Finegan, a congressional employee and the congresswoman’s district chief of staff, and Jeffrey Small, who was her chief of staff from 2021 to 2025.
The code of official conduct prohibits House members from engaging in sexual relationships with employees under their supervision, or the committees on which they serve, unless a couple is married. Consent, the rules state, is not a defense.
Boebert frequently promotes her own Christian values and has previously been publicly critical of same-sex relationships.
JB Pritzker – the governor of Illinois, an expected contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, and one of the country’s heftier political figures – revealed to CBS on Monday that he’s been using GLP-1s to shed weight.
Pritzker told CBS Mornings that he began taking GLP-1s after receiving a diabetes diagnosis two years ago. Since then, he said he’s lost 80 pounds.
Pritzker’s weight has been a source of jabs by political opponents, including President Trump, with whom he has sparred repeatedly during Trump’s second term.
(When pressed by an interviewer on whether he lost weight in part to reshape his image ahead of a presidential run, Pritzker equivocated.)

articles.title: What F-16 Gun Kills Tell Us About the Future of Ukraine’s Air Force
articles.body:
A remarkable cockpit photograph released by Ukraine last week captures far more than the destruction of a Russian Geran jet-powered attack drone. It illustrates both how far the Ukrainian Air Force has come—and the gap between the force it has today and the one it would need to become a major European air power in the future.
This is important because the future of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself does not depend on getting a few more F-16s, but rather on its ability to build an air force capable of the challenge.
The photograph is extraordinary. Taken from the cockpit of a Ukrainian F-16 during a Russian mass air attack on Sept. 10 and released a week later, the image shows a Geran drone falling from the sky, trailing smoke. According to my sources in Ukraine, it was the pilot’s third gun kill of the sortie.
Think about that for a moment.
An aircraft designed during the Cold War and transferred to Ukraine after decades of service in Western Europe, is being flown by a pilot with the Ukrainian Air Force against Russian cruise missiles in an air war unlike anything NATO has previously experienced. And the pilot is shooting them down with the F-16’s 20mm cannon.
On the night of Sept. 9-10, Russia launched 149 Shahed-type cruise missiles, along with decoys and other unmanned aircraft, against Ukraine. According to the Ukrainian Air Force, 128 were destroyed or suppressed. Roughly half of these were Gerans, which are jet-powered variants of the Shahed.
The photograph is not only a terrific advertisement for the ingenuity and skill of airmen in Ukraine, but also a warning to those drawing the wrong conclusions about airpower from this conflict.
Ukraine’s success with the F-16 does not mean these aircraft are sufficient for its long-term needs.
The F-16 Ukraine Has Is Not the F-16 of Today
The European aircraft originally provided to Ukraine are principally F-16AM/BM Mid-Life Update aircraft. They began life as older Block 15 F-16 fighters and subsequently received substantial avionics and weapons upgrades. They remain capable airplanes, and they have been modernized with capabilities comparable to later F-16C/D models. But there is an important distinction between an upgraded aircraft conceived more than 40 years ago and what the F-16 has become today.
The newest F-16 Block 70/72 aircraft are equipped with the APG-83 active electronically scanned array radar, enhanced mission computers and electronic warfare capabilities, advanced datalinks, updated cockpit displays, infrared search-and-track integration, and compatibility with a wide range of modern weapons. Its upgraded airframe is rated for a 12,000-hour structural service life.
The APG-83 is derived from the AESA radars used in the F-22 and F-35, providing pilots greater situational awareness, electronic protection, and the ability to search and track targets more effectively in a complex electromagnetic environment. That matters enormously over Ukraine.
The Ukrainian Air Force is not confronting a single threat. Its pilots face an extraordinarily complicated mixture of slow propeller-driven drones, faster jet-powered Gerans, cruise missiles, Russian fighters, long-range surface-to-air missile systems, electronic warfare, and dense ground-based air defenses.
A modern fighter must therefore do much more than fly fast and carry missiles. It needs to find, identify, prioritize, share, and engage multiple threats while surviving in a heavily contested electromagnetic environment. That is fundamentally an information problem—and modern sensors, electronic warfare and networking are what increasingly determine success.
Shooting Gerans Is Only One Mission
A second lesson from this photograph is the means the pilot used to dispatch the threat. Using the F-16’s gun preserves scarce air-to-air missiles. Ukrainian Air Force officials have acknowledged the pace of Russian air attacks imposes significant pressure on Ukraine’s missile inventories
Ukraine’s air force must perform several missions simultaneously: defend cities and critical infrastructure against cruise missiles; deter or engage Russian air forces; suppress enemy air defenses; conduct precision attacks into Russia; protect Ukrainian ground forces; and contribute to the broader intelligence and command-and-control picture. That requires both highly capable aircraft and scale.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in 2024 that Ukraine needed 120 to 130 F-16s to challenge the number of Russian aircraft committed to the war—many more than they currently possess. That was Ukraine’s stated requirement, not an independent assessment, but it illustrates the difference between possessing F-16s and operating a combat air force of meaningful size. Aircraft numbers by themselves, however, can also be misleading.
A force of 100 fighters is inherently smaller than it seems. At any given moment, some are undergoing maintenance while several must be earmarked for training. The aircraft left must be dispersed, protected, and repaired. Pilots must get enough flying hours to remain proficient. Weapons, engines, spare parts, and ground support equipment must be continuously available.
Airpower depends on a system—not simply an inventory of airplanes.
Building an Air Force, Not Donating Aircraft
One of the more consequential developments in Western assistance to Ukraine is largely unseen, but vitally important. The Air Force Capability Coalition has gradually moved beyond simply transferring F-16s to Ukraine toward creating a Western-style aviation ecosystem encompassing combat aircraft, pilot and maintainer training, weapons, logistics, protected infrastructure, command and control, and airborne early warning.
Ukraine’s future force architecture also includes French-built Mirage 2000s and Swedish Gripens alongside U.S.-made F-16s.
This is the correct way to think about airpower: A modern fighter becomes dramatically more effective when it is properly supported. Airborne early-warning aircraft that can see hundreds of miles, ground-based sensors, secure datalinks for sharing targeting info, and commanders able to assemble those inputs into a common operational picture all enhance operational performance.
There are legitimate questions about cost, training capacity, sustainment, competing aircraft types, and the rate at which any fighter force can realistically be expanded. Discussion about offering newer F-16s miss the point that doing so would not eliminate the need for ground-based air defense, inexpensive drone interceptors, or other cost-effective ways of defeating mass attacks. No country can economically afford to use its most sophisticated weapon against every inexpensive threat.
But the strategic distinction is important. The F-16s flying over Ukraine today began as an emergency wartime capability. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry now describes the broader effort as a transition from its Soviet aviation inheritance toward a modern, networked Western model. That transition will ultimately be far more consequential than any individual aircraft transfer.
The image released this week captures the beginning of that story: A pilot in the Ukrainian Air Force maneuvering an F-16 over Ukraine while the wreckage of a Russian cruise missile falls toward the earth. The next chapter is about whether Ukraine’s wartime collection of fighters evolves into the sustainable, technologically modern, and fully integrated air force it needs, with the capacity to defend its airspace for decades—and carry the fight to the aggressor if required.
That is the difference between providing Ukraine airplanes and helping Ukraine build a credible air force.

articles.title: European intelligence chiefs warn Russia could test NATO within months
articles.body:
European intelligence officials are warning that Russia could seek to test NATO in the coming months, potentially through a limited incursion into alliance territory, drone attacks or other provocations, as concerns grow that Moscow is preparing to escalate its operations in Europe.
One European intelligence chief told The Guardian that such an attack could come within “months, not years,” although other senior officials cautioned that there are no indications an attack is imminent and warned against fueling public panic.
The warnings, published Sunday, came after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told parliament that intelligence assessments indicated Russia could seek to test the military alliance in the coming months. French President Emmanuel Macron described the Polish warnings as well-founded and documented and on Friday summoned political party leaders and candidates in France’s 2027 presidential election for emergency talks in Paris on the issue.
Concerns about escalation are mounting as world leaders gather in New York this week for the annual UN General Assembly and as Russia and Ukraine intensify aerial attacks in the war that began with Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones and missiles at Moscow and other parts of Russia early Sunday in one of its largest aerial operations since the war began. Russia said about 1,600 drones were involved in the attack, including hundreds targeting the Moscow region.
In separate interviews with The Guardian, three senior European intelligence officials described the assessments behind the warnings about Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech Republic’s Security Information Service, or BIS, said that in addition to a large-scale drone attack, a limited Russian incursion into NATO territory bordering Russia could be among the scenarios being considered.
“It's possible,” Koudelka said in a rare interview with the British newspaper. He said possible Russian actions could include “a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” adding that many people were working to prevent such a scenario. Koudelka said an escalation could happen in “months, not years.”
Officials in the Baltic states offered more cautious assessments, warning that amplifying speculation about a Russian attack on NATO territory could itself serve Russian President Vladimir Putin’s objectives.
Normunds Mežviets, director general of Latvia’s State Security Service, said his agency had seen no evidence of an imminent Russian attack.
“We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” he said, while adding that there were indications Moscow was preparing for “more decisive” action in Europe.
Mežviets said it remained unclear whether such preparations were part of a broader strategy to destabilize Europe as the war in Ukraine approaches its fifth year. But he welcomed what he described as a change in attitudes among Western European governments toward the threat posed by Russia.
Before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mežviets said, Baltic governments repeatedly warned their Western European partners about Moscow but were often ignored. That changed after the invasion, he said, when Western officials acknowledged that the Baltic states and Poland had been right about the threat.
‘Social media panic’
Estonian Foreign Ministry Secretary General Jonatan Vseviov also pushed back against what he called “panic on social media” over the possibility that Russia could attack NATO territory to test the alliance.
If there is reason to fear an attack, the Estonian government will say so, Vseviov wrote on X, urging the public in the meantime to remain calm and carry on with their daily lives.
The senior intelligence officials interviewed by The Guardian declined to describe the specific intelligence underlying their assessments.
They also declined to say whether CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s surprise visit to Moscow last month was intended in part to warn the Kremlin against attempting to test NATO.
Thomas Nilsson, head of Sweden’s Military Intelligence and Security Service, also spoke with the British newspaper and expressed skepticism about Moscow’s willingness to negotiate seriously over Ukraine.
Nilsson said he had seen no indication that Moscow genuinely wanted negotiations, adding that his assessment was that Russian leaders still believed they could achieve their strategic objectives and were therefore engaging in what he described as “negotiation theater.”
Nilsson, Koudelka and Mežviets agreed that Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other covert operations in Europe was likely to intensify and expand in the coming months.
Nilsson described an incident in which an explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany as a “gamechanger.” German authorities have blamed Russia for the August incident, saying evidence indicated the Russian state provided expertise and equipment to operatives recruited to carry out the attack. Moscow has denied involvement.
The drone, carrying explosives, was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate, but German authorities said the device could have caused a catastrophe.
Sending an armed drone into a busy airport in the heart of Europe represented a significant escalation because it could have killed people or severely damaged critical infrastructure, Nilsson said.
He said Russia’s intensified sabotage campaign appeared to have several objectives: weakening European support for Ukraine, creating divisions within NATO and spreading fear across Europe.
Mežviets said Russia appeared to be shifting from relatively indiscriminate acts of sabotage and arson intended primarily to create panic toward attacks on specific targets linked to Western support for Ukraine.
“We see them looking to attack railway infrastructure, Ukraine support infrastructure,” he said, adding that European intelligence agencies were now seeing a shift toward targets in the defense industry.
Such operations, he said, could achieve both practical and psychological objectives, disrupting Western support for Ukraine while simultaneously spreading fear.
Koudelka said another consequence of the sabotage campaign was the strain it places on European intelligence services because even fires, accidents and technical failures with no connection to Russia increasingly require investigation as potential acts of sabotage.
Every fire or malfunction must now be examined by intelligence agencies as a possible terrorist attack, Koudelka said, describing that additional burden on security services as an outcome that benefits the Kremlin.
European governments have increasingly accused Russia of conducting what they describe as hybrid warfare across the continent, including sabotage, arson, cyberattacks and disinformation campaigns. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said this month that Russia had become “increasingly reckless,” citing incursions into NATO airspace, fires at factories producing defense equipment for Ukraine and the Leipzig incident.
Trump: ‘This ridiculous war must end’
Meanwhile, following one of Ukraine’s largest attacks on Russia since the start of the war, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday that the “ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended.”
Trump also said Russia had “unfortunately” lost control of parts of its diesel industry because of the war.
Ukraine launched about 1,600 drones toward regions across Russia overnight Saturday into Sunday, according to Russian accounts, with hundreds directed toward Moscow. The operation was among Ukraine’s largest attacks on Russian territory since the beginning of the war.
The assault came a day before results were announced from Russian parliamentary elections that produced an expected victory for Putin’s ruling United Russia party. Voting was also conducted in Russian-occupied regions of Ukraine, which Kyiv and the European Union denounced as illegal.
Reports from Moscow indicated that the Moscow Oil Refinery in Kapotnya, in the southeastern part of the capital, was hit. Videos circulating from the area showed smoke rising from several parts of the energy facility, which had also been targeted in June.
The refinery is a major supplier of fuel to Moscow and the surrounding region and is estimated to provide a significant share of the capital’s fuel needs.
The Ukrainian attack could add to tensions between Kyiv and Washington over strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. Trump has expressed concern that such attacks could disrupt global fuel supplies and drive up energy prices.
Last week, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy not to attack oil refineries deep inside Russia, arguing that the strikes were contributing to global fuel shortages and higher energy prices.
The following day, Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt attacks on energy facilities. Neither side confirmed such an agreement, and strikes on energy infrastructure have continued.
Zelenskyy did not commit to complying with Trump’s demand and responded with a statement disputing the U.S. president’s characterization of the situation.
Ukraine, Zelenskyy said, had proposed that its partners secure an agreement with Russia to stop attacks on critical infrastructure.
Food supplies, energy facilities and other basic infrastructure essential to civilian life should be protected, he said, accusing Russia of routinely attacking those targets.
Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure, logistics networks and even warehouses containing food and medicine continue to come under Russian attack, Zelenskyy said.
The intensifying strikes come as European security officials increasingly warn that the war’s effects are extending beyond Ukraine’s borders. While the intelligence chiefs interviewed by The Guardian differed over how imminent a direct Russian challenge to NATO might be, they agreed that Moscow’s covert and hybrid operations in Europe were likely to increase in the months ahead.

articles.title: Russia’s threat isn’t better missile, it’s 14,000 cheap ones. Its new deadly weapon was built in early 1990s, experts say
articles.body:
Russia wants to build 14,000 of a new cruise missile next year, enough to fire them at Ukrainian cities by the thousand. The weapon, the Dan-T, is a cheap air-launched jet missile that flies hundreds of kilometers on its own, RBC-Ukraine reported.
The danger is volume, not finesse. Russia aims to produce up to 2,000 Dan-T missiles by the end of this year and scale it drastically, RBC-Ukraine's sources say. Fired in large numbers, it would add a fresh layer to the Gerans and the cruise and ballistic missiles that already saturate Ukraine's skies on the worst nights.
Numbers make the threat
The experts are less worried about any single Dan-T than about the swarm. High speed, long range, and the ability to launch the missiles by the thousand would stretch Ukraine's air defense further with every strike, forcing crews to spend scarce interceptors on yet another cheap target.
The missile flies to its objective autonomously, and Russia claims a special flight profile designed to make it harder for air defense to spot and shoot down.
A target drone becomes a weapon
The Dan-T has an unusual pedigree. It began as the Dan-M, a jet-powered target drone Russia's Sokol bureau built in the early 1990s and imitated US Tomahawk cruise missiles for air-defense practice, now planned to be stripped of its recovery parachute, fitted with a warhead, and fired at Ukrainian cities. Like Russia's other new cruise weapons, it carries no operator link, steering itself by satellite and inertial navigation.
The Banderol joins the list
The Dan-T is not the only new weapon unsettling Ukraine's military. The experts named it alongside the S8000 Banderol, a separate cheap cruise missile that Russia already builds at up to 80 a month and has used in some of its heaviest strikes on Kyiv. The Dan-T closely resembles the Banderol and, being cheaper, may end up replacing it.

articles.title: Russia's total oil refining capacity down 45% due to long-range strikes, Ukrainian military says
articles.body:
Russia's total oil refining capacity down 45% due to long-range strikes, Ukrainian military says
Ukraine's ongoing long-range strike campaign against Russian oil refineries has knocked out 45% of the country's total refining capacity, the General Staff reported on Sept. 21.
"One of the consequences is a shortage of high-quality fuel in the Russian Federation," the General Staff report said.
"Among other things, there is a sharp decline in the production of gasoline and diesel fuel of the Euro-5/K5 standard."
The assessment comes a day after major Ukrainian drone and missile strikes on the Moscow Oil Refinery in a mass attacks on the Russian capital.
The Moscow strike was only the latest in a spate of ongoing attacks against Russian refineries, with two others — in Yaroslavl and Samara oblasts respectively — struck since Sept. 14, according to the Ukrainian military.
According to a Reuters report citing industry sources, the Moscow Oil Refinery, owned by state-controlled company Gazprom Neft, stopped production after the Sept. 20 attack.
The refinery's main crude distillation units were hit, Reuters' sources said, with repair likely requiring weeks to bring the facility back online.
Ukraine's ongoing campaign against Russian refineries, meant to hinder Russia's war machine and economy as a whole, has been made possible by a dramatic scaling up in the size and diversity of Kyiv's arsenal.
Ukraine's long-range strike drones and missiles have proved not only capable of regularly reaching targets more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory, but are also launched in sufficient number to overwhelm dense Russian air defense networks, such as the one protecting the Russian capital.
During the Sept. 20 attack, Russian forces shot down more than 1,600 drones across Russia, 450 of which were aimed at Moscow, according to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin.
In his report on the attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine used several largely domestically produced weapons systems in the attack, including the Flamingo cruise missile.
Zelensky also mentioned a "Pelican," with several media outlets mistakenly reporting this was the first confirmed use of the much-anticipated FP-7 ballistic missile. Later reports clarified that the Pelican is a drone.

articles.title: How Washington left Saudi Arabia’s plea for help unanswered
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Trump failed to answer Saudi plea for help against Houthis when Riyadh needed it most
Saudi Arabia has spent decades building its security partnership with Washington, buying billions of dollars in US weapons and cultivating close ties with successive American administrations.
But when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a direct plea to US President Donald Trump for military help against Yemen's Houthis, Washington ultimately stepped away.
For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.
The issue came to a head on Thursday when Mohammed bin Salman called Trump and urged him to intervene against the rapidly advancing Iran-backed group, according to the New York Times.
Trump had told advisers a day earlier that he opposed strikes. After the call, however, he changed course and ordered the Pentagon to prepare for an attack.
By Sunday, US commanders had reportedly approved target lists and troops were loading bombs onto warplanes. Then Trump reversed course again, calling off the strikes, at least for now.
So why did Trump stop short when one of Washington's closest Middle Eastern partners was asking for help?
Why is Saudi Arabia asking for US help?
Riyadh's plea comes at one of its most vulnerable moments in years, as the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi cities, oil infrastructure and shipping while making significant advances in western Yemen, taking the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coast including the area around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The threat has been compounded by the wider war with Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and increased Saudi Arabia's reliance on alternative export routes through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, a crucial route for bypassing Hormuz, has also been largely shut following an attack Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias.
That has left the kingdom facing pressure on its oil export routes from multiple directions.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh had spent decades investing in its US security partnership precisely for such a crisis.
"The reason a country like Saudi Arabia invests so heavily in developing a security partnership with the United States is for just this sort of eventuality," Ratney told the NYT.
Saudi officials have also made clear that they do not want to confront the Houthis alone after the kingdom's previous military campaign in Yemen became a costly, years-long conflict.
Why did Trump hesitate?
For Trump, intervening would mean opening another front while the US is already at war with Iran.
Most of his inner circle were either deeply sceptical of or opposed to joining Saudi Arabia's fight, amid concerns over pressure on the US military and its weapons stockpiles.
There were also doubts that another bombing campaign would work. The US struck more than 1,000 Houthi targets during a campaign lasting more than 50 days in 2025, but the group survived and has since rebuilt much of its military capability.
Trump has also stressed that the Houthis are currently targeting Saudi Arabia rather than the United States.
He said on Sunday that Washington had remained in communication with the group and that the Houthis had so far agreed not to fight the US. Houthi officials have disputed Trump's claim that they contacted Washington.
That gives Trump little incentive to restart a direct confrontation that could bring American ships back into the Houthis' sights and further threaten shipping through Bab al-Mandeb.
What does this mean for the US-Saudi relationship?
The Trump administration last week asked Congress to approve the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal estimated at $24.3 billion, saying it would strengthen the security of a "major non-NATO ally", can be an indication that Washington has not abandoned Riyadh altogether.
But advanced weapons sales are different from direct US military intervention, and the latest crisis has exposed the limits of what Riyadh can expect from Washington when their immediate interests diverge.
Saudi Arabia has already been looking to broaden its security partnerships. Last month, it signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkey and Pakistan, under which an armed attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on all.
Turkey has since said it is prepared to help meet Saudi military needs as Houthi attacks intensify.
For Riyadh, it is a reminder that even close ties with Washington offer no guarantee of US support when American interests lie elsewhere.

articles.title: Houthis target ‘sensitive sites’ in Saudi Arabia (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Houthis target ‘sensitive sites’ in Saudi Arabia (VIDEO)
Houthi missiles and drones struck several “sensitive sites” across Saudi Arabia, including in the capital Riyadh, the Yemeni militant group announced on Sunday, marking a new escalation in their renewed conflict with the kingdom.
Flames and a large column of black smoke was seen rising near King Khalid International Airport on Saturday, as flights were delayed and canceled. Saudi Arabia said its air defenses intercepted a ballistic missile headed toward Riyadh and thwarted several other attacks.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group also targeted facilities belonging to state oil giant Saudi Aramco in the western city of Yanbu. He described the weekend strikes as retaliation for recent Saudi-led coalition attacks on Yemen.
Saudi Arabia has backed Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since intervening in the country’s civil war in 2015. Large-scale fighting largely subsided after a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but the conflict erupted again this summer after an airport in Houthi-controlled Sanaa was bombed to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from Tehran from landing. The Houthis blamed Riyadh, declared the ceasefire over and began a new campaign against Saudi targets.
Houthi forces struck the Saudi capital today, hitting fuel storage infrastructure at Riyadh International Airport. pic.twitter.com/lpRHpyIsXf
— OSINTtechnical (@Osinttechnical) September 19, 2026
They have since seized key territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including positions around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes. Officially known as the Ansarullah movement, the Houthis currently control the capital, Sanaa, and much of the country’s north and west.
Saudi-led forces have responded with renewed airstrikes inside Yemen.
Saudi political analyst Faisal Alshammeri told RT that the latest attacks could force Riyadh to respond more strongly despite its efforts to avoid being dragged back into a major ground war in Yemen.
He also noted that the escalation could become the first major test of the Mecca defense agreement between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan, predicting that Ankara and Islamabad would provide intelligence and air-defense support rather than join direct attacks on the Houthis.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have explicitly warned other countries against joining the Saudi campaign. Senior Houthi official Mohamed al-Bukhaiti told AP on Sunday that the group could fight on multiple fronts if foreign states became involved, while insisting that its current operations in the Red Sea are directed at Saudi Arabia rather than US or other foreign vessels.
The renewed Yemen conflict has increasingly entangled with the wider US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis openly sided with Tehran earlier this year, while fighting around the Strait of Hormuz has forced Saudi Arabia to rely increasingly on Red Sea oil routes now threatened by the Houthi advance.
The mounting pressure on Middle Eastern energy supply routes has kept oil above $100 a barrel, with Brent futures trading around $104 on Friday.

articles.title: Russia Targets 28,000 Additional Strike Drones Per Year via Rosatom Factory Expansion
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Targets 28,000 Additional Strike Drones Per Year via Rosatom Factory Expansion
Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom has drafted internal plans to expand its carbon fiber production capacity at the Alabuga-Volokno factory, Politico reported on September 20, citing leaked documents.
This would enable Moscow to manufacture an additional 28,000 weaponized suicide Iranian-designed Shahed drones per year.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed expansion of the factory—located in Tatarstan’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone—would add 500 tons of aerospace-grade carbon fiber to Russia’s annual output by 2029, according to Politico.
Carbon fiber serves as a critical structural component in long-range drone airframes, reinforcing wings, fuselages, and internal fuel compartments without adding excessive weight.
Ukrainian forces have previously struck the Alabuga drone production plant in Russia’s Tatarstan region—located over 1,200 kilometers from the border—using a towed glider bomb tactic.
During the deep-strike operation, a light unmanned aircraft towed a 100-kilogram explosive-laden glider before releasing it directly into the complex, damaging key manufacturing infrastructure.
“Without the carbon fiber, they can’t make the drone,” David Albright, founder of the Institute for Science and International Security, told Politico. Russia “can’t substitute for the carbon fiber in the drone and keep its weight down.”
The project relies on building a new plant to produce polyacrylonitrile (PAN) precursor materials, producing UMT42S-3K grade carbon fiber directly inside the special economic zone, Politico reported.
Documents verified by the US House Select Committee on China and Ukrainian intelligence indicate the expansion aims to substitute critical imports from China, ensuring a stable domestic supply chain for Moscow’s defense industry.
Satellite images taken between May and August show initial ground-clearing operations adjacent to the existing Alabuga-Volokno facility, according to Politico. Ukrainian estimates indicate Russia currently produces over 36,000 “Geran” strike drones per year, with state plans targeting 130,000 total military drones by 2030.
Security analysts warned that the scaling of Russia’s drone industrial base poses broader risks beyond the Ukrainian theater, according to Politico.
“The expansion of Alabuga and its affiliated enterprises should be viewed not merely as a problem for the Ukrainian front, but as a long-term challenge to the security of the whole of Europe,” said Serhii Kuzan, head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre.
Russia had previously constructed approximately 42,000 square meters of underground production halls at its Alabuga complex in Tatarstan to protect its “Geran” (Shahed-136) drone assembly lines from long-range Ukrainian strikes.
Satellite imagery revealed hardened subterranean facilities and defensive lattice-tower structures designed to shield the site from drone and cruise missile attacks—a tactic modeled after Iranian underground military installations.
