articles.title: Kiev loses about 1,440 troops in special military operation zone in past day — top brass
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 21. /TASS/. The Ukrainian armed forces have lost about 1,440 personnel in Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
Specifically, Ukraine’s losses in the area of responsibility of the Battlegroup North totaled more than 265 troops, in the Battlegroup West’s responsibility area - over 220, in the Battlegroup South’s area - over 215, in the Battlegroup Center’s area - over 430, in the Battlegroup East’s area - over 260, and in the Battlegroup Dnepr’s responsibility area - up to 50 troops.
Russian forces strike logistics centers, ports in Ukraine
Russian forces launched strikes overnight on logistics centers, warehouses and ports in Ukraine, as well as vessels involved in supporting the Ukrainian military, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Tonight, Russian forces launched strikes with UAVs against logistics centers, warehouses and ports in Ukraine, as well as vessels involved in supporting the Ukrainian military," the ministry said.
"As a result of the strike, the following targets were hit: <...> in the Odessa Region: at the port of Odessa, a bulk carrier that had delivered cargo intended to support the Ukrainian military. At the port of Izmail, port infrastructure facilities used to unload and store military cargo. In addition, a bulk carrier carrying cargo intended to support the Ukrainian armed forces to the port of Odessa was hit while crossing the sea," the statement said.
Russian forces hit BDU Logistic center in Kiev Region
Russian forces hit the BDU Logistic center in the Kiev Region, where military products are stored, as a result of strikes, the Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result of the strike, the following target was hit in the Kiev Region: the BDU Logistic center in the settlement of Schastlivoye, where military products were stored and distributed in warehouse facilities," the statement said.
In addition, Russian forces reported hitting a gas distribution station in Boyarka in the Kiev Region that supplies gas to Ukrainian defense industry enterprises.
"A gas distribution station [was hit] in the settlement of Boyarka, which supplies gas to Ukrainian defense industry enterprises," the ministry said.
Air defenses down 244 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 244 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Over the past night, on-duty air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 244 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Volgograd, Kaluga, Kursk, Oryol, Orenburg, Rostov, Ryazan, Samara, Saratov, Tver, Tula, Ulyanovsk, Krasnodar, Adygea, Bashkortostan and Tatarstan Regions, as well as over the waters of the Black Sea," the ministry said.
Russian air defenses down 634 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over past day
Russian air defenses shot down four guided aerial bombs and 634 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) over the past day, the Defense Ministry said in its latest update.
"Air defense systems shot down four guided aerial bombs, four US-made HIMARS multiple-launch rocket system projectiles, and 634 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
According to the ministry, a total of 674 aircraft, 284 helicopters, 242,630 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 30,982 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,780 multiple rocket launcher combat vehicles, 36,529 field artillery guns and mortars, and 72,465 special military motor vehicles have been destroyed since the start of the special military operation.
Russian forces hit Ukrainian drone assembly workshops over past day
Russian forces struck workshops producing unmanned aerial vehicles for Ukraine’s army, drone storage sites and temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian troops and foreign mercenaries in 153 locations, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck logistics centers, energy and transport infrastructure in Ukraine used by the Ukrainian army, military airfields, ammunition, fuel and materiel depots, workshops producing unmanned aerial vehicles and their storage sites and temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 153 locations," the ministry said in a statement.
Russia’s Battlegroup North continues to encircle Ukrainian forces in Kharkov Region
Units of Russia’s Battlegroup North are encircling Ukrainian troops, simultaneously expanding their zone of control in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Units of the Battlegroup North in the Kharkov Region are tightening the ring of encirclement and expanding the external zone of control," the ministry said in a statement.
Ukrainian army loses over 35 troops in Kharkov Region
Ukrainian forces encircled in the Kharkov Region have sustained losses exceeding 35 troops.
"Losses among the encircled Ukrainian forces amounted to more than 35 troops, an armored combat vehicle, an artillery piece, and a ground-based robotic system," the Defense Ministry said.
Russian forces inflict losses on Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
Russian troops within the encirclement in the Kharkov Region have inflicted losses on Ukrainian forces and destroyed their equipment in the areas around five settlements, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Within the encirclement, enemy personnel and equipment were destroyed in the areas surrounding the settlements of Buzovo, Krasny Yar, Reznikovo, Varvarovka, and Khripuny in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces expand external control zone near two communities in Kharkov Region
Units of the Russian Battlegroup North are actively assuming control over areas near the Petropavlovka and Prikolotnoye communities in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Active combat operations are underway to expand the external zone of control near the Petropavlovka and Prikolotnoye communities in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian troops foil Ukraine’s reinforcement attempts in Kharkov Region
Over the past 24 hours, fighters of Russia’s Battlegroup North have foiled three Ukrainian army’s attempts to bring reinforcements from Veliky Burluk to Olkhovatka in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"Three Ukrainian armed forces’ attempts to bring reinforcements from Veliky Burluk to the Olkhovatka settlement in the Kharkov Region were thwarted," the ministry said in a statement.
In the Kharkov Region, Ukraine’s four mechanized brigades and assault regiment suffered losses in personnel and equipment in the areas around the settlements of Sosnovka, Podsredneye, and Sosnovy Bor in the Kharkov Region.
Control over Polnaya, Novoalexandrovka in Kharkov Region to complicate enemy’s supplies
The establishment of control over the Polnaya and Novoalexandrovka communities by the Russian Battlegroup North will significantly complicate the supply of enemy forces encircled in the Kharkov Region, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The establishment of control over the Polnaya and Novoalexandrovka communities in the Kharkov Region will significantly complicate air supplies to the enemy’s encircled group," the ministry said in a statement.

articles.title: Iran is prepared for a protracted war: IRGC
articles.body:
Iran is prepared for a protracted war: IRGC
TEHRAN — The Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) has warned that any renewed US or Israeli aggression against Iran would trigger a substantially different military response, with changes expected in the geography of the conflict, the weapons deployed and the targets struck.
In an extensive interview, IRGC Spokesperson Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi said Iran was prepared for a prolonged confrontation and that the IRGC was now better prepared for such a scenario than it had been before the recent conflict.
From Iran’s perspective, he said, the confrontation involving Iran, the United States, Israel and their allies should not be regarded as a concluded war followed by a new conflict, but as different phases of the same confrontation.
“From our point of view, it is the same war,” Mohebbi said, stressing that although the conflict had passed through different phases, “it has not ended.”
His remarks came alongside a broad assessment of major setbacks for Washington, particularly in the areas of military power, regional security, intelligence and advanced weapons technology.
Hormuz at the center of Iran’s assessment
Mohebbi identified the Strait of Hormuz as one of the clearest examples of a US strategic failure.
He said Washington had entered the region while presenting its military presence as a means of protecting energy flows and freedom of navigation. Yet, despite the United States possessing the world’s largest navy, he argued that Washington had been unable to reopen the strategic waterway.
According to Mohebbi, this outcome had created a contradiction at the heart of the US regional posture: a power that presented itself as a guarantor of maritime security had become an obstacle to security.
He also accused Washington of repeatedly violating agreements and linked the continuation of restrictions in the strait to US actions.
Mohebbi described the developments surrounding Hormuz as one of the United States’ most significant strategic setbacks in the region.
US military bases under Iranian attack
The IRGC spokesman also pointed to US military installations across West Asia, saying the United States had spent decades building a network of bases around the Persian Gulf and to Iran’s east and west.
According to Mohebbi, Iranian missiles and drones subsequently struck these installations, rendering a large number of them unusable and forcing the United States to relocate personnel and equipment to more distant positions.
He referred to US facilities in Jordan and other locations, as well as positions closer to Israel and the Gulf of Aqaba, arguing that even after redeployments Washington had faced difficulties in ensuring their security.
He further added that US warships had been pushed farther away from the Persian Gulf following the confrontation, saying the US Fifth Fleet had moved roughly 400 kilometers farther from the area.
In Mohebbi’s assessment, a significant portion of US military resources had consequently been diverted toward protecting American bases and personnel rather than carrying out Washington’s wider regional mission.
Intelligence capabilities also challenged
Mohebbi described intelligence capabilities as another area in which Washington had suffered a major setback.
He argued that the United States had long been regarded as possessing highly sophisticated intelligence networks and facilities that were difficult for others to penetrate or strike.
The IRGC spokesman said Iranian forces had nevertheless been able to identify and monitor US intelligence facilities in areas around the Persian Gulf and northern Iraq before striking them.
He presented this as evidence that US intelligence infrastructure was not beyond Iran’s reach and said the development had implications not only for Washington’s rivals but also for its allies.
US military technology ‘no longer beyond reach’
Mohebbi also challenged the perception of overwhelming American superiority in military technology.
He referred to systems including the F-35 fighter aircraft, Patriot air-defense systems, offensive missiles, aerial-refueling aircraft, submarines and drones.
According to the IRGC spokesman, the confrontation demonstrated that technologies once regarded as being largely exclusive to the United States could be challenged by Iranian offensive and defensive capabilities.
He said the conflict had conveyed two messages: for US rivals, that American military technology was not necessarily beyond reach; and for US allies, that questions could be raised about Washington’s ability to protect even its own forces and installations, let alone allied countries.
Washington miscalculated Iran’s resilience
A central element of Mohebbi’s assessment was that Washington had underestimated Iran’s ability and willingness to continue fighting.
He said the United States had initially expected Iran to surrender within days, an assessment that he attributed partly to intelligence and political assumptions conveyed to Washington by Israel.
Mohebbi stated that Israeli officials had told the US president that Iran could be forced to surrender within three to five days and that such an outcome would give Washington a result comparable to the Six-Day War.
He said the subsequent failure of that expectation represented a major strategic miscalculation.
The IRGC spokesman also said the United States had been surprised by the range, destructive power, accuracy, and diversity of Iranian missiles and drones, as well their ability to evade detection.
According to Mohebbi, Washington ultimately found itself in a position in which it could neither easily advance its objectives nor reverse course.
'America has not simply lost a war’
Mohebbi framed the consequences of the confrontation in broader strategic terms, arguing that the United States had suffered setbacks in three dimensions that he associated with its regional hegemony: military superiority, the ability to provide security for allies, and political and moral legitimacy.
He argued that military setbacks had challenged the perception of American invulnerability, while attacks on US bases had undermined Washington’s image as a reliable security provider.
He also accused the United States of damaging its international standing through attacks on civilian targets in Iran, citing several incidents.
“America has not simply lost a war; it has lost a system,” Mohebbi said, arguing that a new regional and international order was emerging in which Washington would no longer determine West Asia’s security architecture on its own.
He further argued that regional states had come to understand that the United States could neither provide security against Iran nor guarantee regional security without Iran.
No direct IRGC channel to Washington
On the question of possible communication between the IRGC and the United States, Mohebbi categorically rejected the existence of any direct channel.
He said the IRGC’s constitutional role was military and defensive, while diplomatic affairs fell within the responsibility of Iran’s Foreign Ministry.
Mohebbi insisted that the IRGC had never maintained formal or informal relations with the United States and did not intend to enter the diplomatic arena.
A new attack would mean a different battlefield
The most direct warning in Mohebbi’s interview concerned the consequences of another US or Israeli attack.
He said a renewed assault would bring major changes to Iran’s defensive and retaliatory strategy, beginning with the geographical scope of the conflict.
“We will definitely change the geography of the war,” he said.
Iran would also introduce new weapons and military equipment with new capabilities, he added, warning that “the world will be surprised.”
Mohebbi said Iran had already struck targets that its adversaries had not expected to come under attack and cited the al-Tanf base and the Gulf of Aqaba as examples.
He further stated that Iran had additional targets that had not yet been attacked and remained outside the calculations of its adversaries.
The IRGC spokesman said some of Iran’s strategic weapons had not been used during previous phases of the confrontation and could be deployed if circumstances required.
Iran distinguishes neighbors from US forces
Mohebbi also sought to draw a distinction between Iran’s regional neighbors and the US military presence on their territory.
He said Iran regarded neighboring countries as states with which it shared historical, religious, commercial and cultural ties and stressed that Tehran did not consider these countries themselves to be enemies.
According to Mohebbi, Iranian attacks on locations in Bahrain, Qatar and Saudi Arabia had been directed at US military facilities rather than at those countries themselves.
He nevertheless criticized the presence of American military installations in regional states, questioning why countries in the region would permit a power located thousands of kilometers away to deploy forces on their territory.
“We will never target our neighbors,” he said, while emphasizing that Iran distinguishes between neighboring states and hostile foreign military forces.
Iran’s position on regional resistance groups
Mohebbi briefly addressed Iran’s relationship with resistance groups in Yemen and Lebanon, rejecting the description of these groups as Iranian proxies.
He said such groups made their own political and military decisions and were rooted in their respective societies. He similarly argued that Hezbollah maintained significant social and political roots in Lebanon.
A conflict has entered a new phase
Taken together, Mohebbi’s remarks portray Iran’s assessment of the confrontation as extending well beyond the question of battlefield exchanges.
His central message was that the war remains unfinished, while the IRGC believes the confrontation has exposed vulnerabilities in the US military presence, intelligence infrastructure and technological advantages.
At the same time, his warning about any future attack was explicit: Iran would not simply repeat its previous response.
The geography of the conflict could expand, previously unused weapons could enter the battlefield, and new targets could be selected. Some of the capabilities that Iran describes as strategic weapons, Mohebbi said, have yet to be employed.
Iran, he said, has prepared for a prolonged confrontation—and would enter any renewed conflict with a different battlefield, different weapons and different targets.

articles.title: Russia ‘Unfortunately Lost Control’ of Its Diesel Refineries, Trump Says
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Russia has “unfortunately lost control” of its diesel production and said the war in Ukraine “must be ended.”
Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump called the war “ridiculous” and “never ending,” claiming that “25,000 people, mostly soldiers” are being killed each month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” he wrote. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never-ending War with Ukraine must be ended.”
The statement came a day after his phone call with President Volodymyr Zelensky and a day before the two planned to meet on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
Trump blames diesel crisis on Ukraine
Trump recently blamed Ukraine for rising global diesel prices – which is likely to affect Republicans’ prospects in the US’s November mid-term elections, with diesel having reached over $7 per gallon in the country.
The Financial Times (FT), citing unnamed Ukrainian officials, said Trump pressured Kyiv over the refinery strikes during Sunday’s call. One of them, who reportedly took part in the call, said Trump told Zelensky to cease strikes to relieve the spike in global diesel prices, according to the FT.
Russian Attack Destroys Pet Retailer Warehouse in Kyiv Region
However, while Ukraine’s actions are having some effect, other factors are having a greater influence.
An earlier FT report, citing findings from Ukraine’s Kyiv School of Economics (KSE) Institute, said the US war in Iran has had a larger impact on global diesel prices than the war in Ukraine.
Exports from Gulf states are estimated to have fallen by 152 million barrels between March and August, compared with a 68 million-barrel drop in Russian exports over the same period, according to the KSE’s figures in the FT report.
While another think tank report indicates that Russia’s overall oil exports and revenue fell in August, a new Reuters report said Russia also raised diesel exports to Central Asia despite the ongoing export ban to other regions.
Trump’s Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has previously cited the need to stabilize energy supplies in developing countries as a reason for extending the license exempting certain Russian oil transactions from sanctions.
Zelensky’s response following Sunday call
Zelensky hailed “diplomatic momentum” following the call without mentioning Russia’s diesel production, though he confirmed that he would meet Trump on Tuesday.
“An important conversation, and we got through a lot. We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum,” Zelensky was quoted as saying by his office.
The Ukrainian president hinted at steps towards de-escalation and mentioned the newly signed US sanctions bill against Russian energy.
“We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps. I thanked the American President for signing the Lindsey Graham bill into law. We all concur – there must be peace,” he added.
Zelensky has been pursuing a meeting with Trump after the president’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, visited Kyiv and Moscow, even though the talks produced no breakthrough and the war rages on.
A week earlier, Trump told reporters he told the Ukrainian president “to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” days after claiming an energy truce between Kyiv and Moscow, though both countries tacitly denied reaching an agreement despite voicing openness to the idea.
Russia’s oil crisis
Ukraine has hit Russia’s oil sector hard in 2026.
In summer 2026, Kyiv hit almost, if not all, Russian refineries within range of its current weapon holdings, with its military claiming in July that 43% of Russia’s refining capacity had been forced offline as a result.
Over the weekend, Ukraine hit the Moscow Oil Refinery along with surrounding regional infrastructure in an unprecedented drone and missile attack comprising over 1,600 drones and missiles, including the previously undeployed “Pelican” ballistic missile.
The loss of refining capacity has led to a nationwide automobile fuel crisis and various export bans for the world’s third-largest oil producer. Russian President Vladimir Putin tacitly acknowledged the impact of Ukraine’s actions in a recent remark, despite earlier attempts by Kremlin officials to downplay it.

articles.title: Wars and AI risks top UN General Assembly agenda
articles.body:
Image: U.S. Department of State
World leaders are gathering in New York for the 81st U.N. General Assembly, with wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, climate change and the risks of artificial intelligence expected to dominate discussions.
About 130 heads of state and government are expected to speak alongside dozens of ministers during the general debate, which runs from Sept. 22 to 28.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will deliver his final annual opening address before his second term ends on Dec. 31.
“International cooperation is more necessary than ever,” he said ahead of the gathering, identifying uncontrolled AI development, climate change and widening inequality as existential threats.
U.S. President Donald Trump, French President Emmanuel Macron and President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan are among the opening-day speakers.
Erdoğan is scheduled to speak fourth among national leaders, after the representatives of Brazil, the United States and Jordan.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are scheduled to address the assembly on Sept. 23. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will speak the following day.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas will also address the assembly on Sept. 24, appearing by video after Washington denied him a visa for a second consecutive year.
Chinese President Xi Jinping will not attend, although he is expected to meet Trump in Washington during the week.
Russian President Vladimir Putin is also staying away, with Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov due to address the assembly on Sept. 26.
The wars in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and Sudan will feature prominently in diplomatic meetings, alongside shipping security in the Strait of Hormuz and crises in Yemen, Myanmar and Haiti.
The Security Council is scheduled to hold separate high-level meetings on Ukraine and AI on Sept. 23, with Zelensky attending the Ukraine session.
AI safety has gained attention following calls by industry leaders to slow development.
Guterres has urged governments to coordinate their response, warning that national measures alone cannot address risks that cross borders.
Climate targets, development financing, pandemic preparedness, nuclear disarmament and rising sea levels are also on the week’s agenda.
The gathering will address the U.N.’s own financial difficulties and efforts to reform its institutions, including the Security Council, where the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France hold veto power.
Washington recently paid $725 million toward the U.N.’s regular budget, removing the risk of losing its General Assembly vote in 2027.
It still owed $1.312 billion to that budget, U.N. spokesman Farhan Haq said on Sept. 16.
New York authorities have increased security and restricted traffic around U.N. headquarters.
Temporary flight restrictions, including a ban on unauthorized drones, are in place around the complex through Sept. 26.

articles.title: Ahead of Trump-Xi Summit, North Korea Launches More Missiles
articles.body:
On September 20, North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area on its east coast, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The first, detected around 3 p.m. KST, flew about 450 kilometers (280 miles). The second, fired about 5:50 p.m. KST, flew more than 600 kilometers (373 miles). Both are presumed to be from the Hwasong-11 series.
It was North Korea’s second missile launch in eight days. On September 12, one day after the Japan-South Korea-U.S. Freedom Edge exercise ended, North Korea fired several short-range ballistic missiles from the same area, which it described as part of a “joint firepower drill.” That launch was its first in 23 days.
The September 20 launches followed a statement two days earlier from Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of Kim Jong Un. She said North Korea must answer U.S.-led drills such as the Pacific Vanguard naval exercise near Guam with measures at least as forceful. Her statement added that North Korea’s nuclear buildup would not change.
A day before that, Kim had rejected renewed calls for denuclearization at an International Atomic Energy Agency conference.
Pyongyang has followed each allied exercise this month with missile fire, and the newest launches follow a warning of a tougher response from Kim Yo Jong.
Beyond that, North Korea’s latest missile launches come at a sensitive time. U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping are scheduled to hold a summit on September 24 in Washington, D.C. It will be Xi’s first trip to the U.S. capital in 10 years, and his first official state visit to the United States since 2015. This week also marks the start of the United Nations General Assembly.
Separately, an explosion during a mine-clearing operation in the Demilitarized Zone injured three South Korean military officers on September 21, according to the South’s Joint Chiefs of Staff. The blast came at about 10:50 a.m. KST south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) in the western sector, where soldiers from the Army 25th Division were opening a search route through ground not yet checked for mines and unexploded ordnance. Two of the officers were flown to a military hospital by emergency helicopter and the commander of the reconnaissance battalion reportedly suffered an amputation at the ankle.
The cause of the blast remains unconfirmed, and the JCS said all possibilities remain open. The military is treating a mine as the most likely explanation. It has not said whether the device was one that North Korea planted, an explosive that drifted south in heavy rain, or one that belonged to South Korea. Still, the site lies far from the area in the southern half of the zone where North Korea is believed to have buried mines even as an opposition lawmaker argued that the blast occurred near a North Korean minefield.
It was the first mine explosion to seriously injure South Korean troops south of the MDL line since August 2015 when North Korean wooden-box mines maimed two soldiers. North Korea has been laying mines and building tactical roads near the border since it declared the two Koreas hostile states.
The incident in the DMZ, as well as the missile launches, could increase public skepticism of the Lee administration’s North Korea policy. The Unification Ministry recently devised a plan to support North Korea building hospitals. South Koreans may start to question why Seoul is still making dovish overtures toward Pyongyang, which has repeatedly stressed that it has no intention of renewing the stalled inter-Korean relations.
In a press conference on September 18, before the latest missile launches and the DMZ explosion, Lee said North Korea “is clearly refusing to communicate with South Korea.” He added that Trump wants dialogue with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and that Seoul is coordinating in advance to make talks possible. Lee dismissed concerns that South Korea could be sidelined in North Korea-U.S. diplomacy.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia's oil refining capacity falls as damage from Moscow strikes sets in
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Russia's oil refining capacity falls as damage from Moscow strikes sets in
Key developments on Sept. 21:
- Russia's total oil refining capacity down 45% after mass attack on Moscow
- Exclusive: EU readies biggest-ever sanctions package targeting Russia's war machine
- Russia 'lost control' of its oil refining industry due to Ukraine's attacks, Trump says ahead of Zelensky meeting
- 69% of Russian soldiers on Zaporizhzhia front line have criminal records, Ukrainian military says
- Ukraine's Culture Ministry announces major fundraising initiative to help publishers struggling after Russian attacks
Ukraine's ongoing long-range strike campaign against Russian oil refineries has knocked out 45% of the country's total refining capacity, the General Staff reported on Sept. 21.
"One of the consequences is a shortage of high-quality fuel in the Russian Federation," the General Staff report said.
"Among other things, there is a sharp decline in the production of gasoline and diesel fuel of the Euro-5/K5 standard."
The assessment comes a day after major Ukrainian drone and missile strikes on the Moscow Oil Refinery in a mass attacks on the Russian capital.
The Moscow strike was only the latest in a spate of ongoing attacks against Russian refineries, with two others — in Yaroslavl and Samara oblasts respectively — struck since Sept. 14, according to the Ukrainian military.
According to a Reuters report citing industry sources, the Moscow Oil Refinery, owned by state-controlled company Gazprom Neft, stopped production after the Sept. 20 attack.
The refinery's main crude distillation units were hit, Reuters' sources said, with repair likely requiring weeks to bring the facility back online.

Exclusive: EU readies biggest-ever sanctions package targeting Russia's war machine
The EU's upcoming sanctions package, comprising nearly 1,600 listings, aims to hit Russia's war machine on an unprecedented scale, according to a document obtained by the Kyiv Independent.
The proposal by the European External Action Service (EEAS), the EU's diplomatic arm, calls for adding 827 entities and 744 individuals to the bloc's sanctions list, marking the largest single package of listings to date.
While previous EU sanctions packages have targeted Russia across various sectors — from finance to fossil fuels — or have included high-profile figures, the new listings specifically target companies and executives involved in Russia's defense-industrial complex.
The targeted industry players range from shipyards and aviation companies to electronics manufacturers, armored vehicle repair facilities, and aerospace companies.
The Kyiv Independent has chosen not to name any of the listings so as not to help Russia evade the EU's sanctions efforts.

Russia 'lost control' of its oil refining industry due to Ukraine's attacks, Trump says
Russia has effectively "lost control" of its diesel production sector as a result of the war with Ukraine, U.S. President Donald Trump said on Sept. 21, urging an end to the fighting.
The comments come as President Volodymyr Zelensky travels to New York to meet Trump and discuss a potential mutual Ukrainian-Russian pause in strikes against energy infrastructure and targets on the Black Sea.
The two leaders are scheduled to meet on Sept. 22, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social platform.
The U.S. president added that a large number of Russian "refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission," noting that the "whole world suffers" as a result of the war.
Responding to Trump on social media, Zelensky echoed his sentiment that the war must end, saying, "From the very first minute, Ukraine has sought peace."

69% of Russian soldiers on Zaporizhzhia front line have criminal records, Ukrainian military says
Of the Russian force fighting near the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, 69% of servicemen have criminal records, Anastasiia Shevchenko, a spokesperson for Operational Task Force South, said on Sept. 21.
The figure likely reflects both the overrepresentation of those from poor and disadvantaged parts of Russian society among voluntary recruits, and the widely reported practice of offering men contracts to avoid prison time, often under coercive circumstances.
According to internal analysis conducted by the Ukrainian military, 31% of the overall Russian force had signed up to avoid criminal charges, and 24% were in the military to improve their financial situation, Shevchenko said in comments to Ukrinform.
While Russia still fields special units in its regiments and brigades made up of those taken straight from the penal system with promises of amnesty, many of the regular recruits have also had some form of criminal past.

The Culture Ministry announced a $500,000 fundraising initiative on Sept. 21 for grants that would aid independent Ukrainian publishers struggling with massive financial losses after Russian attacks destroyed 13 million books over the summer.
"For a small publisher, the loss of a single print run can bring operations to a halt for months. Yet it is small publishers that discover new authors, tackle complex and important subjects, and contribute to the diversity of contemporary Ukrainian books," Culture Minister Tetiana Berezhna said.
Russia's escalated attacks over the summer on Ukraine's economy have included strikes on publishers' warehouses and printing houses. According to the Culture Ministry, financial losses for the Ukrainian book industry have already reached at least Hr 1.75 billion ($32 million).

articles.title: Kremlin says no progress made in Ukraine negotiations
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov on Monday said no progress has been made in negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war, state news agency TASS reported.
Peskov said Moscow continues its “special military operation,” the term Russia uses for the war in Ukraine, but remains open to negotiations.
“As for resuming trilateral negotiations, we are open to it. Yes, we are continuing the special military operation, and our military is working to achieve the set objectives. But we do hope that we will ultimately resume trilateral negotiations,” Peskov said.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow on Sept. 5 for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin before traveling to Kyiv on Sept. 6 for discussions with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
While no breakthrough was announced, after the meetings Trump said the Russian president wants to reach a deal to end the war, and suggested a trilateral meeting with Putin and Zelenskyy could take place.
Moscow and Kyiv have also signaled interest in resuming trilateral negotiations, with October discussed as a possible timeframe.
On Russia’s parliamentary election, Peskov said Ukraine launched “massive attacks” during voting in an attempt to disrupt the process. “It constitutes sabotage. It is also an attempt to disrupt these elections. It had no effect,” he said.
Russia’s three-day election for the 450-seat State Duma, the lower house of parliament, ended Sunday amid continuing Ukrainian drone attacks.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said Ukrainian forces attempted a mass attack on Russian territory using drones and Flamingo cruise missiles “to disrupt the State Duma election,” adding that Russian air defenses and military aviation destroyed 1,951 drones and eight long-range cruise missiles over a 24-hour period.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said Russia repelled the largest drone attack on the capital to date, with more than 1,600 drones intercepted, including about 450 approaching Moscow.
It was Russia’s first parliamentary election since the war in Ukraine in February 2022, with voting also held in Russian-controlled parts of Ukraine, a move Kyiv and many Western governments reject as unlawful.

articles.title: Russia’s secret drone math: one Tatarstan plant could yield 28,000 more drone bodies a year
articles.body:
Russia is quietly moving to expand the capacity of the plant behind its long-range attack drones, a step that could sharply raise how many it launches at Ukraine, according to Politico. The plan turns on a single carbon fiber factory in Russia's Tatarstan region and runs to the end of the decade.
These files add something narrower than Russia's known intent to fight on: they identify carbon fiber as a critical material capping how many drones it can build. To break that cap, the Kremlin is funding production lines that will not run until the decade's end—a bet on winning by out-building Ukraine, even as the strikes grind on.
The bottleneck Russia wants to break
Politico obtained internal documents from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom showing its Alabuga-Volokno plant would add 500 tons of military-grade aerospace carbon fiber a year by 2029. Rosatom declined to comment. Weapons expert David Albright, who heads the Institute for Science and International Security, estimated that volume could yield airframes for about 28,000 more attack drones a year—a 78% jump.
Ukraine already estimates Russia can build more than 36,000 Shahed/Geran kamikaze drones a year. Carbon fiber is the choke point: it keeps the airframes light and strong, and Russia has no cheap substitute.
"Without the carbon fiber, they can't make the drone. Can't substitute for the carbon fiber in the drone and keep its weight down," Albright said.
Moscow is investing in the raw material, not just more assembly halls—the fiber, not floor space, is what caps output.
Ground already cleared in Tatarstan
Documents gathered by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center describe a new factory on the site designed to produce UMT42S-3K aerospace-grade fiber. Satellite images from May to July show land cleared for construction. Albright's own August imagery shows foundations going in. He said the stated 2027 completion date "requires rapid construction." Russia has spent the past year adding new assembly halls at the same site.
The plant and its parent, Rosatom's Umatex Group, already sit under US, UK, and other Western sanctions. The US House Select Committee on China and the Ukrainian government both verified the documents, officials told Politico.
The push comes as Russia leans harder on jet-powered Shaheds, which Ukraine's Air Force says are hard to down with conventional defenses. Kyiv has fielded its first jet interceptor and tested a new one in September—but the plant is a bid to out-build those defenses faster than Ukraine can scale them.

articles.title: China prepares for Trump-Xi summit in Washington
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From a position of strength, China prepares for Trump-Xi summit in Washington
Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump in Washington within a few days, as global attention turns to whether the two countries can fulfil their agreement to work towards constructive steps towards international stability.
Beijing is preparing to begin this week's summit with Washington from a position of strength, backed by a series of recent diplomatic efforts.
The two sides have held intensive preparatory talks in New York to negotiate possible outcomes on trade, artificial intelligence and rare earth minerals.
Beijing announced on Monday, 21 September, that it was ready to work with Washington to build "strategic stability" and "manage differences".
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China "will work with the United States to enrich the substance of constructive strategic stability in China-US relations, strengthen dialogue and cooperation, and properly manage differences".
The South China Morning Post reported on Sunday, 20 September, citing Chinese experts, that Beijing's confidence "could be strengthened by US efforts to make progress in its war with Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, given that Washington may need Beijing's cooperation to help resolve them, even if reaching a truce in the near term remains unlikely."
"In recent months, the Trump administration has explicitly asked Beijing for greater diplomatic cooperation to manage ongoing conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, particularly those involving Iran," the paper added.
Moreover, China maintains a structural advantage through its dominance of rare earth elements and critical minerals, creating deep dependencies for US defence and technology manufacturers.
There is a belief in Chinese circles that US President Donald Trump's claim of permanent security control over Greenland just days before his Chinese counterpart's state visit is an attempt to strengthen US influence.
Based on this, warnings have emerged about a potentially negative impact on high-stakes talks, which could affect trust between major powers and peaceful development projects in the Arctic, according to the Chinese assessment.
Despite the cordial rhetoric between the two leaders, with Trump planning to personally welcome Xi at Andrews military base, many issues threaten to disrupt the positive atmosphere for the summit.
Rumours are abound regarding a potential US arms package for Taiwan have led to threats in the media to cancel the meeting altogether.
Trump also recently signed the Lindsey Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, which directly penalises China's energy imports from Russia just days before Xi's arrival.
The White House also recently classified China as the main source of essential chemicals for synthetic drugs.
Trump's public complaints about Chinese interference in elections ahead of the 2026 midterm elections have further exacerbated bilateral tensions.
A few weeks before his trip to Washington, Chinese President Xi Jinping embarked on one of his most intensive foreign tours.
He made a state visit to Egypt after concluding the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, and then attended the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
The BRICS summit formed a united front against US tariffs and sanctions, which Beijing describes as unilateral.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to meet his US counterpart Donald Trump at the White House on 24 September, four months after Trump's official visit to Beijing in May.
The latest summit produced a series of economic agreements, the establishment of a new US-China Trade and Investment Council, an agreement to open a dialogue between the two governments on artificial intelligence, and a commitment by the two leaders to build what the two governments described as a "constructive relationship of strategic stability".

articles.title: Trump set to press Zelenskyy at UN to agree energy ceasefire with Russia
articles.body:
Donald Trump is expected to press Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy on an energy ceasefire during a face-to-face meeting this week during United Nations high-level week, as world diesel prices have soared due to the war in Iran, as well as Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Ukraine stepped up its attacks on Russia’s energy sector over the weekend, launching its largest reported strike yet on the Moscow region in a barrage that struck a major Moscow oil refinery and killed three people.
On Monday, Trump said the whole world was suffering due to an energy shortage that he said was being exacerbated by the war in Ukraine.
“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump said in a Truths Social post on Monday morning. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission.”
“This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” Trump said. “The whole World suffers as 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are being killed each month. What a shame!”
Trump had earlier blamed Kyiv for the escalating energy war even as Russia has decimated Ukraine’s economy and launched night barrages of drones and ballistic missiles against Ukrainian cities.
Zelenskyy on Monday said negotiations were continuing and that that there are “ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, starting with strong de-escalation steps”.
“Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to matching de-escalation steps on our part,” he said in a statement. “Solutions are possible.”
The two leaders are expected to meet on Tuesday during a rare sitdown on the sidelines of the high-level week of the United Nations general assembly. Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov will also be in Washington this week, and is expected to meet with secretary of state Marco Rubio.
During a trip to Ireland last week, Trump directly addressed Zelenskyy, saying he has to do “one thing: he has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia”.
“Let him go after targets but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage,” he said.
Trump spoke with Zelenskyy on Sunday in a phone call that one senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times was about “diesel, diesel, diesel”.
Average diesel prices in the United States hit a record $6.50 per gallon on Monday, up from $3.19 per gallon this time last year before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran and Tehran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz to most international trade. The rise in prices is seen as a liability for Trump’s Republican party in the US midterm elections, which will take place in November.
Trump is expected to deliver a speech to the UN general assembly on Tuesday morning, and is expected to meet with major energy producers including the Gulf Cooperation Council and Venezuela’s recently installed leader Delcy Rodriguez.
In a preview, Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, said Trump would speak about how he has “confronted complex problems head-on around the world. Many of the peace deals that he has driven to conclusion, or is in the process of driving to conclusion.”
Trump last week prematurely announced an energy ceasefire under which Ukraine had agreed not to hit Russian energy targets and that “Russia has agreed to do likewise!” The deal had not been agreed, however, and Russian strikes against Ukrainian energy and other critical infrastructure have continued.

articles.title: 'Scorched earth': How Israel is remaking south Lebanon
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Scorched earth': How Israel is remaking south Lebanon
Beirut, Lebanon - Israel’s military is continuing a “scorched earth” strategy in southern Lebanon, despite a framework peace deal and ongoing direct negotiations between Beirut and Tel Aviv, analysts told The New Arab.
Airstrikes and controlled demolitions have rocked southern towns and villages almost daily, while US-mediated talks aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah’s disarmament have stalled ahead of the Israeli legislative elections in October.
Earlier this month, Israeli ground troops took control of the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge - allegedly containing a Hezbollah command centre, tunnels and weapons stores - after months of fighting in southern Lebanon.
“Ali al-Taher is considered a linchpin for the Israeli security system of today,” Elias Hanna, a retired Lebanese army general, told The New Arab.
Hanna added that from this vantage point, Israeli forces can consolidate their position in the previously captured Beaufort Castle and dominate the area south of the Litani River.
But it is not clear whether the Israeli military’s seizure of the Ali al-Taher ridge signals an intent to expand its occupation deeper into Lebanese territory.
The subsequent destruction of the alleged Hezbollah command centre – Israeli troops detonated the hilltop, causing a 4.1-magnitude seismic tremor – has been touted as a strategic and symbolic victory by Israel.
However, Hanna said the Ali al-Taher ridge was not as valuable a stronghold for Hezbollah as it was before this war began, as the armed group has switched to guerrilla-style warfare that precludes the use of large bases.
According to Hanna, Israel’s military, for its part, is also pursuing a new strategy in the south.
“This time it’s totally different from the 1982 invasion – now they are destroying everything,” Hanna said.
Israel historically occupied a swathe of southern Lebanon from 1982 to 2000, when Israeli forces withdrew completely. This time, however, Hanna argued that Israel cannot afford to put a large number of boots on the ground and is opting instead for a “scorched earth” approach.
“If you want to destroy your enemy, you destroy the ecosystem of your enemy, so he won’t be able to ever recover and come back,” Hanna explained.
The remaking of south Lebanon
Israel has flattened entire villages inside the “yellow line”, a 10km-deep ribbon of land occupied by Israel along the Lebanese-Israeli border.
At least 46 of 54 towns and villages in this area have been heavily damaged or completely levelled by airstrikes and controlled demolitions, according to satellite analysis by Bellingcat. More than 340,000 people remain internally displaced.
In August, Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz visited southern Lebanon and said the military was destroying underground infrastructure and “all the houses” in the area. Lebanon’s Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has called the destruction a serious violation of international humanitarian law.
“Israel is consolidating its control over this dead security zone that it has demarcated in the south, in which it is attempting to erase any evidence of civilian life and then any possible social or infrastructural base for Hezbollah,” Sam Heller, a Beirut-based analyst with the Center for International Policy, told The New Arab.
The direct negotiations between Lebanon and Israel were announced in April, shortly before the latest ceasefire, despite heavy opposition from Hezbollah.
In June, a framework deal was agreed between Beirut and Tel Aviv that included a plan to launch “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon where the Lebanese army would disarm Hezbollah.
The last round of talks, held in Rome in August, reached a deadlock after Beirut failed to achieve either of its two key objectives: to secure a genuine ceasefire and to make progress on Israel’s withdrawal from the areas it occupies in southern Lebanon.
Israel, by contrast, prioritised Hezbollah’s disarmament and rejected a proposal to launch additional pilot zones.
Asked whether the Lebanese army was capable of disarming Hezbollah, which is widely considered to be the more powerful force, Hanna said: “It’s not about the Lebanese army’s capabilities, it’s about the political will of Hezbollah.”
One of the main obstacles to the negotiations has been the failure to appoint a third party to verify the agreement’s implementation on the ground. Italy and France emerged as potential candidates, but Israel objected to both options.
“The Israelis likely have basically nil confidence in Lebanese authorities’ ability or willingness to really confront Hezbollah or disarm it,” Heller said. “Instead, Israel will seek to legitimate internationally its continued direct role in Lebanon and to make that maximally sustainable politically,” he added.
“Israel has gotten most of what it wanted, which is a step towards the normalisation of relations, the opening of direct negotiations, and the legitimation by Lebanese authorities – as part of this agreement – of Israel’s indefinite presence inside South Lebanon.”
The diplomacy of an indefinite occupation
The next round of talks, which has been postponed to October, is due to take place as Israel gears up for what could be pivotal elections.
“The negotiations themselves have stalled, given the upcoming Israeli elections. The Lebanese President is hopeful that a change in government would yield positive results; the PM and his team are less so,” Mohanad Hage Ali, with the Carnegie Middle East Center, told The New Arab.
While progress on the negotiations before the end of October remains unlikely, Heller doubts that the Israeli elections will deliver a government more amenable to making the concessions Beirut is trying to secure.
The Lebanese government, which says it has no option but to negotiate, is seeking to garner international support for the Lebanese Armed Forces, especially as the UN peacekeeping mission in the south is set to withdraw at the end of the year.
Last week, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun met French President Emmanuel Macron in Paris, as well as Arab, European and US military officials.
While France affirmed its support, observers say this remains largely symbolic, as any meaningful change to the status quo in southern Lebanon will rely heavily on action and mediation from Washington.
“Regardless of how the Lebanese government feel about the prospects of negotiations, the process itself is now all about conflict management and de-escalation, buying time, and the fact is they have no other tools,” Hage Ali said.
Alex Martin Astley is a freelance journalist based in Beirut, covering conflict, foreign policy, and social justice issues
Follow him on X: @AlexMAstley

articles.title: Russian drones slam southern Ukraine city after Kyiv's 1,000-drone weekend barrage
articles.body:
The war's relentless daily attacks underscore the absence of any significant progress in diplomatic efforts to stop the fighting, more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour.
Russian drones blasted Ukraine’s southern city of Zaporizhzhia a day after Kyiv’s forces fired more than 1,000 at Russia, officials said on Monday.
The war's relentless daily attacks underscore the absence of any significant progress in diplomatic efforts to stop the fighting, more than four years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour.
There is no sign the war is abating as world leaders gather this week at the UN General Assembly. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he expects to meet with US President Donald Trump at the annual event in New York.
Russian President Vladimir Putin isn’t due to attend.
European leaders, fearing Moscow has malicious intentions on their continent, are keen to put further pressure on Putin to withdraw from Ukraine, but the Russian leader has given no indication he is ready to give up his goals.
Russia hits apartment blocks and shopping mall
The Russian bombardment of Zaporizhzhia late on Sunday hit apartment blocks, a university and a shopping mall, among other sites, and wounded five people, Zelenskyy said on social media Monday.
Russia also struck nine other regions of Ukraine, he said.
“Russia is not backing down from its escalation and is sending many signals that it is ready to expand the war,” Zelenskyy said. “At the UN General Assembly, we will discuss how we can achieve peace through joint efforts.”
The Russian military overnight targeted Ukrainian logistics hubs, warehouses and ports, among other military-related sites, the Russian Defence Ministry said in a statement on Monday.
The attacks came after Ukraine launched a huge swarm of drones at Russia from Saturday to Sunday, including hundreds aimed at Moscow, as voters turned out for the third and last day of a carefully orchestrated parliamentary election.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday that its air defences overnight downed 244 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the waters of the Black Sea.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s air force said on Monday it shot down or suppressed 148 Russian drones in an overnight attack.
Moldova reports another drone incursion
During the aerial barrages, drones have repeatedly strayed into neighbouring countries, unnerving leaders who are war of Russia and fear being dragged into conflict.
Moldova’s Ministry of Defence said on Monday that part of the country's airspace in the north was temporarily closed overnight after surveillance systems detected an “aerial object” entering its national airspace shortly after midnight.
In recent weeks, Moldova’s airspace has been violated multiple times and drone debris has been found on its territory.
With electronic jamming knocking drones off course, it was not clear whether the drones were Russian or Ukrainian, though officials have often singled out Moscow for blame.
Moldova’s pro-Western President Maia Sandu has repeatedly condemned Russia for its war on Ukraine and earlier this month said Moscow’s “brutal war is reaching our border” following Russian strikes along Moldova’s frontier with Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine spent year ignoring one Russian drone-control tech, and now Geran-5 flies on it. President’s adviser warns next one, from space, is worse
articles.body:
Russia's newest military satellites keep stalling short of orbit, and Ukraine's top technology adviser says that is exactly why no one should relax. Serhii Beskrestnov, the presidential adviser on defense technology known as Flash, warns that once Russia completes its "Rassvet" satellite network, Moscow could steer its Gerans and missiles from space, and that Ukraine has to build the jamming to stop it before that day comes.
A working Rassvet would hand Russia a permanent link to its long-range weapons, letting it control drones and missiles online through satellites, what Flash calls "a small catastrophe."
Russia is nowhere near that yet: it has launched around 32 satellites but needs 200 to 250 for stable, round-the-clock coverage, and its most recent batch stalled in low orbit. Flash's point is that the reprieve is temporary.
"Russia is a space power," he wrote, and one heavy Angara rocket could loft much of the constellation in a single launch once its engines are fixed.
Ukraine has tried to choke the program at its source, striking a Russian space-rocket plant in mid-August and reaching for the Plesetsk cosmodrome days later, though the effort has only slowed it.
The MESH failure sets the warning
His alarm rests on a mistake, he says, Ukraine already made. For a year, he wrote, no one in the armed forces systematically worked on countering the MESH radio networks Russia uses to fly its jet Gerans, and no one shielded the capital with electronic warfare, even as the enemy openly built out the technology.
Breaking what he called a lifelong rule against criticizing colleagues, he "thanked" the former commander-in-chief and his electronic-warfare chief for the lapse, he wrote a bit earlier.
The result, he said, is that Russian Geran-5 are now striking under MESH control while Ukrainian specialists scramble to catch up.
The jamming must come first
With Rassvet, Flash argues, Ukraine cannot afford the same delay. The counter-system must not only be designed but actually fielded before the constellation is up, with the country's key infrastructure shielded by the time Russia's satellites reach orbit.
"This electronic warfare must ALREADY have closed all key infrastructure sites," he wrote.
Building it, he cautioned, will be neither fast nor cheap.

articles.title: Documents from Russia’s state nuclear corporation show plans to expand output of carbon fiber used in Geran-2 attack drones
articles.body:
Documents from Russia’s state nuclear corporation show plans to expand output of carbon fiber used in Geran-2 attack drones
European officials are increasingly worried about the growing number of sabotage attacks and Russian drone incidents in NATO countries. According to The Guardian, European intelligence agencies believe Russia may take more aggressive action in Europe in the coming months.
Michal Koudelka, head of the Czech counterintelligence service BIS, said Moscow could launch a small incursion into one of the NATO countries that border Russia. “It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign,” he said. Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned of a similar threat.
Officials in the Baltic states say they see no signs of an “imminent attack” yet, but they acknowledge that Russia may be preparing for more aggressive action. Jonatan Vseviov, secretary general of Estonia’s Foreign Ministry, said on social media that if the authorities had reason to fear a Russian attack, they would tell the public. “Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine.”
The debate over the likelihood of a direct escalation comes amid a very real rise in Russian hybrid operations in Europe. Last week, Bloomberg laid out in detail how those operations grew both more frequent and riskier over the summer. Their true scale may be much larger, since the authorities don’t publicly disclose many incidents. Bloomberg’s sources said Moscow intends to make life in Europe “hell” as punishment for supporting Ukraine.
Russia is also building up its capacity for further escalation, according to Politico. The outlet reviewed Rosatom documents on expanding production at the Alabuga-Volokno plant in Tatarstan.
In May, the Russian authorities approved building a new production line at the plant that would be able to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber a year. The material is used in the airframes of Russia’s Geran-2 attack drones, and the new line would allow Russia to expand drone production significantly. Experts estimate that 500 tons of carbon fiber is enough for 28,000 drone airframes a year. Ukraine currently puts Russia’s capacity at 36,000 Gerans a year.
Satellite images suggest that construction has already begun. It’s scheduled for completion in 2027. Serhiy Kuzan, chairman of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, which obtained the Rosatom documents, warned that the planned expansion at Alabuga should be seen not just as a problem for Ukraine’s front line but as a long-term threat to all of Europe.
The war in photos: Kramatorsk
Russia struck an evacuation center in Kramatorsk, in the Donetsk region. The center was housed in a school building, and evacuated civilians and staff were inside when the strike hit. Two people were injured.

articles.title: Warning sirens are going west: Russian jet-powered drones bring strikes closer to NATO country
articles.body:
Poland will have more than 1,000 automated warning sirens in Lublin Voivodeship by the end of 2026, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said on 19 September, up from nearly 350 now. The region had about 30 remotely activated sirens at the beginning of 2024.
The expansion comes as Russian attacks on the west of Ukraine are reaching closer to Poland. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Russia is expected to intensify attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure and warned of possible "accidental" drone or missile strikes on NATO countries, including Poland. He also said Russia is introducing jet-powered drones that move much faster and at higher altitudes.
Sirens sound as drones approach the border
A Russian air attack on western Ukraine triggered air-raid warnings in Poland's Lublin and Podkarpackie regions on 17 September. Sirens sounded in Lublin and Rzeszów, while residents received an SMS warning: "ATTENTION! ATTENTION! ATTENTION! Threat of an air attack. Find a safe place. Follow the instructions of the emergency services. Await further announcements."
The Polish military said its aircraft were activated in response to Russian strikes involving jet-powered drones against western Ukraine. A Russian drone flying toward Poland fell on Ukrainian territory about four kilometers from the Polish border, according to Polish authorities. Polish airspace was not violated.
Airports in Lublin and Rzeszów temporarily suspended operations to give military aircraft freedom of movement. Polish authorities said the measures were preventive and intended to protect Polish airspace.
More strikes on the border zone
On 13 September, Russian strikes near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing damaged a gas station and hit the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train about two kilometers from the Polish border. No deaths were reported, and the border crossing temporarily halted operations.
On 19 September, Poland again activated ground-based air-defense systems and increased radar reconnaissance in response to another wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine. The operation ended the same day with no violation of Polish airspace recorded.
Shelters, sirens, and a 1939 echo
Beyond sirens, authorities have marked nearly 3,500 official shelter locations in Lublin Voivodeship. More than 500 State Fire Service stations and volunteer fire units took part in special exercises on 19 September to practice responses to warning signals and emergency alerts.
"We are building a civil-protection system virtually from scratch," Kierwiński said at a briefing in Lublin. "We have very, very little time."
The 17 September strikes fell on the anniversary of the Soviet Union's 1939 invasion of Poland. Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the Russian attack as "massive, extremely brutal."
The 13 September strikes near the border also drew a response from Kyiv. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described them as Putin's terror "knocking" directly on the doors of the EU and NATO and called for a "full trade embargo, a total entry ban, and complete sanctions against Russia's military-industrial complex."

articles.title: Finland’s Stubb warns Europe not to ‘overreact’ to Russian threats and sabotage
articles.body:
Finland’s Stubb warns Europe not to ‘overreact’ to Russian threats and sabotage
Moscow isn’t seeking a full-scale war with NATO but instead trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine, Finnish President tells POLITICO.
NEW YORK — Finnish President Alexander Stubb has a message to European partners amid growing warnings of further Russian escalation: Keep calm and carry on.
In recent days, top European officials have ever-more-loudly sounded the alarm about intensifying Russian hybrid warfare, with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warning that Moscow could send drones or missiles into the territory of NATO countries supporting Ukraine in “the next few months.” The head of the Czech security service warned that Russia could undertake “a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign” in a matter of “months, not years.”
Yet Stubb has a different message. Although he acknowledges that Europe needs to prepare for “continued hybrid and sabotage attacks” by Russia, the Finnish president warns that Europe shouldn't “overreact,” as Moscow aims to scare allies into slowing down support for Ukraine.
Advertisement
“We have to be very careful and understand that Russia is trying to destabilize and scare Europe. And any time we overreact to a hybrid attack, they have actually won the battle in that particular way,” Stubb told POLITICO during an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
“We also have to understand that it is not in the interest of Russia nor in the capacity of Russia to go full-scale” with military escalation, Stubb added. “So they will continue to intimidate and we just have to be, as I say, cool, calm and collected in this situation.”
In contrast, however, Stubb pointed to the “overreaction” from some intelligence services which “basically say that, well, you’re next” for a Russian invasion.
“We don’t see the evidence of that,” he said, adding: “We think we have to be vigilant and awake. But, you know, we have the longest border in NATO with Russia, it’s half the border. In our intelligence we see that there is activity but no imminent military threat right now.”
Stubb also expressed tentative hopefulness concerning a meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on Tuesday.
Advertisement
“Obviously, we’re not going to be getting a peace deal here this week,” he said. “But if we were to get, for instance, an idea or a framework for a ceasefire in the Black Sea linked to grain or to energy, I think this would be a move in the right direction.”
Stubb added that he was hoping for further peace talks in the coming weeks, including potentially a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Zelenskyy at the G20 summit in Miami in December.
“Let’s see what President Trump is able to do for the G20 meeting. Is he able to get Zelenskyy and Putin around the same table?” Stubb said, adding that this was “a possibility” and would be “a jackpot,” even though currently negotiations were still “far from that.”
The Finnish president also pushed back against suggestions that he could be Europe’s top negotiator in upcoming peace talks with Russia.
“No, I don’t think that’s sort of in the cards,” Stubb said. “I don’t think Europe will have one representative as such,” he argued, while describing his role as trying “to help in the back office.”
