Zelensky floated single state idea to drag Warsaw into war – Polish opposition leader
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky sought to drag Poland into war with Russia in 2022, even floating the prospect of creating a single state, Polish opposition leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski has claimed.
The head of the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party recalled how the government of Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki reacted to the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. Kaczynski was deputy prime minister at the time and chaired the government committee responsible for national security and defense affairs.
“The Ukrainians sometimes expected things that – for various reasons I cannot discuss here – we simply could not agree to,” the veteran politician said during a meeting with the PiS youth congress last weekend.
“Initially, they held a somewhat strange concept, namely, that they would drag us into the war, perhaps even to the point of creating a single state,” he added, noting that Zelensky’s speech in the Polish parliament was “heading in that direction.”
Zelensky addressed the Sejm remotely in March 2022 as part of his efforts to rally Western support. Warsaw went on to provide Kiev with additional military aid while pressing other NATO members to increase their contributions, Kaczynski said.
Other Polish politicians made similar criticisms of Zelensky
Krzysztof Gawkowski, a deputy to incumbent Prime Minister Donald Turk, similarly accused Kiev of trying to drag Poland into the war in 2024, as he rebuked Zelensky for “pestering” Warsaw with demands for greater military involvement.
Poland suffered casualties early in the conflict when a missile fired by Ukrainian air defenses struck a farm near the border village of Przewodow in November 2022, killing two civilians. Zelensky initially insisted that the projectile was Russian and urged for a collective NATO retaliation.
Former Polish President Andrzej Duda, a PiS ally, later described Kiev’s reaction to the incident as part of an effort to draw NATO nations directly into the conflict.
Moscow has repeatedly warned that deeper NATO involvement in Ukraine risks a direct conflict. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that if Europe attacked Russia, the resulting war would be “different” in nature and “very short.”
Historic grievances divide Poland and Ukraine
Poland and Ukraine have a long-running dispute over the legacy of the Nazi-collaborating Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which Warsaw holds responsible for mass killings of Polish civilians during World War II.
The issue flared again earlier this year after Zelensky gave an elite military unit the honorary name “Heroes of the UPA,” prompting sharp criticism from Warsaw.
The historic grudge feeds into tensions over territories that belonged to interwar Poland and became part of Soviet Ukraine after World War II. A reference to lost Polish lands sparked a public quarrel last week between Tusk and conservative President Karol Nawrocki.
Nawrocki wrote on X that Poland “may lose territory, but we will never lose [its] soul.” The prime minister rebuked the sentiment, saying: “We do not intend to give up even a scrap of our territory.”

articles.title: The ‘stab in the back’ that wasn’t: Why Stalin sent the Red Army into Poland
articles.body:
The ‘stab in the back’ that wasn’t: Why Stalin sent the Red Army into Poland
On September 17, 1939, Soviet troops crossed into eastern Poland. By that time, the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth was about to collapse under the assault of Nazi forces. Soon, the Soviet military moved westward to meet the advancing Germans. Moscow and Berlin established a demarcation line according to which the USSR acquired parts of eastern Poland. Today, these territories belong to Belarus, Ukraine, and Lithuania.
This event still sparks debates both in Russia and Europe, and particularly in Poland. In Ukraine and Lithuania, political discourse has taken a surprising turn, suggesting that while the USSR was the aggressor state that invaded Poland on September 17, neither Ukraine nor Lithuania will yield any territory that they gained as a result of this aggression. For Lithuania, the situation is quite ironic, since it acquired its capital, Vilnius, precisely as a result of the Red Army’s Polish campaign.
Any commentary on this event provokes an intense and painful reaction from all sides that consider themselves victims of it. Nevertheless, it is essential to examine the circumstances surrounding the Soviet army’s invasion of Poland. For Russians, who lost countless lives during the Second World War, this topic is particularly sensitive; but the same holds true for Poles, who suffered comparable losses relative to their population size, and for Belarusians and Ukrainians, who found themselves in the middle of this significant territorial reallocation.
History can often be distorted by politics. From the late 1930s to the present day, interpretations of this event have evolved in various countries. It would be best to take a measured approach to assess what really happened, recognizing that each country has its own perspective shaped by its unique experience. We also need to remember that all parties had rational interests, yet none of them possessed enough information or the benefit of hindsight provided by post-war historians.
Buffer zone of discord
By 1939, both the Soviet Union and Poland were new states established on the basis of old nations. They had come into existence following the disintegration of the Russian Empire and the subsequent Russian Civil War. However, from the outset, there was a significant territorial dispute between Russia’s reincarnation in the form of the Soviet Union and Poland’s rebirth as the Second Polish Republic. The Poles laid claim not only to their own lands but also to all the lands Poland had once possessed, which included vast territories in Belarus and Ukraine. In Poland, this region is referred to as “Kresy Wschodnie,” which means “Eastern Borderlands.”
Overall, Poland’s ambitions extended even further. During the Russian Civil War, Polish forces advanced deep into Ukraine and captured Kiev before ultimately being defeated. The Red Army then launched its Polish campaign which also ended in failure a short way from Warsaw. Ultimately, the Poles acquired what they referred to as “Kresy” – the western regions of Ukraine and Belarus. For the most part, these territories weren’t populated by Poles, yet Poland had governed them before the territorial divisions of the 18th century and viewed them as its historical lands. During the interwar period, these regions underwent a process of polonization, with Ukrainian and Belarusian populations facing discrimination. One somewhat counterintuitive fact is that Ukrainian nationalist terrorism during that period was directed primarily not against the USSR, but against Poland.
Meanwhile, the Soviet Union regarded these lost territories as unjustly seized and was unwilling to relinquish its claims on them. In short, neither party was satisfied with such ‘peace’ and there was no warming of relations between the USSR and Poland.
The territorial dispute over the Vilnius region caused additional challenges. Poland seized Vilna (Vilnius), a city that Lithuania claimed as its historical capital and which was highly important to it both historically and culturally.
This atmosphere of ‘cold peace’ lasted throughout the 1920s. In the 1930s, the Nazis came to power in Germany. In 1938, Hitler annexed a significant part of Czechoslovakia (a few months later, he came to fully control the country). This crisis put the USSR and Poland at odds once again. The Soviet Union viewed the Nazis as a grave threat, and Moscow even considered intervening on behalf of Czechoslovakia. However, this required USSR troops to pass through Poland, which Warsaw resolutely rejected. It was opposed to any military cooperation with the USSR, even for transit purposes. Furthermore, during the German occupation of Czechoslovakia, Poland annexed the Teschen region (an area of 805 square kilometers with a population of 277,000) which was a small but notable territorial gain.
Throughout the negotiations regarding Czechoslovakia, the interests and positions of the USSR were overtly disregarded by Western allies – i.e. England, France, and Poland. The Soviet Union gained considerable political weight on the global stage only after WWII. Before that, its influence hardly rose to the level of a superpower. Consequently, Stalin had to swallow this bitter pill and prepare for the events to come.
Meanwhile, Hitler was determined to continue his aggressive expansion. The regime he constructed in Germany had a significant yet subtle flaw – its structure resembled a financial pyramid. The rapid growth of the country’s military industrial complex threatened to undermine its economy. The only salvation for the Third Reich lay in war or the unconditional submission of neighboring countries to its demands and threats. Poland was next on Hitler’s list of intended victims. He used the “Polish Corridor” – the strip of land separating mainland Germany from East Prussia – as leverage. The Germans maintained contact with this exclave solely by sea. Today, this area remains an exclave, but belongs to Russia: the current Russian city of Kaliningrad is the former German city of Königsberg. Additionally, Hitler demanded reconsideration of the status of Danzig, a city with a significant German population that had been designated a “free city” under the League of Nations’ protection.
Understandably, Poland wasn’t satisfied with these demands. The question was, how could it stand up to Germany, which was much more powerful. Clearly, the best option was to seek help from Western allies – Britain and France. They readily provided Poland with security guarantees and did indeed declare war on the Third Reich on September 3, just two days after it invaded Poland. However, what the Polish leaders didn’t realize was that their allies weren’t prepared to offer immediate assistance. Britain needed time to transport troops across the English Channel, while France had to mobilize and strategically deploy its troops. This couldn’t be done immediately, but it was uncertain whether Poland could hold out long enough.
Poland’s dialogue with Soviet diplomats was quite rude. Polish officials bluntly told People’s Commissar for Foreign Affairs Maxim Litvinov that they would ask for help “when it will be needed.” Throughout this time, the Polish government believed that “the dismemberment of Russia is at the heart of Poland’s eastern policy.”
It’s no secret that there were significant territorial disputes between the USSR and Poland, and that the two countries felt an aversion towards each other. In hindsight, Warsaw’s behavior appears reckless, but at the time, Poland believed that the guarantees from Western allies would suffice. They thought that by allowing even one Russian soldier into Poland, they could easily become hostages of such an ally. Strictly speaking, one can’t say that they were wrong. Nevertheless, the Soviet regime turned out to be a lot less strict than the German regime in Poland.
The USSR aimed to safeguard its interests in Eastern Europe. Moscow had no doubt that a large-scale war was imminent. And the USSR found itself in a vulnerable position. The key centers of Soviet power were located too close to the border. Leningrad (currently St. Petersburg) faced threats from both Finland and Estonia which it bordered, while Minsk and Kiev were dangerously close to the Polish border. The USSR wasn’t concerned about a threat coming directly from Estonia or Poland, but rather feared that a third party could use these regions as a launchpad for an attack on the USSR (by 1939, it was clear that this would be Germany). Stalin and his inner circle understood that the USSR would eventually confront Germany and were eager to secure the most advantageous position before the inevitable confrontation.
Mistrust and the fog of war
The USSR still had another option – direct negotiations with Western allies. Stalin was primarily interested in a coordinated plan of action against the Nazis. However, the Soviet Union had its own fears and biases. It’s important to note that, just like in the situation with Poland, neither British nor French leaders could foresee the future any better than their Soviet counterparts. And in 1939 they considered such an alliance no better than one with Hitler.
This might sound odd in 2026, but in the summer of 1939, Hitler wasn’t yet “the Hitler” that we’ve come to know. The Third Reich was still largely focused on repressing its own citizens. Anti-semitism with its discriminatory laws was abominable, yet not necessarily worse than the repressions in the US against African-Americans or the colonial practices of European powers. On the other hand, Stalin’s USSR, with its own repressions and ideology aimed at dismantling the capitalist world, certainly didn’t present itself as a beacon of virtue. This is why Moscow had its doubts about whether Britain and France were more reliable negotiating partners than Germany, and the same skepticism was shared by Paris and London in regard to Moscow. Additionally, Britain and France significantly underestimated the real weight of the USSR as an ally – and this was an error they would soon regret.
On August 11, an Anglo-French delegation arrived in Moscow. The problem was that the allies came with a very vague battle plan. The Soviet side insisted on including the term “indirect aggression” in the agreement, which implied using the territories of neighboring countries to wage war against the USSR. The allies believed that Stalin wanted free rein to act against the Baltic states, Finland, and wherever else he pleased. However, the Soviet Union needed this complicated wording to safeguard itself against a possible surprise alliance between Germany and Finland or the Baltic nations, leading to a potential invasion of the USSR from those territories.
Both sides distrusted each other and preferred to secure maximum guarantees with minimal commitments. Ultimately, the negotiations failed.
In response, the Soviet Union made a controversial move: it struck a deal with Hitler. On August 23, a non-aggression pact was signed between the USSR and Germany, outlining spheres of influence in Europe.
Under the famous Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, the USSR aimed to buy time and establish a buffer zone in Eastern Europe. Moscow secured a significant condition – the incorporation of Eastern Poland (currently Western Ukraine and Belarus) into the Soviet sphere of interest.
Even today, this pact is often regarded as a deal with the devil. However, it did not serve as an immediate trigger for war. For Hitler, war was inevitable. Stopping the war would lead to the collapse of his entire foreign policy, and Germany’s bloated military system could not come to a stop without causing economic disaster. Moreover, Hitler did not regard the Soviet Union as a formidable opponent; he even devised plans of a complete military defeat of the USSR in three months.
Looking back, we may say that the 1938-1939 negotiations represent one of the greatest failures in the history of diplomacy. Had the world powers united against the Nazis in 1939 – or better yet, in 1938 – there might have been no WWII, but only a major clean-up of issues left over from WWI. However, there’s no way to change history.
The barrier to Blitzkrieg
Poland’s pre-war planning was based on several questionable assumptions. Poland believed that its army was sufficiently large and was capable of holding off the Nazis long enough for Western allies to come to its aid. Ideas to form a defensive line along the Vistula River and use the river as a natural barrier were ultimately dismissed. Marshal Edward Rydz-Smigly, who led Poland’s defense, aimed to cover all fronts and surrender nothing. However, in reality, Poland had far fewer military resources than the enemy and couldn’t seize the initiative. Moreover, after the annexation of Czechoslovakia, the Third Reich bordered Poland on three sides. Even without additional complications, this combination spelled disaster for Poland. Yet another problem existed: between the wars, the Germans developed a range of operational, tactical, and technical solutions known as “Blitzkrieg,” which prioritized rapid, decisive maneuvers. And Poland became the testing ground for this strategy in real-life conditions.
On September 1, 1939, Hitler invaded Poland, marking the start of WWII. On September 3, the Allies declared war on Germany. The Wehrmacht charged at the Polish army like a gorilla breaking free from its cage. Within the first week, the Polish forces retreated chaotically on all fronts, and some units became encircled. By September 5, the Polish government fled toward the border. On September 16, before the USSR entered the conflict, the Polish leadership was already negotiating with Romania regarding evacuation. The high command moved to Brest and lost contact with the main body of troops.
After September 10, there was no longer any centralized control of the Polish army. By September 16, German forces reached Bialystok, Brest, and Lviv. Most organized Polish units remained to the west and were encircled. The Allies were unable to assist Poland; French troops were slowly deployed and managed to carry out only a limited offensive that pushed the front back a few kilometers into German territory. The Allies could have saved Poland by 1940, if only it could hold out until then – but this was clearly an insurmountable task for the country.
Soviet political leaders decided that further delay was pointless. On September 6, Moscow announced “large-scale military exercises” which in reality meant that the country mobilized its armed forces. However, it soon became apparent that the Soviet military was not as combat ready as was anticipated. The troops weren’t ready for combat, military equipment required repairs, and there was a great shortage of additional vehicles.
Regardless of this, the Polish forces were completely disorganized and could not offer fierce resistance. The notion that the Soviets “stabbed Poland in the back as it fought” the Nazis sounds quite dramatic, but by that time, all that remained of the Polish army were some isolated battalions. Poland had lost all its industrial regions, mobilization was impossible, the army was defeated, and the remaining troops tried to defend Warsaw. In essence, there was no one to “stab in the back.” Formally, the Polish army still numbered in the hundreds of thousands of soldiers and officers, but in reality they moved around chaotically in the rear. There was no one to lead them into battle.
On the night of September 17, Stalin personally informed German ambassador to the USSR Friedrich-Werner Graf von der Schulenburg that the Red Army was about to start its operation. A similar note was delivered to the Polish ambassador to the USSR. The next morning, Soviet mechanized columns crossed the border into Poland.
The Polish government promptly fled the country. Commander of the Polish armed forces Marshal Rydz-Smigly ordered, “I command an immediate retreat to Romania and Hungary by the shortest routes. Do not engage in combat with the Soviets.”
The entry of the Red Army into Poland was accompanied by considerable disorder. Polish resistance was sporadic and was largely initiated by local junior commanders. The advance of Soviet troops was marked by confusion and there were many non-combat losses. In areas where the Poles put up resistance, the Soviet army fought, but generally for the Poles, it looked more like disarmament than defeat in battle. For instance, during the assault on Grodno, 57 Red Army soldiers were killed, while about 1,500 Polish soldiers and officers surrendered. During the campaign, an estimated 737-1,475 Soviet soldiers and officers died – many of them for non-combat reasons; and about 240,000 soldiers were taken prisoner.
While Polish soldiers and officers offered some resistance, the Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Jewish people often sympathized with or even assisted the advancing Red Army units. Poland’s ideology was one of triumphant nationalism, so non-Polish cultures found themselves in a subordinate position and were often openly discriminated against.
The Wehrmacht immediately halted its advance into territories that were claimed by the USSR. A few days later, the demarcation line was finalized. Tensions arose only in Lviv, where Soviet forces encountered German troops. As a result, all three sides – the Red Army, the Polish garrison, and the German army – lost both soldiers and equipment.
A separate story unfolded in Brest. On September 22, a Red Army tank brigade entered the city, which had been occupied by German forces. Depending on the narrator, this event is often described as either the passage of troops or a joint parade. Soviet commander Semyon Krivoshein and German General Heinz Guderian watched as German soldiers withdrew from Brest and Soviet troops took their place. The situation was all the more awkward since Krivoshein was Jewish and felt as uncomfortable standing next to a Nazi commander as Guderian did standing next to him.
By September 29, the Red Army’s campaign in Poland was essentially over. The Soviet Union expanded its territory by 196,000 square km (half of the territory of Poland) with a population of up to 13 million people. The Vilna region, including the city of Vilnius, was handed over to Lithuania, while areas populated by Belarusians and Ukrainians were assigned to the respective Soviet republics.
The fate of prisoners of war and the people detained by Soviet security agencies raised further questions. Many Polish officers were later executed at Katyn. But most captives were either sent home or fled to the West through third counties where they formed the Anders’ Army, which became part of the Western coalition. In western Belarus and Ukraine, Soviet authority was established, which caused certain upheavals that always accompany such transitions. Many people suspected of disloyalty were deported further east. However, considering the war which would soon break out, such exile often saved their lives.
Liberation for some, occupation for others
Setting politics aside and focusing on the actual circumstances surrounding the Soviet campaign and its alternatives, we see that the situation didn’t look flattering from any side.
Firstly, we need to dismiss the idea that Hitler would not have started the war without the pact or that the war was started jointly by the Nazis and the USSR. The Soviet Union lacked the diplomatic weight to impose its will on partners in negotiations. Indeed, the Nazis didn’t want more problems in the East. However, from Hitler’s perspective, he struck a fantastic deal: he resolved a potentially contentious issue and rid himself of possible complications by ceding territories that he considered worthless – that didn’t have any significant resources or industrial centers – to the Soviet Union.
For the USSR, this meant gaining a buffer zone in case of a future confrontation with the Nazis and reuniting two important national republics. Did the decision regarding Poland align with strict moral standards? Not really. But Poland had little reason to complain – after all, its army had forcefully seized the disputed territories a few decades earlier, only to lose them in another military conflict. And while we may vehemently denounce USSR aggression, we must also ask: what were the alternatives? In fact, there were only two viable options. The first one was to fight against Hitler with a weak military force and with no solid guarantees from Western allies. Negotiations on a joint action plan with those allies had just failed, so why would Stalin trust them?
As for Poland, it was outright opposed to an alliance with Moscow. Indeed, there was another option: to do nothing. This meant handing over the Kresy to Hitler. On September 17, 1939, the choice was not “Poland or Hitler” or “totalitarians or democrats”; it was simply “Hitler or Stalin.” Given this reality, it’s worth asking the moralists whether they consider Hitler a more legitimate or humane ruler of Lviv and Grodno than Stalin.
In this grim world of ‘realpolitik’, Poland’s position proved to be extremely vulnerable. The leaders of the Second Polish Republic consistently rejected any ideas of jointly fighting against Hitler with the USSR. Of course, they reasonably feared being drawn into Moscow’s orbit and ultimately finding themselves living in a socialist Poland. Ironically, by the end of the war, this is indeed what happened, but by that time Poland had lost one-fifth of its population due to the war and the Nazi occupation, and Warsaw and the entire country were in ruins. Should Poland have considered making political concessions to the USSR earlier instead of waiting until Moscow controlled Poland’s territory, army, and political institutions? That’s a question only the Polish people can answer. Indeed, it’s hard to shake the feeling that in 1939, faced with two evils, Poland chose to do nothing and simply perish. The idea of doing nothing in such a situation might look good in a novel, but it’s hardly practical in politics.
For Western allies, 1939 clearly became the year of lost opportunities. One could argue that an allied operation against the Nazis involving Britain, France, the USSR, and what remained of Poland could have been a better option than what happened in reality: Germany’s swift occupation of France, followed by Britain and the USSR fighting Germany on their own – Britain at sea and in the air, and the USSR on land. However, at the time, deep mutual distrust and a poor understanding of the situation played a fatal role in forming an alliance between Western democracies and the Soviet Union.
The USSR ultimately benefited from the events of September 1939, but not as much as it had hoped. Its territorial gains included western Belarus and Ukraine, and this was soon followed by the annexation of the Baltic states. Since a larger war loomed on the horizon, this territory became valuable only as square kilometers. These buffer zones proved crucial in 1941 when the USSR entered the war against Germany. The issue of Finland’s status, which the USSR declared war on several months later, remained unresolved.
Most importantly, Stalin hoped that he would gain far more time than he actually did. The USSR had hoped that it would have several years to prepare for war, while France put up active resistance. In reality, the defense of France collapsed in the summer of 1940, and the USSR gained only one year and nine months of breathing room. And rather than becoming weaker, the Wehrmacht grew even stronger in the course of the conflict against Western allies.
In 1939, politicians gave more candid and sensible assessments of the situation. Winston Churchill observed:
“Russia has pursued a cold policy of self-interest. We could have wished that the Russian armies should be standing on their present lines as the friends of the allies in Poland, instead of as invaders. But that the Russian armies should stand on this line was clearly necessary for the safety of Russia against the Nazi menace. In any case, this line exists, and this means that an Eastern Front has been established that Nazi Germany would not dare attack.”
The Soviet Union operated within the framework of ‘realpolitik’, which didn’t look either nice or noble.
But in less than two years, the Russians found themselves engaged in the greatest war in history, which was a battle for their very survival. And undoubtedly, the Soviet Union used every means at its disposal to strengthen its position before that day arrived.

articles.title: Ukrainians are preparing for the most difficult wartime winter due to the threat of prolonged outages of electricity, heating, and water – Bloomberg
articles.body:
Ukrainians are preparing for the most difficult wartime winter due to the threat of prolonged outages of electricity, heating, and water – Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
russia may have reduced ballistic missile launches, stockpiling them for winter strikes on energy infrastructure. Ukraine lacks missiles for Patriot.
Ukraine is preparing for a winter that could become the hardest since the beginning of the full-scale war due to the threat of new massive Russian strikes on energy and heating infrastructure. Russia has recently reduced its use of ballistic missiles, which may indicate that it is stockpiling them ahead of the cold season, Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
Concerns intensified after last winter, when prolonged freezing temperatures and Russian strikes led to days-long disruptions to electricity, heating, and water supplies in major cities. In Kyiv, temperatures fell below -20°C, while some residents of Troieshchyna were left without centralized heating.
Amid expected attacks, Ukrainians are already preparing backup options. Some people are moving to homes with autonomous heating, buying generators, warm clothing, and firewood. According to one of Bloomberg's sources, firewood prices have risen by approximately 70–80% over the year.
Ukraine lacks missiles for Patriot systems
One of the main problems remains the shortage of air defense assets, particularly interceptor missiles for Patriot systems, which are needed to counter Russian ballistic missiles.
Since August, Russia has significantly reduced its use of ballistic missiles in favor of jet-powered drones. Bloomberg notes that this may indicate the accumulation of missiles for strikes on Ukraine's energy and heating systems during the cold season, which usually begins in late October or early November.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously stated that Ukraine needs at least 300 Patriot interceptor missiles to get through the winter. European allies plan to raise the issue of additional deliveries during meetings in New York this week.
Government preparations
The Ukrainian government, meanwhile, is preparing for the worst-case scenario. The authorities plan to expand the network of "Points of Invincibility," while European partners are supplying spare parts for power plants and equipment for heating systems.
According to Bloomberg, Ukraine's energy infrastructure is now better protected against Russian strikes than before. At the same time, Kyiv's allies fear that Russia will try to use winter attacks on critical infrastructure to increase pressure on Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
articles.body:
This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: September 21, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
September 21 marks the fourth anniversary of Vladimir Putin’s 2022 “partial” mobilisation, yet the true fate of the men drafted into the war remains highly opaque. Because recent obituaries rarely mention recruitment details and there are no indirect ways to identify the draftees, our current figure of 20,500 KIA mobilised soldiers is a significant underestimate. To overcome this lack of public data, we are now analysing two major military leaks to track what has actually happened to these troops over the past two years.
Read the report here:
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By September 21, 2026, the death of 7,692 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 241,600 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 244,700 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

Breadcrumb
Iran says conveyed conditions to US for reopening Hormuz
Iran's top negotiator said Sunday that Tehran conveyed to Washington, through mediators, its conditions for ending its blockade of the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
The two foes are locked in a stalemate, months into the conflict that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Tehran has maintained a stranglehold on the strait, a vital shipping route for the world's oil and gas, while Washington is pushing its own campaign to choke the Islamic Republic's ports and economy.
"Our messages and the explanation of our conditions have been clearly conveyed to the other party through mediators," said Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has acted as chief negotiator in talks to end the war.
"As long as the conditions are not met...and the US commitments are not honoured, it will be impossible to return to the situation from before the negotiations and to an open strait," he added, according to state television.
Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's supreme national security council, said on Saturday that the Islamic Republic had conveyed its conditions to the US via mediator Qatar.
"Our conditions are an end to the war on all fronts, the release of our frozen funds and an end to the naval blockade," he said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
He warned that the US would face an Iran that was better prepared than at the start of the war.
"We will confront America with greater force, and with more numerous and more painful strikes," he said, singling out US bases and US commercial interests in the region as targets for an Iranian military and economic response to any US strike.
"We are prepared for a decisive war."
The Iranian security chief said in the interview that Iran had increased the speed of its hypersonic missiles "from Mach 6 to Mach 10", as well as improved its air defences and developed "electronic warfare systems".
"Therefore, should war break out again, US ships, unless they withdraw from the Indian Ocean, will be subject to attack," he said.
Iranian authorities have said that mediator Pakistan's Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi will travel to Tehran on Sunday for talks.
Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya central military command, meanwhile, issued a threat against the United States on Sunday, in a statement carried by state television.
"We warn that if the US makes a mistake in dealing with Islamic Iran, all of that country's bases and interests in the region will become the target of continuous, effective and painful attacks, without any limit or restraint," it said.

articles.title: Ukraine disables over 45% of Russia's refining capacity – General Staff
articles.body:
Ukrainian Defense Forces, following the strike on the Moscow Oil Refinery, have disabled more than 45% of the design capacity of Russia's oil refining industry as of September 21, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said in a weekly summary covering strikes on key enemy facilities in Russia and the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine from September 14 to 20.
"From September 14 to 20, units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a number of important enemy facilities in Russia and the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. First and foremost, these were enterprises supporting Russia's military and economic potential," the General Staff said.
On the night of September 15, the Syzran Oil Refinery in Russia's Samara region was struck. The AVT-6 primary oil refining unit and a tank farm were hit. In Taganrog, Rostov region, the Atlant Aero facility, which produces Molniya strike and reconnaissance UAVs and components for Orion drones, was also struck.
On the night of September 17, the Slavneft-YANOS oil refinery in Yaroslavl, with an annual refining capacity of about 15 million tonnes of oil, was struck. The AVT-3 primary refining unit was hit.
On September 20, the Gazprom Neft Moscow Oil Refinery in Moscow was struck, including the AVT-6 unit, a comprehensive oil refining unit and an isomerization unit.
"Thus, as of September 21, 2026, following the strike on the Moscow Oil Refinery, more than 45% of the design capacity of Russia's oil refining industry has been disabled," the General Staff said.
One consequence, it said, was a shortage of quality fuel in Russia. In particular, production of Euro-5/K5 standard gasoline and diesel fuel has fallen sharply.
"Another area is the systematic targeting of air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare systems and command-and-control assets," the General Staff said.
In particular, a 92N6 radar from the S-400 Triumf system was struck in Sochi; two S-400 launchers were struck near Vyhonichi in Russia's Bryansk region; and a Buk-M3 surface-to-air missile system was struck near Ukrainka in Zaporizhia region. A Nebo-U radar was struck in Donetsk region. Electronic warfare stations, radars and repeaters were also struck in Bryansk region.
"Significant attention was paid to the infrastructure supporting the occupiers' strike UAVs. Storage, preparation, launch and production sites for unmanned aerial vehicles were struck in the areas of Donetsk, Kursk and Sievierodonetsk. At Saki airfield, an Orion UAV ground control station was struck. Numerous command posts for Russian aggressor UAVs were also struck," the General Staff said.
In addition, two An-26 aircraft, an An-12 and three helicopters were struck at Rostov-on-Don (Central) airfield. A Su-24 aircraft was struck at Saki airfield.
During the week, Ukrainian forces also struck ammunition, fuel and lubricants, and materiel storage facilities belonging to Russian forces.
"Striking such facilities of the Russian aggressor is Ukraine's exercise of its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military and economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said.

articles.title: Houthis move to seize strategic terrain after Trump calls off airstrikes at last minute
articles.body:
Houthi fighters are moving to seize strategic heights in Yemen that would cut the Red Sea coast off from areas held by Saudi-backed forces after Donald Trump called off US strikes on the group at the last minute, reportedly as bombs were being loaded on to aircraft.
Amid increasingly heavy fighting in Yemen, which has displaced tens of thousands of people in recent weeks, the New York Times reported on Monday that the US president had flip-flopped wildly in recent days after a call from Saudi Arabia for US strikes on the Houthis.
It comes amid the Houthis’ rapid advance on the ground with the group gaining control over much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and advancing to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia has used as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the strait of Hormuz.
In the call reported by the New York Times, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, implored Trump to step in to help halt the Houthi advance after weeks of such appeals. Trump, who had been resisting joining the Saudi war in Yemen, after the call then told the Pentagon to prepare for airstrikes against the Houthis before reversing course once again, the report said.
Trump has frequently given mixed signals to Riyadh, telling reporters during a visit to Ireland earlier this month that the Houthis “called us, and they don’t want to fight us”, adding that the group was “allowing ships to pass” the Bab al-Mandab strait and that the situation would “work out very well”.
He added that the Houthi problem was limited to “one country” an apparent reference to Saudi Arabia promising to “take care of fixing that”.
The UN says hostilities in Yemen have displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September. Taiz city has received the largest number of displaced persons, taking in up to 86,000 Yemenis since the recent escalation began.
The rapid advance by the Iran-aligned group this month has extended the wider Middle East conflict to a new theatre and further threatened global energy supplies.
Washington has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Prince Mohammed to join the fight in Yemen with the Houthis claiming on Saturday they had fired on Riyadh, where columns of smoke were visible near the main airport.
The Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, spoke to Trump on Sunday, requesting support for his UN-recognised government in its fight against the Houthis. Trump made no direct pledge of military support during the call, sources said.
Saudi Arabia has launched hundreds of strikes in recent days on Houthi positions in the strategic Kahboub mountains, according to the group, but making little impact on the advance of its fighters.
Fighting has centred on the outskirts of the remote Al-Wazi’iyah district in Taiz province and Ras al-Ara along the Indian Ocean coast, which separate the Red Sea coast from the city of Aden, where the government is based. The Houthis aim to secure the rear of their forces around the Bab al-Mandab strait by taking control of the mountains, which would also allow them to open new fronts, according to sources who spoke to Reuters.
The surge in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has created a new dilemma for Trump, under pressure to help defend Washington’s close Saudi allies but anxious not to further expand the deeply unpopular war he launched in February against Iran.
The US bombed the Houthis for two months in early 2025, but Trump called off those strikes after reaching a ceasefire with the group and has kept out of the conflict since.
Amid the broad failure of the US-Israeli war against Iran, and with the US midterm elections looming, the Trump administration’s priorities appear to be to secure at least some oil supplies through the strait of Hormuz, while avoiding a wider entanglement in Yemen.
That, however, invites longer-term risks, not least the growing alienation of key US allies in the Gulf, including Saudi Arabia, where Washington is increasingly seen as an unreliable ally, that could also undermine the so-called “security for oil” understanding where the US provides a defence umbrella for Gulf states in exchange for energy supplies.
Reuters contributed to this report

articles.title: Putin consolidates grip on Russia as 49 Ukraine war veterans elected to parliament
articles.body:
Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine, officials have said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections.
The pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures. The result further consolidates Vladimir Putin’s grip on power and gives United Russia a super-majority bigger than its previous 2016 record of 343 seats.
The polls are the first to be held since Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion. United Russia’s general secretary, Vladimir Yakushev, said 86 veterans from Moscow’s “special military operation” were likely to have been elected. “This is quite a substantial contribution,” he said. He later revised the number to 49.
Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the vote showed that Russians supported their longtime leader, who has ruled as prime minister or president since 2000. “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Peskov said.
Western governments denounced the polls held in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine as a “sham”. Russia’s supreme court last month banned the only party that opposes the war, Yabloko, from participating, leaving liberal voters with no option to express discontent.
Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, called the election “another major setback for Russian democracy”. “The Kremlin silenced dissent and shut out international election monitors,” Kallas wrote on X, adding: “The veneer of democracy is all that remains.”
The elections come amid speculation that Putin may announce a large mobilisation campaign this autumn, in an attempt to inject fresh momentum to Russia’s bogged down military campaign. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has suggested the Kremlin wants to recruit another 300,000 troops.
In recent months, Russia has escalated its bombardment, pummelling Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine has launched its own deep strikes, hitting Moscow’s oil refinery on Sunday, as part of what Zelenskyy has dubbed “long-range sanctions”.
Russia’s has also intensified its campaign to seize a string of cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. So far, it has been unable to break through, with Ukrainian commanders reporting their own counteroffensive near the city of Lyman.
Inside Russia, criticism of the conflict is banned. Anti-war bloggers have been arrested and jailed. A local politician, Boris Nadezhdin, who previously tried to stand in presidential elections on a peace ticket, was barred from September’s elections and accused of being a “foreign agent”.
The other parties that won seats in this month’s poll all support the “special military operation”. They include the communists, who came second with 40 seats, the ultra-nationalist LDPR party, with 25, and the New People party, with 20. Chechnya’s leader, Ramzan Kadyrov, a Putin ally, was re-elected and said to have won more than 99% of the votes.
Russia’s elections chief, Ella Pamfilova, said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83%, with 95% of ballots counted, up from the 49.8% it won in the last parliamentary election, in 2021. She praised voters for resisting “psychological pressure”.
Overnight, Russia carried out what Zelenskyy called a “brutal, targeted attack” on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. He said a nine-storey residential building, a university building, a shopping centre, and a boiler house were all damaged, with five people injured. A woman in Kharkiv region was killed in a drone strike.
Zelenskyy said: “Russia is not scaling back its escalatory actions and is signalling a readiness to expand the war. All this is happening against the backdrop of global stability already having been shattered by this war. We must continue to pressure the aggressor to bring this war to an end.”

articles.title: Targets picked, bombs loaded: Trump called off strikes on Houthis at the last minute
articles.body:
After days of shifting positions in the office of U.S. President Donald Trump, and despite his latest conversation with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the president called off a series of planned airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen at the last minute. According to The New York Times, citing senior U.S. officials, munitions had already been loaded onto fighter jets that were ready for takeoff when Trump announced the change in plans.
The president and crown prince spoke on Thursday about a week and a half ago, when bin Salman urged Trump to launch strikes and help Saudi Arabia in its campaign. Two U.S. officials told Axios at the time that the Trump administration was not inclined to take direct military action against the Houthi group.
Something apparently changed, however. According to The New York Times, fighter jets were preparing for an attack and the target list had already been approved. The newspaper reported that the conversation influenced Trump, who instructed the Pentagon to prepare for action before changing his mind again. The White House declined to comment, but a senior U.S. official stressed that Washington has a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and remains committed to defending its allies.
The decision to cancel the attack, or at least delay it, was driven in part by concern in Washington that opening another front could further complicate the parallel conflict with Iran, which has also made little progress.
Trump said Sunday, in response to a question from Fox News reporter Trey Yingst, that he would consider meeting Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian this week on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. He added that he was still weighing his options, suggested major developments were imminent and warned Iran against taking provocative action.
The Saudi request weighed heavily on Trump, who knows that Washington ultimately needs Riyadh’s help in confronting Iran. U.S. military officials who spoke to The New York Times on condition of anonymity said the United States could not manage without Saudi Arabia. They said Saudi officials had “shown a willingness” to use the leverage available to them against Washington if their ally did not cooperate in the campaign against the Houthis.
In May, for example, the officials said Saudi Arabia blocked a U.S. plan to escort commercial oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. The kingdom refused to allow the U.S. military to use its airspace.
Other officials said that if the United States joins the campaign, the move could be carried out alongside a ground offensive planned by forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognized government. Those forces, however, have yet to prove effective against the Houthis, and U.S. officials questioned the value of supporting what they described as a dysfunctional force that has repeatedly been defeated in fighting with the rebels.
Several U.S. military commanders also warned that a limited attack would not defeat the Houthis, who have already withstood nearly two months of sustained U.S. bombing in the past.
The developments come alongside a Reuters report that U.S. officials met early last week in Oman with Houthi representatives, several days after the Iran-backed militia seized a strategic stretch of coastline along the Red Sea in an offensive that defeated Saudi-backed forces of the Yemeni government.
According to the report, the Houthis told the United States at the meeting that they intended to refrain from attacking American vessels in the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait, over which they had effectively taken control.
Reuters reported that the meeting, which was not publicly disclosed but was confirmed by three sources, took place the previous Sunday at the U.S. Embassy in the Omani capital, Muscat.
The Houthis told U.S. officials that they remained committed to the ceasefire reached with the United States in 2025 and therefore had no intention of attacking American vessels. One source, a Yemeni official, told Reuters that the group also said it would not attack Israeli ships or other commercial vessels, except those belonging to Saudi Arabia.

This came as the Houthis also advanced toward Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Saudi Arabia has now faced a potential two-front conflict over the last 10 days. Now Saudi Arabia has sent officials to the UN General Assembly (UNGA). Riyadh has also been wondering whether it will get military support from the US.
What is happening is that the US has advanced a sale of F-35s to Saudi Arabia. However, if the sale proceeds, the 5th-generation warplanes won’t arrive in Saudi Arabia for years. Riyadh needs to decide what to do now.
The Houthis have continued their threats over the last week. They have been fortifying the positions they captured near Bab el-Mandeb; they are pushing propaganda against Saudi Arabia and launching attacks on the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. They have even threatened Mecca. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia’s allies, Pakistan and Turkey, do not appear to be stepping up.
Saudi Arabia is wary of going it alone. Arab News noted on Saturday that “Yemeni government forces clashed with Houthi fighters on several fronts in Marib on Saturday, advancing on Al-Mashjah front west of the city and forcing the Houthis to retreat, military sources said.” The sources added that the Armed Forces destroyed several Houthi vehicles during the fighting, according to an Al Arabiya report.
Saudi Arabia left alone in its time of need
Meanwhile, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan arrived in New York on Saturday to lead the Kingdom’s delegation at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Arab News noted.
“The delegation includes Saudi Ambassador to the US Princess Reema bint Bandar, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Adel Al-Jubeir, and King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Center Supervisor General Dr. Abdullah Al-Rabeeah, along with other officials.”
Saudi Arabia also said it had postponed its Red Sea International Film Festival to 2027. The New Arab media outlet noted that “Saudi Arabia has spent decades building its security partnership with Washington, buying billions of dollars in US weapons and cultivating close ties with successive American administrations.”
It said that “when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a direct plea to US President Donald Trump for military help against Yemen’s Houthis, Washington ultimately stepped away. For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.”
The report, along with others, noted that the US has stepped back from strikes on the Houthis. This is important. Riyadh wants commitment. It has been fighting since 2015 in Yemen. Saudi Arabia has faced this dilemma before. In 2019, Iran attacked Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq energy facility on the coast. This is similar to the September 11 attack on the East-West pipeline.
The message was clear both times. If Saudi Arabia responds, the attacks on strategic infrastructure will continue. Riyadh has more to lose than Iran or the Houthis or militias in Iraq. Saudi Arabia and US Central Command retaliated in July for militia attacks from Iraq. The attacks stopped for several weeks.
This big question for Riyadh at the UNGA is whether it can rally support and also work with Washington regarding the next steps in Yemen. The Houthis believe they are winning. Saudi Arabia will have to see how it can avoid a two-front conflict and also restore deterrence.

articles.title: Pakistan carried out airstrikes on Afghanistan and said it had killed dozens of militants
articles.body:
Pakistan carried out airstrikes on Afghanistan and said it had killed dozens of militants
Kyiv • UNN
Pakistani fighter jets struck suspected militant hideouts in eastern Afghanistan. Kabul reported at least three deaths.
On Monday, Pakistani fighter jets carried out airstrikes on sites in eastern Afghanistan that Pakistani officials described as suspected militant hideouts. Pakistan said 28 militants had been killed, while authorities in Kabul reported at least three deaths, UNN reports, citing AP.
Details
The strikes near the countries’ shared border marked a new escalation of tensions, raising the risk of further cross-border fighting. They also threatened to complicate mediation efforts by regional states, including China.
The strikes came after Pakistan warned that it might attack militants in Afghanistan following two deadly attacks on Pakistani security forces near the border in recent days.
Militant attacks targeting Pakistan’s police and security forces have increased in recent years. The escalation followed months of military operations. Hundreds of people have been killed in cross-border fighting since February, when Afghanistan retaliated with strikes after Pakistan carried out airstrikes on Afghan territory.
Islamabad authorities accused the Pakistani Taliban and militant groups allied with it of being responsible for most of the violence. The Pakistani Taliban is a separate but allied group to the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in 2021.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said security forces had conducted a planned, intelligence-led ground operation in the northwest following a series of militant attacks in the country. The operation was followed by "calibrated airstrikes on the hideouts and safe havens of terrorist organizations responsible for these attacks."
The ministry said in a post on X that the airstrikes had killed 28 militants along the Afghan border.
However, the Afghan government said the strikes had killed three civilians and wounded four others. The claims from both sides could not be independently verified immediately.

articles.title: Russia has warned its cities about every strike for years. During the heaviest raid yet, on election day, it left the sirens silent
articles.body:
Russian authorities left residents in and around Moscow without air raid sirens or phone alerts during Ukraine's largest combined strike on Moscow Oblast, apparently to guard turnout at Russia's parliamentary elections, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said. The silence angered residents and even pro-war commentators as a major oil refinery burned.
For most of this war, Russia has handled strikes on its cities as a routine to be announced, warned about, and waited out. Withholding warnings during the heaviest raid yet, in the middle of a national vote, suggests authorities will trade residents' safety for the look of a calm election when a political milestone is on the line.
Sirens stayed off during the biggest raid
Ukraine hit strategic sites across the Moscow area overnight on 19-20 September, the last day of Russia's State Duma vote. Moscow Oblast officials did not switch on air alert sirens or send the SMS warnings they had used during far smaller attacks. They quietly restricted mobile service without major public notice. Ukraine struck oil and logistics targets, not polling stations, according to the experts, and authorities appeared to place high turnout above protecting civilians.
Moscow Oblast residents complained that no alert reached them, some posting on the Telegram channel of regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov before it closed comments. A prominent Kremlin-linked military blogger attacked the official response, saying it erodes public trust and that cutting mobile service does "not really help."
What the drones hit
Ukraine's General Staff reported striking the Gazpromneft-Moscow Oil Refinery in the city's Kapotnya district, one of Russia's largest plants, causing a large fire. Ukrainian manufacturer Fire Point said its FP-1 drones completely shut down the refinery, with all primary processing units damaged.
Governor Andrei Vorobyov claimed air defenses countered 249 drones across 17 municipal districts. The strike was part of Ukraine's widening campaign against the fuel sector funding Russia's war, with about a fifth of Russian refining capacity offline.
