articles.title: "Mastercard for travelling, Visa for shopping": how Russians get round financial isolation
articles.body:
"Mastercard for travelling, Visa for shopping": how Russians get round financial isolation
"Our plans are the same as they have always been. Our firm position – not to work with the aggressor country – remains unchanged," Tetiana Chorna, Visa's country manager in Ukraine, told Ekonomichna Pravda in March 2025.
Visa and Mastercard pulled out of Russia back in spring 2022. Cards issued by Russian banks under these payment systems stopped working abroad, and Russian nationals lost the access to international payments they had been accustomed to using for everything from booking hotels and paying for Spotify or Netflix to simply paying for groceries at a supermarket checkout with a smartphone.
This gave rise to a new market. Through Telegram bots, little-known financial services offer Russians the chance to obtain a virtual Visa or Mastercard in a matter of minutes, top it up with cryptocurrency or even roubles, and become part of the global payments infrastructure once again.
Some of these services carry out almost no Know Your Customer (KYC) procedures, advertise sky-high payment limits, and explicitly offer the opportunity to pay for foreign services that are unavailable to holders of Russian-issued cards. It's not even Russian banks that are behind them, but chains of intermediaries, offshore companies and licensed financial institutions in various countries.
Ekonomichna Pravda has investigated how this market works, who issues these cards, and how Visa and Mastercard products ultimately end up in Russians' hands, even though the payment systems have officially withdrawn from the country.
A world without Apple Music, Netflix or Steam
Visa and Mastercard payment services ceased to operate in Russia on 10 March 2022. But the cards still worked within Russia because domestic payments were processed through Russia's National Payment Card System (NSPK).
In other words, the Visa or Mastercard logo was still on the physical card, but payments in Russian shops were now processed through Russia's domestic infrastructure.
Outside Russia, Russian-issued cards were now just pieces of plastic. They could no longer be used to pay in shops or withdraw cash abroad, or to buy from online retailers based in other countries.
To enable such cards to continue to be used domestically, Russian banks effectively declared them valid indefinitely. This didn't entirely fix the problem, though. Over time, the international security certificates embedded in the cards' chips began to expire, increasing the risk of technical malfunctions, security vulnerabilities and fraud.
As a result, Russia began to talk about phasing out old Mastercard and Visa cards. According to Russian media reports, the National Payment Card System plans to achieve this by putting economic pressure on banks. This will involve a phased reduction of interchange fees for cards issued under international payment systems.
The plan is expected to be implemented in two stages. The interchange rate is set to be reduced to 1% from the start of 2027, then to zero from the start of 2028. Interchange fees are a source of revenue for the bank that issued the card. If the rate is reduced to zero, banks will have little economic incentive to continue supporting old Mastercard and Visa cards.
In that case, these cards will gradually disappear from circulation, and ultimately Russians will be moved entirely to the domestic payment system, Mir.
The shift to Mir
Although Mir is widely used in Russia, demand for access to global services has not gone away. Russians still want to order products from abroad and use bank cards when travelling.
A new segment of financial services has emerged to meet this demand, consisting mainly of crypto exchanges and little-known platforms that offer virtual cards for cross-border payments.
Ekonomichna Pravda has identified around 50 such services. A significant proportion of them have emerged over the past year or two.
Most of these platforms operate in a similar way. Users obtain a foreign-issued virtual card via a website, Telegram bot or app, top it up with cryptocurrency – usually stablecoins – and receive a balance in dollars or euros.
The card can then be used to pay for online purchases, subscriptions and advertising services, or while travelling. Some platforms also offer physical cards delivered by post.
There are different cards for different purposes. Some are designed to be used with Apple Pay and Google Pay, while others are intended for specific services, subscriptions or advertising platforms. In some cases users are required to undergo KYC procedures, meaning they must verify their identity. But there are also services that explicitly state that no such verification is required.
The key feature of these cards is that they operate through international payment systems. That is what gives Russian users renewed access to the payments that became unavailable to them after Visa and Mastercard withdrew from the Russian market.
An international payment card you can get on Telegram
One of the most popular services that enables Russians to access international payment systems is called CinCin.
CinCin is heavily promoted by Russian and Russian-speaking bloggers. Back in August 2026, they included the rapper and blogger Albert Vasyliev, better known as Kyivstoner, who was later accused by the FSB of being involved in supplying drones used in attacks on Moscow.
CinCin offers virtual Mastercard and Visa cards for international payments. All interaction with users takes place via Telegram. A card can be issued within minutes, after which the user receives the full card number, expiry date, CVV and payment details.
CinCin has a near-identical counterpart, Cinazes. A preview of its website invites users to obtain a virtual Mastercard or Visa card. Cinazes is also actively promoted by Russian bloggers.
"Forget lengthy application forms and tedious checks – your virtual card will be ready in minutes. Want to travel or shop online? Get instant access to a wide range of payment options without the hassle," the website says.
The minimum amount required to create a card is around US$55 for CinCin and US$75 for Cinazes. Part of this covers the card issuance fee, with the remainder credited to the initial balance. The service also charges a 4.5% top-up fee.
Users can top up their balance via the service's internal wallet by transferring USDT on the TRC-20 network. USDT, or Tether, is a digital token known as a stablecoin. Its value is pegged to the US dollar, meaning that one USDT is generally worth around one dollar. TRC-20 is a technical standard used on the Tron network, through which these tokens can be transferred between wallets.
The process is fairly straightforward for users. The service generates a cryptocurrency address to which the user transfers USDT from their crypto wallet or exchange platform. The funds then appear in the service's internal balance and can be used to issue or top up a virtual card.
The service also offers account top-ups through Russia's Faster Payments System. This is a payment infrastructure that enables money to be transferred between banks using a phone number or QR code.
For the user, this works much like an ordinary bank transfer in roubles: the funds are credited to the balance of their account with the service and can then be spent using the virtual card.
Verification is minimal or virtually non-existent. For certain types of cards, the service requires only an email address and even accepts temporary or disposable addresses. A phone number may not be required, and during testing there was no identity verification against reliable sources of identification data.
CinCin claims that its cards can be used to make payments of up to US$50,000 per transaction, US$200,000 per day and US$2 million per month.
Transaction limits on this scale with minimal or no customer identification constitute a serious breach of the generally accepted financial monitoring standards. Essentially this means that CinCin, Cinazes and other similar services may be doing more than just giving Russians access to "prohibited" international payment systems. They could also enable anyone to conduct illicit transactions such as laundering money, financing terrorists, and trafficking weapons, drugs or people.
Through BIN partners in Asia
This gives rise to the question: how is it that services like CinCin and Cinazes are able to offer Mastercard or Visa cards?
They don't generally work with Visa or Mastercard directly. Their cards are issued by a separate issuer, known as a BIN sponsor, which is authorised to work with the relevant payment system. The service enters into an agreement with the BIN sponsor and uses its infrastructure to offer cards to users under its own brand.
According to Ekonomichna Pravda's analysis of two CinCin cards in its possession, CinCin operated through at least two such sponsors until at least autumn 2025. One card had a BIN associated with Sunrate Solutions Limited in Hong Kong, the other with Sunrate Partners UK Limited in Britain.
These findings indicate that Sunrate's card infrastructure was being used, although they do not prove that CinCin works with the company directly rather than through intermediaries.
Sunrate is an international Singapore-based fintech group that provides businesses with international payment, foreign exchange and corporate card issuance services. The company also has offices in Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta, Hong Kong, Shanghai and London.
Sunrate Partners UK Limited is an Electronic Money Institution regulated by the UK's Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), while Sunrate Solutions Limited in Hong Kong holds a Money Service Operator licence.
Sunrate says it became a Mastercard Principal Member in 2020 and obtained the equivalent status with Visa in 2021. This grants the company direct access to the payment networks and the ability to issue cards. Sunrate also issues virtual cards through its own platform and API.
Generally, the use of BIN sponsors through Asian fintech companies is common practice among services of this kind. In various platforms' terms of service, Ekonomichna Pravda repeatedly found references to Hong Kong and Singapore-based companies through which cards are issued.
Cinazes has a similar arrangement which allows users to obtain virtual cards with almost no identity checks. By examining one such card, for example, Ekonomichna Pravda was able to establish that it operates through Singapore-based fintech company UQPAY.
UQPAY provides businesses with payment infrastructure, including international money transfers, payment acceptance, foreign exchange and the issuance of physical and virtual cards. The company's status as a payment institution is confirmed by Singapore's financial regulator.
The company also says it is authorised to issue and service Visa cards. Separately, UQPAY says it is a Mastercard Principal Member for acquiring, i.e. the acceptance and processing of payments.
Why this works at all
Visa and Mastercard themselves have not entered into any agreements with CinCin or similar services, and this is where one of the main problems lies.
Payment systems do not necessarily open accounts for individual users themselves. They operate global payment networks, while cards are issued by banks and financial companies that have access to those networks. Those institutions, in turn, may work with other fintech companies, processing platforms and card programmes. The longer this chain becomes, the harder it is to determine who has ultimately obtained a card and what they are using it for.
Formally, Visa and Mastercard's withdrawal from Russia primarily means that Russian banks can no longer issue cards under these payment systems. But if, for example, a company in the UK, Hong Kong or another jurisdiction issues such a card, and an intermediary then sells it on to a Russian customer, the nature of the relationship is completely different.
Visa and Mastercard may not work with Russian banks at the level of their publicly stated policies, but their cards can still reach Russian users through third parties. It is this loophole that CinCin, Cinazes and other services are exploiting to restore Russians' access to international payments.
Ekonomichna Pravda contacted Visa and Mastercard to ask whether they were aware of the existence of services being used to circumvent these restrictions. We received the following responses.
Visa's press office said: "Visa announced the suspension of its operations in Russia on 5 March 2022, and that decision remains in effect today. Under Visa's rules, an issuer must not solicit customers or issue Visa cards outside the country in which it is licensed to conduct card-issuing activities. This rule has been in place for many years, applies across all regions and was not introduced in connection with Visa's withdrawal from Russia in 2022. All Visa products must be issued in accordance with Visa's rules and applicable law, including Know Your Customer (KYC) and anti-money laundering (AML) requirements."
Mastercard gave a similar response: "Mastercard operates in accordance with applicable laws, regulatory and sanctions requirements, and requires all participants in its network to comply with them. The use of reloadable cards on the Mastercard network without completing KYC procedures, with the exception of gift cards, is not permitted. If we identify indications of, or receive information about, such activity, we conduct a review to ensure that all parties comply with local laws as well as our rules and standards."
The issue is that the services investigated by Ekonomichna Pravda did not comply with either KYC or AML procedures. It is therefore reasonable to assume that such cards could be used not only by a hypothetical "Vanya from Uryupinsk" [an ordinary Russian citizen from a small village out in the sticks – ed.] who wants to pay for ChatGPT, but also by an organ trafficker or weapons manufacturer. The cards' limits are high enough to accommodate transactions of that kind.
Visa and Mastercard do not operate like banks. They don't issue cards to end customers or hold their money in accounts. Their core business is running the global networks through which payments are processed. The more cards are used and the more transactions pass through these networks, the more revenue the payment systems generate from various network and processing fees.
So for Visa and Mastercard, increasing transaction volumes and the number of cards in circulation is part of their business model. Of course, that does not prove that the companies benefit from the market for workaround cards or that they are knowingly allowing sanctions to be circumvented. To reach that conclusion one would require data on specific card programmes, their transaction volumes, and what the payment systems themselves knew about them.
This business model does, however, create an apparent conflict of incentives. On the one hand, Visa and Mastercard have an interest in their networks being used as extensively as possible. On the other, they are responsible for setting the rules for participants in those networks and for monitoring the associated risks.
Officially, of course, neither Visa nor Mastercard has returned to the Russian market.
But the question is: how clearly can the world's biggest payment systems see what is happening at the second, third or fourth tier of their partner networks? And what action do they take when their infrastructure ultimately ends up being used for precisely the kind of activity they publicly withdrew from in 2022?
Ihor Pylypiv, Alina Poliakova
Translated by Myroslava Zavadska
Edited by Teresa Pearce

articles.title: 22 countries back call to keep AI ‘under human control’
articles.body:
The motto "The future is human", used prominently by "The Be Human Company", a Canadian AI strategy and transformation company, is seen during day two of the "ALL IN 2026" conference at the Palais des Congres de Montreal in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, on September 17, 2026. | Andrek Ivanov / AFP via Getty Images
NEW YORK — Several European countries were among a group of 22 nations that adopted a declaration Monday saying that artificial intelligence “must remain under human direction, oversight and control” and suggesting to create a global supervisory regime.
The declaration, adopted on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week, acknowledged AI’s “potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen our economies” but warned that “the rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed.”
The push comes ahead of the meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the leaders of the world’s leading AI-developing nations, in Washington Thursday.
Advertisement
Neither the U.S. nor China are part of the new declaration. But Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. And our message here is that we need human intervention, so humans need to be in charge,” he said in an interview.
Referring to the recent cyberattack by rogue AI agents on the Hugging Face platform, the declaration urges to “address these risks” by obliging AI companies “to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.”
Yet the document falls short of calling for slowing down or pausing AI development, with organizers saying they want to focus on managing risks instead.
Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. | Alessandro Rampazzo/ AFP via Getty Images
To do that, countries should “further develop and coordinate common standards” and strengthen transparency, “including shared reporting of serious safety incidents.” Moreover, UN member countries should “build on existing international mechanisms and explore creating an international institution” to oversee AI.
Stubb, who spoke to POLITICO at Finland’s consular office in New York, said that “our preference personally” would be to create a new institution similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency “within the U.N. framework.” Yet he added, with a nod to Trump’s skepticism of the United Nations, “we have to leave it open-ended so that people don’t reject it just because it would be within the U.N. framework.”
Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who initiated the declaration together with Stubb and who joined the interview via video, said that, “we would be very encouraged to see both G7 and the upcoming G20 presidency of the United Kingdom take on this ... The U.N. is big, but the G7, G20 is a bit more focused.”
Advertisement
However, the U.K. has not signed up to the declaration yet. Among the big European countries, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz supports the initiative, while signatures from France, Italy and Poland are notably absent.
Stubb added that neither he nor Støre were “doomsdayers” about artificial intelligence but named three reasons why the lack of effective oversight is threatening: AI-created bioweapons, cyberattacks by AI agents and killer robots using AI for lethal attacks.
Stubb stressed that the upside of AI can be “much higher” — if the tech is used correctly — ranging from “the eradication of diseases, productivity, information and many other things.”

articles.title: Ukraine has ‘lost its steel industry’ – Metinvest exec
articles.body:
Ukraine has ‘lost its steel industry’ – Metinvest exec
Ukraine has effectively lost its steel industry after Russian strikes brought production at the country’s three largest plants to a halt, a senior Metinvest executive has told the Financial Times.
Ballistic missiles have disabled major steelworks in Kiev-controlled parts of Russia’s Zaporozhye Region and Ukraine’s Dnepropetrovsk Region, repeatedly striking Metinvest’s Zaporozhstal and Kamet Steel plants and ArcelorMittal’s facility in Krivoy Rog. The latest attack on Thursday damaged production equipment, workshops and railway infrastructure, the outlet reported on Sunday.
The three plants, which together accounted for about 90% of Ukraine’s steel output, are now idle, Aleksandr Vodoviz, head of the CEO’s office at Metinvest – owned by Ukrainian oligarch Rinat Akhmetov – told the FT. “As of today, [Ukraine] doesn’t have a steel industry any more,” he said.
The Russian Defense Ministry said the strikes targeted Zaporozhstal, describing the facility as a key producer of pig iron and rolled steel used by Ukrainian and European military enterprises.
Vodoviz said it was unclear when production could resume, with repairs potentially taking “days, weeks, months, or years.” The plants employ more than 15,000 people, and their shutdown could have a major impact on tax revenues for the Ukrainian budget, he added.
Zaporozhstal has been struck several times over the past month, with Vodoviz claiming the attacks had targeted its blast furnaces. “They knew everything about the plant, they knew exactly where to hit,” he said.
Moscow has also reported strikes on industrial and logistics facilities related to Kiev’s military. Russian forces last week hit the Radionix electronics plant and a data center in Kiev, which were involved in missile production and data processing for the Ukrainian Army, according to the Defense Ministry.
Other recent targets cited by the ministry include drone production and storage sites, power infrastructure, bridges, ports, warehouses, and logistics hubs. It also reported hitting a Fire Point warehouse in Kiev Region that it said stored drone components.
The attacks come as Kiev has ramped up long-range strikes on Russian energy, industrial, and civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings, warehouses, and oil refineries.
Kiev claims it considers Russian oil facilities legitimate military targets because they allegedly help finance and supply Moscow’s military campaign. Russia has condemned strikes on civilians as acts of terrorism, while maintaining that its forces only target military and defense-related facilities.
“There is a war of attrition, and now an economic war of attrition – Russia is trying to hurt Ukraine’s economy as much as possible and so does Ukraine,” Alyona Bilan, chief economist at investment bank Dragon Capital, told the FT, adding that Ukraine is unlikely to record any economic growth this year.
The damage extends beyond steelmaking. Some 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s roughly 5 million square meters of modern warehouse space has been destroyed, including 900,000 square meters in recent months, retailer Ruslan Shostak told the FT. The attacks could also cost Kiev around $1.5 billion in tax revenue, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ukraine’s steel industry was already shrinking before the latest strikes. The country produced around 7.4 million tons of crude steel in 2025, down from 7.6 million tons a year earlier and far below pre-conflict levels, according to the World Steel Association.
Producers have also faced growing pressure from cheaper Turkish steel made with Russian raw materials and tighter EU import restrictions. Metinvest COO Aleksandr Mironenko said last week that Kiev had been too slow to protect domestic producers with anti-dumping measures, adding to pressure on an industry now left without its three biggest plants.

articles.title: Europe is under attack from three sides – but the EU and Nato are unfit to defend us | Nathalie Tocci
articles.body:
Europe’s strategic predicament is ever clearer, and ever darker. The continent is at war, which is being fought militarily in Ukraine, but is escalating rapidly across Europe through hybrid attacks. Germany’s disclosure that it blames Russia for the explosion at Leipzig airport; a Russian drone strike on a train near the Ukraine-Poland border; an Italian jet shooting down a Russian drone over Lithuania; flares fired from a Russian warship at a Danish helicopter – all within the space of a couple of weeks – tell a coherent story. Whether because Russia is bogged down and unable to advance in Ukraine, or because it believes the US will not come to Europe’s rescue, Vladimir Putin’s regime is ever more bent on escalating its aggression in Europe.
Putin’s calculus is not irrational. Trump never misses a chance to lash out at Europe – the latest example being his threats of further tariffs on the EU if Brussels proceeds to offer Canada “associate membership”. Europeans have grown numb to Trump’s insults and threats, but these threats do underline his deep antipathy, suggesting that if a Russian attack warranted a response, Trump might look the other way. The US certainly can’t be relied on to have Europe’s back.
This is the context in which Ursula von der Leyen caused surprise last week by proposing associate membership of the EU for Canada. To bolster Europe’s defences, the European Commission president also wants a “European security council”, and a mutual solidarity mechanism to respond to hybrid attacks.
While they have distinct rationales, these ideas fit into the same strategic logic: in a world of predatory powers, the “rest of the west” must huddle together.
The threats are not only external. Along with Putin’s Russia and Maga America, the rise of the far right in Europe completes a triangle of threats. The far right is a threat to liberal democracy. But by instigating internal division and pushing for disintegration, it also supports the divide-and-rule designs of predatory external powers, representing a challenge to Europe’s independence and sovereignty. It has taken the earthquake of the AfD’s successes in German regional elections for von der Leyen to acknowledge openly that Europe’s threats are also homegrown. Better late than never.
Faced with this unprecedented convergence of threats from three sides, leaders are scrambling for a response. Nato has what it takes to defend Europe against Russia. But if its majority shareholder – the US – is unwilling to step in, the question of its plans, structures and capacities is moot. If a hybrid attack on a European country caused civilian casualties, would Nato be bypassed if Washington signalled its unwillingness to act? Collective defence would not even be invoked if the anticipated result were the US’s betrayal of its European allies.
This is where von der Leyen’s emergency protocol comes in, filling the gap between the high-water mark of mutual assistance – article 42.7 of the EU’s founding treaty, which covers armed aggression – and nothing at all. The attacked state would activate the protocol, an emergency European Council would convene, and the commission and EU high representative would propose responses, including evacuation and medical support, stockpiling and energy security, economic coercion, military mobility and more. The mechanism could extend to like-minded non-EU partners, starting with Canada, Norway, the UK and Ukraine. The proposal to offer Canada associate membership, while still undefined, can be read in this light as well.
On paper, it all makes sense. In practice, it is hard to see such a mechanism operating seamlessly, let alone rapidly, given the EU’s organisational complexities, its slowness to act and its internal divisions.
Hence the proposal for a European security council, consisting of those countries willing and able to contribute to the defence of Europe, without the US if need be. Some of these countries would be EU members, but not all – again, Canada, the UK, Ukraine and possibly Turkey.
Both the problem and the solution are clear. To protect itself against predatory powers, what remains of the west must cooperate ever more closely. But the existing multilateral organisations – Nato and the EU – are unfit for purpose. Nato will remain anchored to the US, while the EU is slow and cumbersome, built for peacetime. Its membership, while large, is not wide enough, excluding key players in the wider European space.
Developing alternative forms of EU membership could be of interest not just to Canada, but to the UK, too. The idea was first raised by Berlin for Ukraine, in fact, but Kyiv turned down the offer, seeing it as second-class. Ukraine deserves full EU membership, but if a substantial associate membership is on the table in the short term, it should take that, while continuing to press for more.
The rise of far-right nationalism means that reaching consensus within the EU will become harder, not easier – which is precisely where the proposal for a smaller, more agile European security council comes in, provided far-right governments do not simultaneously come to power across major European countries.
Von der Leyen’s security proposals are sensible and urgently needed. The potential pitfall lies not in the message, but in the messenger. In her years at the helm of the commission she has grown a reputation for centralising power and overstepping boundaries, irking other EU officials in Brussels as well as European capitals. When it comes to security and defence especially, sovereignty is jealously guarded by the EU’s nation state governments. It would be tragic if European governments ended up killing off a set of good ideas because of Europe’s institutional turf wars. Rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic is the last thing Europe and its partners need right now.
- 
  Nathalie Tocci is a Guardian Europe columnist

articles.title: Ukrainian company unveils interceptor for jet-powered Shahed drones: top speed of 416 km/h
articles.body:
Ukrainian company unveils interceptor for jet-powered Shahed drones: top speed of 416 km/h
Ukrainian company Vluchnyk has completed internal testing of the Zorelit v5 (Starship), an anti-aircraft interceptor drone designed specifically to counter jet-powered attack UAVs.
Source: Vluchnyk, speaking to Militarnyi, a Ukrainian military news outlet; the company's website
Quote from Stepan Radiboh, Vluchnyk's CEO: "Zorelit v5 has completed all testing and is ready for military use. We are open to direct contracts with military units, and once the product is codified, we will also make it available through the e-Points system E-points are earned by Ukrainian units for confirmed strikes on Russian soldiers and equipment ."
Details: The drone has a stated top speed of 416 km/h and a range of up to 47 km on a single charge. At a cruising speed of around 200 km/h, it can remain airborne for approximately 17 minutes. The UAV is designed to carry a warhead weighing between 300 and 600 g.
The manufacturer says Zorelit v5 is designed to intercept Russian reconnaissance UAVs, Gerbera-type and Geran-2 drones and high-speed jet-powered Geran-3 and Geran-4 drones.
The interceptor can also be equipped with an AI-based system that automatically detects and tracks targets and provides terminal guidance during the final stage of flight. Separately, it can be integrated with the SkyMap system to enable automatic guidance to the target area.
Zorelit v5 was developed from the earlier Zorelit v4 interceptor, which the company says has been used in combat, entered service and received a NATO Stock Number (NSN). Some technical solutions proved in combat were carried over to the new version.
Vluchnyk's website lists the price of one Zorelit v5 at UAH 89,500 (US$2,000).
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported that an interceptor drone developed by the Security Service of Ukraine's military counterintelligence division to counter jet-powered Shahed-type drones had successfully completed testing.

articles.title: A 21-year-old candidate for Russia’s antiwar Yabloko party documented her campaign for the St. Petersburg legislature
articles.body:
A 21-year-old candidate for Russia’s antiwar Yabloko party documented her campaign for the St. Petersburg legislature
Russia’s elections are over, and Yabloko faced unprecedented pressure throughout them. The party’s federal list was removed from the ballot back in the summer, and its regional lists followed. Only one survived, in the Novgorod region. Yabloko candidates running for regional legislatures in single-member districts complained of pressure, and several were removed from the ballot. The outlet Bereg has published the diary of Marina Peslyak, a 21-year-old antiwar candidate for St. Petersburg’s Legislative Assembly who managed to defend her place on the ballot. For more than a month, Peslyak recorded the election commission’s absurd demands, pressure from law enforcement, and the everyday work of running a campaign. Meduza is translating the diary here.
Bereg shortened and lightly edited Peslyak’s diary and added a timeline of the pressure on Yabloko to her entries.
August 11, thirty-eight days until the election
The day before, on August 10, the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the State Duma election. Yabloko would have been the only party on the ballot calling for a ceasefire with Ukraine as soon as possible.
The district election commission (DEC) got in touch: one person’s donation doesn’t meet legal requirements, even though he filled in all his details correctly. I’m annoyed. One more formality I have to deal with.
Every message from the commission is insanely stressful. I’m afraid they’ve found another reason to kick me off the ballot.
Spent two hours sorting things out with Sberbank — even the staff don’t know how to return a payment like this. But I got it done. It seems like a small thing, but after two hours on one transaction, you just want to shut everything down and not do anything else today.
In the evening, The New York Times reached out. They asked me to comment on my campaign, my motivation, and Yabloko’s list being thrown out. It’s a really strange feeling: a few hours ago I was dealing with the bank, and now the NYT is writing to me.
August 12
I arranged to speak with the NYT journalist, but I’m worried about the possible consequences. Yabloko’s headquarters ignored my question about whether I should agree to the interview.
I wouldn’t want to be answering for the whole party when I’m a candidate for the city legislature. I’m anxious. I want to speak honestly, but I keep thinking about where my personal views end and where I start speaking on behalf of the party.
Lyudmila Vasilyeva wrote to me. She’s asking how she can help.
Gave the interview. It seems like it went fine, but I still have the feeling that now I’m going to replay every sentence [and worry].
August 13
Woke up in the night with a panic attack, thinking I might have said too much in the interview. I’m scared they’ll kick me off the ballot. Scared law enforcement officers will break into my home. Scared for my mom and my sister, who are staying with me right now. At night it all felt completely real, but by morning it was clear how badly I’d worked myself up.
Still, I just have to get up and keep going. I’m writing to everyone who signed up to volunteer.
Talking with the BBC about filming a documentary on my campaign. I don’t even know yet what there is to film: there are hardly any people involved, there’s no money either, and I can’t even get the campaigning off the ground. It’s awkward: it’s supposed to be a film about a campaign, but there’s practically no active campaign.
August 14
Yabloko appealed the Supreme Court’s decision to bar it from the election.
Met with Yabloko’s people in my district, and we talked about our next steps — what we can pull off with the resources I have. For the first time in several days, I felt a little calmer. It’s starting to feel like we at least have some kind of plan.
Messaging volunteers, setting up a meeting. Late at night, I’m writing a post asking for donations. It’s a little awkward to ask people for money again, but without it there’s nothing to run this campaign on.
August 15
Police issued warnings against taking part in unauthorized rallies to several people who had come out to support Yabloko outside the Supreme Court in Moscow on August 10.
Meeting with Lyudmila Vasilyeva and a BBC cameraman, taking photos, talking about the campaign’s problems. I’m filmed for an interview. Of course, she didn’t tell me anything new, but I was glad to see her two years after we last met. Back then I was collecting signatures for her myself, and now I’m the candidate.
It’s uncomfortable to sit in a café next to a metro station and film a conversation about what’s wrong in the country and what’s ahead for us. In a public place, on camera, we’re talking about things people don’t usually say out loud.
August 16
Yabloko found more than a billion rubles in donations to parliamentary parties from donors with foreign ties and demanded that those parties be removed from the election. One of the grounds for removing Yabloko itself was 16,900 rubles “from certain citizens who allegedly received funds from abroad.”
Taking part in a Yabloko photo shoot.
August 17
Russia’s Supreme Court rejected the appeal by Yabloko’s lawyers against the ruling that removed the party’s federal list. During the hearing, police outside the court detained more than 85 people who had come to support the party.
The same day, a court in Pskov sentenced Lev Shlosberg, Yabloko’s 63-year-old deputy chairman, to 11 years and one month in a penal colony in a case over repeatedly “discrediting” the Russian army and spreading “fake news” about the military.
The BBC film about my campaign isn’t happening: the cameraman suddenly left Russia, and the active phase of my campaign started pretty late.
Working on notifying the territorial election commission (TEC) about my printed campaign materials.
August 18, one month until the election
Three Muscovites who had come to the Supreme Court to support Yabloko on August 10 were detained a week later and accused of taking part in an unauthorized rally that obstructed traffic. They were jailed for 10–15 days for administrative offenses.
Yabloko was taken off the ballots. Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova said that Russians who “left and betrayed the country” should be stripped of the right to vote.
The ballot draw.
When I handed over my passport at the ID check at the entrance to the city election commission, a commission member said: “Oh, you’re the one we reinstated! Make sure she gets in, and everyone should know her face. Other complaints are citing her case now.” Funny.
August 19
Apple Savior Day. Went to a meeting at Yabloko’s city headquarters and handed over the results of the drawing so they could sign the contracts with media outlets.
August 20
Eight thousand people applied to join Yabloko after it was removed from the State Duma election, Kirill Goncharov, the head of its Moscow branch, told Bereg. At that point, the party had half that many members.
Going over legal issues with volunteers. Signing contracts with TV companies, writing the script for a video to air on TV. To get the video into the airtime slots the channels assigned me, I’ll have to hand it in in just a few days.
Yabloko can’t record videos for all its candidates: State Duma candidates get priority. We’ll try to do it on our own.
August 21
The Rodina party filed a lawsuit with the Pskov Regional Court demanding that Yabloko’s list be removed from the election for the regional legislature.
We’re trying to find a video editor. Not many responses so far. The price people are asking is sky-high [for the campaign’s budget] — 15,000 rubles.
August 22
Out of nowhere, they wrote to say Yabloko’s headquarters had found time to shoot the video. I need to be at headquarters at 5:00 p.m. and send the script by 3:00.
In the end, everything gets postponed because of bad weather: they were planning to shoot outside.
August 23
Drafting and signing a contract so I can use a special font developed by Yabloko [in my campaign materials]: the party is worried about copyright lawsuits.
August 24
Signing a contract to pay for the finished website, running to the St. Petersburg TV channel to hand over the video recorded at the Yabloko office, then to the TEC to hand in all the contracts and the video and audio materials.
By law, I only have to give the commission a cover letter and the campaign material itself, but they’re demanding every single contract for every transaction that went through my campaign account, the acceptance certificates, the payment orders…
A TEC staffer complained that I supposedly criticize them all the time in the media or on social media, even though they’re trying to help me “out of kindness”: “You seem like a smart girl, you should have known about requirements like this.” I’m not even angry. I’m tired of being surprised.
August 25
Yabloko was removed from the ballot for the Pskov regional legislature election.
Videos made for St. Petersburg’s State Duma candidates are being pulled en masse. Almost all the candidates got letters from TV channels saying their videos had been found to contain “extremism” and “discrediting the armed forces.” The St. Petersburg Election Commission sent them similar letters.
My video has different content, and the script is my own. So far, they’re leaving it alone.
August 26
The St. Petersburg TV channel calls and begs me to withdraw the video voluntarily. They say, “It’s not up to us.” Supposedly the St. Petersburg Election Commission sent them a notice to that effect. I didn’t get any letter from the St. Petersburg Election Commission.
VGTRK also sends a letter about pulling it from the air.
We’re shooting a second video. Since the first script was as toothless as possible (on purpose), the only things that could bother them are the party slogan and the call for peace. I’m sitting here crossing the words “peace,” “freedom,” and “life” out of my own script. I feel angry.
The worst part isn’t even that the video got pulled. What bugs me more is that I have no idea who’s making this decision. The TV people say one thing, the St. Petersburg Election Commission says another, and the TEC says nothing at all.
In the evening, the cameraman and I go to Nikolai Rybakov’s meeting with supporters. To be honest, I expected more. A routine speech in an intimate setting.
August 27
Filing a complaint with the Central Election Commission over the St. Petersburg Election Commission pulling my video.
I contact a print shop and realize I haven’t raised enough to print even 5,000 flyers. They cost 14,658 rubles. For a big campaign, that’s probably not a huge amount. But when you’re raising the money yourself, you feel every expense like that. I decide to put 30,000 rubles of my own into the campaign.
August 28, three weeks until the election
A court removed Yabloko from the elections for the Sverdlovsk and Kaliningrad regional legislatures. VKontakte cut off Yabloko’s broadcast “Mirny strim” (“Peace Stream”), during which the party was raising money for its election campaign.
Spend half the day writing the text for flyers and posters and send edits to the video editor. At first, I really didn’t like the video at all. It came out more creepy than hopeful, and hopeful is what I wanted despite the censorship. I really want to lift people’s spirits somehow, not make yet another unsettling video.
Heading to a meeting with supporters.
August 30
Finally sorted things out with the print shop (there wasn’t enough money, so in the end I paid for it myself). Going around to the TV companies again — this time to submit the censored video.
August 31
In a single day, Russian courts removed three Yabloko candidates running in single-member districts from the ballot — in the Tula region, Tatarstan, and Bashkortostan. In Moscow, Yabloko candidate Artyom Snegovsky was detained over alleged “discrediting” of the army.
Hi, I’m N.
I report for Meduza from inside Russia. I could go to prison for my work. To stay safe, I have to follow strict security protocols. I know my lawyer’s phone number by heart. And, of course, my articles are published anonymously.
Working for an independent news outlet while still living in Russia feels like something out of a spy film. My friends know me by one name. My colleagues and sources know me by another. But sometimes there’s a glitch. At a close friend’s birthday party, someone I don’t know reaches out to shake my hand. “Hi, I’m Lyosha.” It takes me a few seconds to decide how to introduce myself. Do I use my real name or my pseudonym? I’m trying to figure out whether this is someone I might one day end up writing about.
What I do is journalism in exile, even though I’m not in exile myself. I have the rare opportunity to do uncensored, on-the-ground reporting in Russia. Please support Meduza so I can continue this work.
September 1
Handing in the new video and an audio recording for radio to the TEC. Broadcasting starts tomorrow.
September 2
In the end, none of my video or audio materials were allowed on the air.
Going to the TEC again — they called me in to discuss the design of the campaign boards. The commission chair says three more donations were made in violation of the rules (I didn’t find any violations), so the money went to the state. And apparently I’m also supposed to reimburse the donors for those amounts. The law doesn’t say a word about this. I guess I’m supposed to do it out of my own pocket.
At the TEC, they say “the prosecutor’s office has taken an interest” in me. The best part is that all these transfers were made in accordance with the law.
I’m really nervous. I reread the law the TEC cited. It finally sinks in that they’re just trying to slow me down and keep me from running my campaign in peace. There’s very little time left as it is.
September 3
Get a reply from the St. Petersburg Election Commission saying they have nothing to do with my video and audio materials being kept off the air and that I need to go to the TEC (DEC). Then I don’t understand why the TV channels are telling me something else.
Get a letter from VGTRK saying my new video contains “extremism.” The channel’s management cites a demand to that effect from the St. Petersburg Election Commission.
It hurts that the new video won’t air either. So I’ll post it myself.
September 4, two weeks until the election
Two more Yabloko candidates were detained in Moscow: Anna Shatunovskaya-Byurno (Preobrazhensky single-member district) and Grigory Grishin (Leningradsky single-member district).
We’re setting up a group chat for volunteers. Going to the TEC again with booklets and all the contracts, which I spend a couple of hours filling out, copying, and signing every time before I submit them. Writing posts to explain the situation to my supporters.
September 5
Brought my flyers to Yabloko’s headquarters.
September 6
Brought flyers to supporters, and we’re also looking for volunteers. We don’t have enough people, though I’m grateful to every single one. The same day, we start canvassing neighborhoods.
September 7
In Yekaterinburg, six Yabloko candidates were detained. All of them were cited for displaying “extremist” symbols. A penalty for that administrative offense bars a person from running in elections for 12 months.
I’m officially invited to take part in a debate. I meet with my opponents, and we discuss safety: three of the participants, including me, have already faced attempts to get them removed from the ballot.
The conversation was surprisingly constructive, even though our main rival [United Russia candidate Alexei Kulkov] refused to take part in the debate. After all the trouble with commissions and paperwork, it’s nice to just have a normal conversation with other candidates.
Today’s my birthday. I’d like to keep at least the evening for myself.
September 8, ten days until the election
In the morning I get a bunch of calls. Turns out they’re from the prosecutor’s office. There’s a letter from them in my inbox too, dated September 7. Very ironic — thanks for the present. The letter came in the afternoon and went to spam, but I’m supposed to show up today at 5:00 p.m. I answered the call at four.
At the prosecutor’s office, they spoke to me politely and calmly. The staffer who took down my statement listened carefully and, as far as I could see, wrote down what I said without distorting it.
I came away feeling that even they didn’t fully understand why my video counted as a violation. The staffer saw it for the first time herself during our conversation and called the words in the video “prophetic.”
They gave me an official warning and told me to be more careful. They said several times that they were “forced” to issue the warning. Naturally, they didn’t open any case, because there’s nothing to open one over.
At first the whole situation scared me, but then the fear gave way to calm: I’m not the first person in Yabloko summoned to the prosecutor’s office over a video. After that, I mostly found the whole thing funny because it was so surreal.
It also turns out someone reported me for missing the deadline for submitting campaign materials. Supposedly I brought the video to the commission after it had already been distributed.
September 9
Media requests are coming in: Bumaga, SOTA Vision. Campaigning in my district.
In the evening, I go to Yabloko’s headquarters, sign papers related to election monitoring, and bring the flyers that were missing. Recruiting observers is hard: people whose official residence is outside a candidate’s district can’t serve as observers anymore.
By the way, nobody told me the flyers had run out until I asked. I don’t really get why people at Yabloko keep blowing me off. Is that normal for them, or am I just the lucky one?
Coming home, designing posters.
September 10
Handing out flyers in my district. There was a horrible downpour, and only one other person showed up besides me.
The Central Election Commission sent a brush-off reply saying it found no fault with the St. Petersburg Election Commission for pulling my video off the air. It took the Central Election Commission two weeks to answer.
September 11
Yabloko’s list was removed from the election in the Tomsk region. Only the Novgorod region is left.
Groundhog Day. I get up and head out to the district. Campaign, get home by 11:00 p.m. Almost every day looks the same now, and I can physically feel the exhaustion piling up.
In the afternoon, I was messaging with the print shop. There’s not much time left, and the posters still aren’t ready. I’m worried I’m some kind of “half-candidate.”
September 12
Picking up the posters and going straight to the TEC to submit the campaign materials. Then to the district to campaign.
September 13, five days until the election
Before, I felt like I was mostly carrying the campaign on my own. And then suddenly people showed up — on their own, too. It’s probably the first time in the whole campaign I felt like this matters to someone besides me. I’m really tired, but after that it got a little easier.
Actually, I got really lucky with my district — in terms of how people react. Everyone’s pretty positive about me as a candidate and about the party I’m running with. Although today, for the first time in the whole campaign, we met people who were “not going to” talk to Yabloko.
Writing a post about how we campaign. Asking people to help.
September 14, four days until the election
Still campaigning. The flyers ran out — turns out 5,000 isn’t that many. Urgently writing to the print shop. Panicking a little over how much there is to get done.
September 15, three days until the election
In St. Petersburg, Yabloko-appointed election commission members received summonses to report to the military enlistment office on the first day of voting.
Waiting for my flyers. Going to the district. Waiting for my flyers. Going to the TEC. Going to the district.
Going to Nikolai Rybakov’s meeting with supporters. Out of nowhere, they handed me the mic. They had introduced the candidates at the start, but I was late, so I decided to use the chance to introduce myself and ask people to help me. They handed me the mic so suddenly that I didn’t really know what I was saying. There were a thousand people in the room, and the stress was awful. Surprisingly, the appeal worked — quite a lot of people came up to me after the meeting.
Physically, I feel terrible. I haven’t eaten properly in more than a week. I can feel myself starting to get sick from the stress.
September 16, two days until the election
The debate is today. The first one of my life.
Honestly, it didn’t go very well for me. I was nervous. Sometimes I didn’t manage to say what I wanted; other times I could have answered better. But just taking part matters. At least now I know what a live debate is like and what I need to do differently next time.
The main topics were the environment, transportation, urban development, and how the campaign was going. It was more like a discussion than a debate. I got lost amid my opponents’ loud slogans. On top of that, I’d felt awful since morning, and the tension before the debate took its toll.
Yuri Kulikov, Yelena Belyaeva, Ivan Changli, and I attended the debate. Mikhail Amosov and Alexei Kulkov didn’t show up.
I think I got sick after the debate. Slept at home for an hour, and I’m back to campaigning. Stopped by Yabloko’s headquarters to drop off a batch of flyers, then brought campaign materials to Yabloko activists in the district. We’re going to hand out flyers and canvass apartment buildings.
The last few weeks of the campaign were almost identical: I get up at 10:00, leave the house at noon, and get back around midnight. I’m physically and emotionally drained, but I keep going anyway.
September 17, one day until the election
In the Rostov region, where early voting had started, police officers in balaclavas detained Yabloko observer Boris Miklyukov.
Last day of campaigning. I want to sleep for several days straight, but I have to keep going. We need as many people as possible to come out [to campaign] today — we’ll be handing out the last 2,000 flyers.
In the morning, voting members of one of the precinct commissions wrote to me asking for help if something goes wrong. I’m trying to set up a chat for observers, write a post, answer everyone who’s written to me, and get ready to go campaigning, all at the same time.
By now I’m so used to stress that it’s become my normal state. It’s scary, it’s hard, I’m tired, but I still get ready and go. Honestly, I have almost no strength left. But I feel it’s my duty to see the campaign through to the end myself.
Even if I don’t win, I’ve gained a tremendous amount of experience. I had the chance to speak out for peace legally, in times like these. I can do it, and I’m doing it.
September 18, first day of the election
Polling stations in Sochi suspended voting because of the threat of drones.
Yabloko chairman Nikolai Rybakov asked Central Election Commission head Ella Pamfilova to intervene over the pressure on Yabloko’s observers, who were being kept out of polling stations. In total, nearly 1,300 observers from the Communist Party and Yabloko were barred from polling stations.
My assistant and I bought water and snacks and went around to our observers and voting commission members so they wouldn’t go hungry. All day I went from one precinct commission to another, talked with commission chairs, and checked on how things were going at polling stations where we don’t have observers.
Something funny: one precinct commission complained that they didn’t have enough gifts for first-time voters. Usually the state provides commissions with those gifts. The chair asked me to “buy them gifts.” He said they’d be very grateful and would tell everyone who voted for me that the gifts were from me: “We’ll be able to see who voted for you, after all.” Is it stupidity or what? I don’t know. Surreal. Maybe United Russia people came by and did that…
Overall, the commission chairs were pretty polite with me. They all said turnout at their polling stations was about 30%.
September 19, second day of the election
Yabloko observers are still being kept out of polling stations. And at Precinct Election Commission No. 3104 in Perm, a Communist Party observer was turned away along with a Yabloko representative.
In St. Petersburg, police used force while detaining a Yabloko observer, and he lost consciousness. He was later cited for “disobeying” the police, and the commission chair accused him of “attempting to disrupt the election.” The observer’s name wasn’t released.
Still making the rounds of precinct commissions. The Communist Party got in touch — we’re trading news. Lots of their observers weren’t allowed in. Mine, thankfully, were.
September 20, last day of the election
A St. Petersburg precinct commission member named Darya (her surname wasn’t given) was detained over a complaint of “discrediting” the army filed by the precinct commission chair, according to Yabloko’s St. Petersburg branch. The complaint was prompted by her use of the word “war” in a private conversation. Darya believes the real reason may have been to remove her from the polling station. A Yabloko observer was taken to the same police station over filming that the commission considered illegal.
At one precinct commission, the chair (a participant in the “special military operation”) clashed with one of my observers. She was accused of talking to a voter — according to her, she said hi to her mom, who had come to vote. The observer was given a warning.
At another precinct commission, something strange happened. My observer stepped out during the vote count — as she said later, she felt unwell. One of the voting commission members later told me that the ballots were swapped at that moment. It’s hard to verify.
I ask commission chairs about turnout, and they give roughly the same figure: 50–60% over the three days.
Really tired. Late in the evening, I stopped by Yabloko’s headquarters on Shpalernaya Street and talked with other candidates.
Around 3:00 a.m., an acquaintance from one precinct commission sent me the tally sheet with the preliminary results for the precinct. The result was disappointing, of course. I was in second-to-last place, with just over 30 votes. The United Russia candidate [Alexei Kulkov], who didn’t campaign at all, had around 150. And [incumbent deputy] Amosov had around 300.
September 21, results
According to the Novgorod region election commission, with 96.86% of ballots counted, Yabloko is set to win representation in the regional duma with 6.2% of the vote. The Novgorod region is the only region where Yabloko was allowed to run in the regional legislative election.
According to preliminary data, I came in last. Considering that at almost every polling station I visited, another 400 votes appeared after voting ended, I’m not surprised. At one precinct commission, they told me I originally had 90-something votes, and then they falsified the count down to 40-something. According to preliminary data, the United Russia candidate came in second and Amosov first.
Above all, what mattered to me in this campaign was speaking up for peace — and showing people they’re not alone. This whole time, my team and I were able to talk with people about their real problems. Having the chance to speak out is very important to us.

articles.title: Inquest into British aid workers killed in Gaza may call on Israeli and UK military chiefs
articles.body:
Israeli and UK military commanders could be requested to give evidence to an inquest concerning three British workers killed in Gaza when aid vehicles they were travelling in were hit by an airstrike.
It is also possible that the inquest into the deaths of John Chapman, 57, Jim Henderson, 33, and James Kirby, 47, may examine whether the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK.
Until now, the focus of the inquest has been on the role played by the aid organisation in charge of the convoy and the security firm that was protecting it. But at a pre-inquest review, Maria Voisin, the senior coroner for Avon, indicated that the scope of the final hearing would probably be widened to include the role of Israeli authorities in the deaths.
The coroner said she was “minded” to designate the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and the colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, as “interested parties” for the inquest. Interested parties are often relatives of the person who died or an organisation or individual believed to be closely involved in what happened.
Israeli military authorities last month said they would not open criminal investigations into the strike which, along with the three Britons, also killed the Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, and one each from Poland, Palestine and the US. The UK, Australian and Canadian governments called the Israeli decision “shameful”.
In a written submission to the court, Pete Weatherby KC, for Henderson, compared the case to that of the novichok attack by the Russian state in Salisbury, in which the British woman Dawn Sturgess was killed.
In that case, the high court in London ruled the lack of any criminal investigation by the Russian authorities and the strong public concern surrounding the circumstances of Sturgess’s death necessitated the expansion of the scope of the investigation.
Lawyers for the three men accepted that it was possible Israel would not cooperate with the inquest but called for UK ministers to try to apply pressure if needed. Another element the families are keen to have investigated is the role the British military may have played in the incident in April 2024.
Weatherby’s submission says that a Royal Air Force surveillance plane spent about five hours above Gaza on the day of the attack, seemingly returning to base minutes before the airstrikes were launched. The families want to know what, if any, surveillance the plane gathered about the convoy – and what was shared with the Israeli authorities.
The barrister also told the review hearing in Flax Bourton, near Bristol, it was a “matter of public concern” and “great importance to the family” to find out if the weaponry that killed the men was made in the UK.
Voisin said she was open minded about which issues the inquest would consider and would keep some under review. “It’s very much a case of throwing the net wide at the moment,” she said.
Henderson’s father, Neil Henderson, said in a statement: “We hope the coroner will carry out a thorough investigation into the attack that killed Jim and the others [including] an exploration of all the issues relevant to his death, encompassing the decisions and policies leading to the attack, and what role, if any, UK authorities or military equipment originating from the UK may have played.”
Tayab Ali, who is representing the Kirby family, said: “On behalf of the Kirby family they are very pleased that the coroner took onboard their concerns and extended the scope of the inquiry to include those actors that actually caused James’s death.”
The scope of the inquiry has also been widened to include inquiries of the IDF and the Israeli defence ministry. It is understood that inquiries will be made of the UK Foreign Office, Ministry of Defence (MoD) and the Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems as well.
Ali said after Monday’s hearing: “In order for the inquiry to establish the real circumstances of James’s death it’s crucial that information is provided by the Israeli authorities including the IDF and MoD there, that’s the only way we’ll get to the bottom of how and why he was killed.”
A further pre-inquest review will take place in March. No date for the final hearing has been set.

articles.title: New systems could turn the Bayraktar TB2 into “hunters” of Russian radars and air defense systems
articles.body:
New systems could turn the Bayraktar TB2 into “hunters” of Russian radars and air defense systems
Kyiv • UNN
Aselsan has equipped the Bayraktar TB2 with intelligence-gathering and electronic warfare systems. They detect radars, create interference, and help suppress air defense systems.
Turkish Bayraktar TB2 drones have received new electronic intelligence and warfare systems that allow them to detect and suppress enemy radars and air defense systems. Such equipment could theoretically expand the capabilities of Ukrainian drones, Defense Express reports, writes UNN.
Details
Turkey’s Aselsan has integrated three external pods onto the Bayraktar TB2: the Antidot 2ES 100, Antidot 2EA 200, and Fulmar 200.
The Antidot 2ES 100 is designed for electronic intelligence. The system can detect, identify, and determine the coordinates of radio-emission sources, including radar stations.
Bayraktar receives air defense countermeasure systems
The second pod, the Antidot 2EA 200, is designed for electronic warfare. It can jam radar operations and increase the drone’s protection against missiles with radar homing seekers.
The simultaneous use of the two systems gives the Bayraktar TB2 the ability to detect air defense elements and counter their radars. In Aselsan’s promotional materials, the Russian Pantsir-S1 air defense gun-missile system is shown among the potential targets.
Another pod, the Fulmar 200, makes it possible to obtain SAR images at a distance of up to 40 km and from an altitude of up to 9 km.
Defense Express notes that, due to dense Russian air defenses, the strike use of Bayraktar TB2 drones in Ukraine is currently limited. The new equipment could theoretically give these drones a different role: reconnaissance, locating Russian radars and surface-to-air missile systems, and participating in the suppression of air defenses.

articles.title: As Fears of Post-Election Mobilization Swirl, Russian Activists Prepare for the Worst
articles.body:
Rumors that the Kremlin could order another mobilization to sustain its invasion of Ukraine after this month’s parliamentary elections have circulated in Russian media for months.
Now that the ruling, pro-Kremlin United Russia party has secured a record majority, anti-war activists and lawyers told The Moscow Times that anxiety is rising, even though helping Russians avoid military service has long been a routine part of their work.
When the Kremlin called up 300,000 reservists in September 2022 in Russia’s first mobilization since World War II, the announcement sparked an exodus of tens of thousands of Russians and protests in dozens of cities. At least 20,468 of the men who were mobilized in 2022 were confirmed killed as of this month, according to an independent tally.
Activists told The Moscow Times that the renewed speculation about another mobilization “echoes with pain” — and that a new call-up could be faster and harder to evade than the one in 2022.
“Almost everyone here has friends or relatives who have already been affected by [the draft],” said an activist for New Tuva, an exiled anti-war and Indigenous rights movement from Tyva, a southern Siberian republic bordering Mongolia. The activist spoke on condition of anonymity for safety reasons.
A region the size of Tunisia with a predominantly Indigenous population of less than 350,000 people, Tyva has suffered the highest per capita losses of any Russian region in the war. More than 2,100 men and women from the republic have been killed, according to figures compiled by activists.
During the 2022 mobilization, men in the region were taken from their workplaces, detained on the street or collected from their homes at night to be sent to the front, said Sholbaana Kuular of New Tuva.
“We have been living with anxiety and fear since June because we have not yet recovered from the so-called ‘first wave’,” she said.
President Vladimir Putin directly linked the Sept. 18-20 elections to public support for the war, urging Russians to vote and “demonstrate that millions of people stand behind our soldiers.”
Yet Russian officials, including Putin himself, have repeatedly sought to dispel speculation over a new draft. Over the past three months, they have denied planning a new mobilization 18 times.
After the 2022 mobilization triggered widespread discontent, the Kremlin has relied on contract soldiers lured to sign up through payments of up to 5.5 million rubles ($70,000) for a year of service — or simply forced to sign military contracts.
Because military contracts cannot be annulled while the 2022 mobilization decree remains in force, lawyers say that contract soldiers and mobilized servicemen remain bound to serve until the war ends or the authorities release them.
Activists have documented cases in at least 17 regions in which security forces and military enlistment officers detained men and pressured them to sign contracts following coordinated street raids. Some were reportedly threatened with having drugs planted on them.
Idite Lesom (“Get Lost”), a group that helps Russian men avoid military service, said pressure on potential recruits and conscripts performing their mandatory military service has risen sharply in recent months.
“The authorities are making extremely effective use of the fear of mobilization,” Idite Lesom spokesman Ivan Chuviliayev told The Moscow Times.
Recruiters tell men that they can still choose some of the terms of their service if they sign a contract voluntarily while warning that they would have no such choice during a mobilization, he said.
“They are building this very effective narrative: ‘Sign a contract now, before mobilization begins. Once mobilization starts, it will be too late’,” Chuviliayev said.
In 2024, Russia introduced an electronic military register containing records on citizens liable for military service, which could make a new mobilization easier to carry out.
The register allows authorities to use electronic summonses to prevent conscripts from leaving the country. Russians subject to mandatory military service are barred from leaving Russia from the date a summons is deemed served. An electronic summons is considered served seven days after it appears in the register, regardless of whether the recipient has seen it.
New Tuva volunteers help fellow Tyvans by connecting them with military lawyers or translating guidance on avoiding military service into Tyvan, the republic’s widely spoken Indigenous Turkic language.
“Covert mobilization in Tyva has not stopped for a single day, and so our work has continued uninterrupted,” Kuular said.
Tyva is one of many regions and ethnic republics where fears of a second mobilization are particularly acute, as these places are still grappling with the effects of the first wave.
Maria Vyushkova, a leading expert on regional and ethnic disparities in Russia’s war casualties, has attributed this disparity to the disproportionate mobilization of ethnic minorities and Indigenous peoples in 2022.
“It cannot be ruled out that the same will happen in the event of a second mobilization,” Vyushkova warned in an interview with The Moscow Times in January.
The election results could also help indicate which regions might face the heaviest recruitment pressure in the event of another mobilization, exiled political commentator Ekaterina Schulmann said.
“Every Russian citizen has a vital interest in ensuring that, in their own region, United Russia gets as small a number of votes as possible,” Schulmann said.
“Because if United Russia performs particularly well, that will be seen as evidence that the local administration is working well and effectively and that the population is disciplined and compliant,” she added, suggesting that the authorities see such regions as easier places to draft men.
Sargylana Kondakova, co-founder of the Free Yakutia Foundation, an anti-war and Indigenous rights group from the republic of Sakha (Yakutia), likewise said that if a second mobilization happens, it would be “nothing like the first,” especially because of the introduction of digital summonses.
“We are seeing a large wave of emigration from the republic. People often ask us what documents to prepare before leaving the country,” said Kondakova. “And those people who can’t leave are preparing to hide locally.”
In Tyva, men who could afford to leave the country did so over the summer, while those who lacked the financial means to go abroad relocated to nearby regions in hopes of evading a call-up, according to the anonymous New Tuva volunteer based in the republic.
Estimates of the number of people who have left Russia since February 2022 range from 500,000 to 1.3 million. Yet it is hard to measure how many more are considering leaving this year.
Despite widespread fatigue with the war, activist Kondakova ruled out a return of the street protests seen in 2022 — even in Sakha, where Russia’s largest women-led anti-mobilization protest took place.
“Most of those who were willing to protest left and the remaining people are apathetic and depressed. It would be wrong to say that they came to terms with their fate,” said Kondakova. “They will resist, but in their own quiet way.”
For now, experts say the Kremlin is still recruiting enough soldiers to cover its battlefield losses.
Military analyst Dmitry Kuznets told The Moscow Times that Russia is recruiting around 30,000 people a month, allowing it to offset the number of troops killed, seriously wounded, captured or missing. He said the recruitment rate had remained unchanged since July.
“There is no need for an urgent mobilization” in Russia, he said. “Whether [Putin] is assessing the situation rationally remains an open question.”
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
Remind me later.

articles.title: Ukrainian hackers say they obtained classified documents on 70 Russian ship and submarine projects
articles.body:
Ukrainian hacking group Ukrainian Militant said in a Sept. 17 Telegram post that it had obtained a large cache of technical documents on Russian naval projects. The materials it published include documents from 2024 to 2026 on navigation systems for Russia’s Project 636.3 Varshavyanka-class attack submarines, Project 955M Borei-A ballistic missile submarines, and Project 22350 frigates.
The operation was dubbed “Poseidon.” The hackers said they obtained scientific, technical, design, testing, and operational documentation from Russian companies developing systems for the navy. They said the cache includes documents marked “secret” and “top secret.” The full scale and contents of the documents could not be independently verified.
Screenshots published by Ukrainian Militant show documents from the Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering, among others. One example from 2024 concerns development work on the Andoga-M2 navigation system with “advanced positional correction capabilities” for Project 636.3 submarines. Another, dated 2025, concerns development of a modified navigation system for Project 955M nuclear-powered submarines.
Another published document, dated March 2026, concerns the results of interagency testing of the Simfoniya-PM navigation system. Among other things, it says the stability of navigation data generated by the onboard inertial navigation system after maneuvers needs to be improved, as does the system’s interaction with other onboard equipment.
The published materials also include a test program for the Chardash-22350 automated navigation and gyro-stabilization system for a Project 22350 frigate, as well as documentation for the KAMA integrated marine navigation and stabilization system.
Despite the terminology, these are not simply shipboard “navigation devices.” A submarine that is underwater cannot rely on GPS, meaning it has to calculate its position independently and periodically correct its coordinates by other means. Some of the published documents concern newer methods of correcting navigation data.
Ukrainian Militant said the full cache is far broader than the excerpts released publicly and that the larger trove includes technical specifications and requirements, operating manuals, structural and functional diagrams, algorithms, accuracy and reliability parameters, test programs and results, and acceptance documents.
According to the group, the obtained documents cover not only navigation but also sonar, digital hydrography, marine robotics, and autonomous navigation for underwater vehicles. The systems mentioned include Simfoniya, Chardash, KAMA-NS-VK, Sprut-N1, Priliv, and 14Ts217, among others.
The hackers also said the documentation as a whole makes it possible to trace the work of Russian specialists across 70 projects involving ships, vessels, and submarines under construction or modernization. Organizations whose materials were said to be included in the cache include the Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering, the Malachite Marine Engineering Bureau, the Elektropribor Central Research Institute, the Okeanpribor concern, Elara, the Vega concern, and the State Research Navigation and Hydrographic Institute.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces strike Russian Kasta radar, UAV control post in Donetsk region

Ukrainian forces strike Russian Kasta radar, UAV control post in Donetsk region
As reported by Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced this on Facebook.
