articles.title: WATCH Ukrainian press gang snatch TV crew member outside Kiev studio
articles.body:
WATCH Ukrainian press gang snatch TV crew member outside Kiev studio
A Ukrainian TV employee has been forcibly detained by a press gang outside his workplace in Kiev, with footage showing police and draft enforcers in military fatigues shoving the resisting man into a vehicle.
The incident occurred outside the main studio of Inter, one of Ukraine’s major national television channels. The detained man was identified by local media as an editing director working for the broadcaster’s news operation.
The clip, posted on Telegram on Sunday, captures a chaotic scene outside the studio as several officers surround the employee while other people attempt to intervene.
Scuffles can also be seen nearby, with a man in military fatigues pushing a civilian to the ground.
The footage appears to have been recorded by the detained man’s colleagues, who can be heard warning the officers that their conduct will be shown on television.
Российское "ипсо" в виде бусификации нагрянуло к сотрудникам телеканала Интер.
Вот тут поддерживаю, пропагандонов войны нужно отправлять на передовую в первую очередь pic.twitter.com/3APXt7qi1e
The Kiev branch of the Territorial Center of Recruitment and Social Support (TCC), the body overseeing mobilization, later defended the detention, insisting that the officers had done nothing unlawful.
According to the TCC, the editing director had no registered deferment from military service and was wanted for violating Ukraine’s mobilization rules. The agency added that neither the employee nor his employer had taken steps to secure his exemption.
Ukraine barred most military-age men from leaving the country after the conflict with Russia escalated in February 2022 and later lowered the minimum mobilization age from 27 to 25.
The country’s conscription drive has become increasingly contentious amid Kiev’s battlefield setbacks and a shortage of willing recruits.
Ukraine does not provide regular updates on its battlefield losses, but Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last week that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month, citing information from Ukrainian partners.
Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov, meanwhile, said in December that Ukraine had lost nearly 500,000 troops killed or wounded in 2025 alone.
Numerous videos of so-called “busification” – a term Ukrainians use for the forcible detention and transportation of military-age men to recruitment centers – have circulated online. Such incidents have repeatedly triggered confrontations between TCC personnel and civilians.
Moscow has long accused Kiev of seeking to fight “to the last Ukrainian” at the behest of Western powers that are waging a proxy war against Russia.

articles.title: ‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now’: diesel crisis ripples across Britain
articles.body:
The smoke rising from the Kapotnya oil refinery to the south-east of Moscow marks one of Ukraine’s biggest air raids on the Russian capital since the start of the war, and the latest salvo in an energy crisis that threatens to affect households and businesses across the globe.
More than 1,500 miles away, British motorists are braced for the ripple effect from that conflict, and the US-Israel war on Iran. Average UK diesel prices are expected to reach record highs within days – while across Europe and the US, pump prices have already surpassed all-time highs.
In a call on Sunday, Donald Trump pressed Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries over concerns that the attacks were pushing up global fuel prices, the Financial Times reported. On Truth Social, Trump said Russia has “unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry” and called for an end to “this ridiculous and never ending war”.
While the price of Brent crude oil – which briefly fell below $100 a barel on Monday – remains in flux, already hard-pressed households and small firms face a far greater cost threat at forecourt pumps as the combined impact of Russia’s war-damaged refineries and the Middle East crisis has erased about a fifth of the world’s diesel supplies.
“Around half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car now,” says Jon Barden, a former humanitarian adviser turned handyman, who says his fuel costs have doubled. His diesel Ford estate, once used for camping trips, is now used to carry heavy tools to jobs around Tottenham in north London.
Across Britain’s forecourts, the average price of diesel has climbed by 54% to 196.28p a litre since the Middle East crisis began in late February. It is expected to reach a record £2 a litre within days, with some forecourts already charging above the psychologically important mark.
In Europe, pump prices have already hit record highs in recent weeks, leading to unrest and growing calls for government leaders to protect consumers from the surge in cost.
While the popularity of fully electric and hybrid petrol vehicles may be on the rise in the UK and Europe amid attempts to move away from polluting fossil fuels, diesel remains the overwhelmingly dominant fuel. It is the single biggest cost for many independent traders and small business owners, powering transport, tools and services. It is also the economic lifeblood for farmers, and logistics and haulage businesses, layering costs on to grocery bills and consumer purchases.
“I’ve had to put my prices up,” says Barden. “I don’t want to because the people around here don’t have a lot of money. But when fuel prices go up everything else follows. The things I need to buy from Wickes to do a job will cost more before I even fill up,” he says.
In part, the surge in fuel prices is due to the rise in global oil prices following Iran’s effective blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, a vital trade route for Gulf oil. The price of Brent crude has climbed to a four-year high, raising the cost of refined oil products such as diesel and gas oil.
Yet the most pressing energy crisis is not a shortage of crude, but a shortage of the refining capacity to turn crude into the fuels consumers need. The Middle East crisis has severely damaged many of the region’s refineries, which once supplied 10% of the world’s fuels. What little can be produced has struggled to circumvent the blocked trade artery.
Output from Russia’s war-damaged refineries has fallen by almost a third over the past year to reach a 20-year low following sustained drone attacks by Ukraine, according to the International Energy Agency. The latest strike on Kapotnya came after a similar attack by Ukraine in June.
Although Russian oil exports have been subject to toughened EU sanctions since 2022, a reduction in exports to other parts of the world, including Asia, is likely to push up global prices.
In China, which hosts the world’s largest refining capacity, and had been the largest importer of Iranian crude, exports of refined oil products have been capped since March to safeguard the country’s domestic supply.
The global refining slump has helped to keep oil market prices down by dampening the demand for crude. But this is cold comfort for economists who warn that the ‘crack spread’ – or the price difference between crude oil and its refined products – has climbed above $100 a barrel on the continent for the first time and is likely to rip through the economy by raising the cost of all transported goods, as well as household bills.
Diesel in particular is “the workhorse fuel that powers business, haulage, deliveries and rural communities”, according to Luke Bosdet, the AA spokesperson on fuel prices. “Increased fuel costs are passed on to customers, and then on to consumers, which adds to inflation.”
While sales of new diesel passenger cars have plummeted over recent years as motorists increasingly opt for petrol, hybrids, and electric vehicles, the UK’s consumption of diesel has continued to climb because of its role as a crucial industrial fuel.
“Almost everything on supermarket shelves got there on a lorry,” Richard Smith, the managing director of the Road Haulage Association said. “When diesel goes up that cost has nowhere to go but on to the price of goods.”
The AA’s chief concern is for “small businesses, such as taxis and vehicle-based services, and rural communities who already do higher mileages even before diesel costs went through the roof”, Bosdet adds. “They don’t get to add diesel surcharges to invoices, like many of the big companies, for fear of losing customers.”
Mehmet, from Clacton, began driving black cabs in central London 35 years ago. “When I first started, diesel cost 10 bob a gallon,” he laughs. In modern terms this would be 11p a litre, or a fraction of the looming £2 a litre average expected nationwide within days, while cab fares remain capped.
Diesel taxis are easily outnumbered by EVs in London, but they still make up about a third of the black cabs. Drivers were told in February that they would be allowed to raise their fares by 4% this year. At the time, the rise was above inflation – amid concerns over an exodus of black cab drivers. However, the US-Israeli bombardment of Iran ignited a war that has caused fuel costs to surge and inflation to remain well above the Bank of England’s 2% target, at 3.1% last month.
“We’re stuck with it,” says Mehmet. “We don’t want the meter price to go up, because then we lose custom. But we can see oil companies making billions in profit while we take home less. How can that be right?”
The UK may be acutely exposed to the global squeeze on road fuel supplies. The number of refineries in the UK has dwindled since the start of the century from nine to four, causing the UK’s reliance on diesel imports to climb from 14% of the UK’s diesel consumption in the early 2000s to 54% last year, according to Fuels Industry UK.
Elizabeth de Jong, chief executive of Fuel Industry UK, said: “Our latest annual statistics, published earlier this week, show that UK demand for petroleum products increased by 1% in 2025 to almost 61m tonnes, while the closure of the Grangemouth and Lindsey refineries reduced UK refining capacity by almost a quarter.
“We are currently having to import about 55% of our road diesel, meaning a growing dependence on overseas supply. Global events such as the conflict in the Middle East demonstrate the vital role that UK refineries play and why they are crucial to our economy,” she said.

articles.title: Diplomacy or war? Trump weighs next move on Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Diplomacy or war? Trump weighs next move on Iran
US President Donald Trump is weighing whether to pursue renewed diplomacy with Iran or further military action as he prepares for high-level talks with Gulf leaders in New York this week.
Trump is expected to meet representatives from all six Gulf Cooperation Council states - Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman - on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly's 81st session. The talks are expected to focus heavily on Iran and the future of the conflict.
The meeting comes as Qatar intensifies efforts to bring Washington and Tehran back to the negotiating table, with Qatari mediators exchanging proposals with both sides for nearly two weeks and shuttling between capitals in search of a breakthrough.
The diplomatic push is unfolding against an increasingly volatile regional backdrop.
Renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure, the group's advances around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and tensions around the Strait of Hormuz have raised fears of further disruption to regional and global trade.
US embassies across the Middle East have also issued security alerts urging American citizens to exercise heightened vigilance amid the possibility of a rapid escalation, warning of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruption.
'An earthquake'
Qatar is trying to create a diplomatic opening before the conflict enters another phase.
Speaking at the Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatar's Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani called for Gulf states and Iran to work towards a new regional security framework.
"Our region has experienced what I can only describe as an earthquake," Sheikh Mohammed said, arguing that Gulf states needed to work collectively to restore stability and improve relations with Iran.
Qatar's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said on Sunday that Doha had spent nearly two weeks exchanging ideas with Washington and Tehran over the possibility of restarting negotiations.
"For around two weeks, we have been exchanging different ideas on resuming talks between Washington and Tehran," Qatari media reports cited Al Ansari as saying.
"We are working through our mediation team with Tehran and Washington to explore whether the talks can be resumed, and our mediators are currently travelling between different capitals in the hope of making progress on this track," he added.
"We have heard assurances from US administration officials that Washington wants to reach an agreement," Al Ansari said.
He also called for "a regional solution that brings stability and an international understanding that protects waterways such as the Strait of Hormuz", warning that "placing waterways under the sovereignty of a particular state and using it as a weapon would set a dangerous precedent for all of us".
The mediation effort could receive another opening in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are due to attend the UN General Assembly. Washington has agreed to allow a core Iranian delegation to attend despite the ongoing conflict.
Trump has also signalled that he would be open to meeting Pezeshkian during the gathering, although no such meeting has been announced.
'Blow the entire nation up'
The diplomatic manoeuvring comes as Trump publicly weighs whether to pursue negotiations or launch further military action against Iran.
Speaking to Fox News over the weekend, Trump said he was in "deciding mode" and warned that "very big things" would happen in the "not-so-distant future".
He described the options before him as destroying Iran, allowing the country to "rot" economically or reaching a deal.
"My question is, if and when, do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave," Trump said.
His comments followed similar remarks to Axios last week, when he said he faced a "big decision" over whether to resume large-scale attacks on Iran.
Trump had previously suggested the war could end after the November midterm elections, while accusing Tehran of seeking to influence the vote.
Iran, meanwhile, has warned that it was prepared for renewed large-scale fighting and would retaliate against another US attack.
Iranian media quoted Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Hossein Mahdavi as saying Tehran would deploy new weapons and strike targets that had not previously come under attack if Washington launched another assault.

articles.title: For first time in war, Ukraine drops small robot vehicles behind Russian lines from heavy bombers, and clears 125 square kilometers of Donetsk Oblast
articles.body:
For the first time, Ukraine has dropped ground robots behind Russian lines from the air. The 3rd Army Corps, behind the mission, says its heavy drones delivered kamikaze unmanned ground vehicles more than 10 kilometers into the Russian rear during the "second season" of Operation Vivaldi, letting Ukrainian troops flank them and clear another 40 square kilometers.
Vivaldi is the counteroffensive the corps is running near Lyman in northern Donetsk. Over its first two "seasons," the 3rd Army Corps and attached units have retaken more than 125 square kilometers, half of it de-occupied outright, and inflicted more than 3,000 casualties on Russian forces.
The operation, run under an information blackout for months, has also disrupted Russia's push and, the Institute for the Study of War found, its plan to encircle the fortified belt of Donetsk cities.
Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, corps commander, has said the operation, which he named after Vivaldi's Four Seasons, will run through four phases, and only two have been completed. The air-dropped robot is the newest report on how the corps fights.
Machines go first, infantry follows
The corps casts the tactic as a means of expending robots rather than people.
"In assault operations, drones and ground robots always go ahead of the infantry," Biletskyi says.
The 3rd Army Corps was the first in the world to begin air-dropping ground robotic systems. Our heavy bombers deliver kamikaze robots more than 10 kilometers into the Russian rear.
Wars are won by infantry, one of the corps' soldiers added, "but we protect ours, so the robots go to the enemy first."
A dome hides the assault
As the assault groups advanced amid the operation, Ukrainian air defense and electronic warfare threw a protective dome over the battle area, blinding Russian drones so they could not read the operation's design.
Meanwhile, artillery and strike drones hit command posts, communications nodes, logistics, crossings, and reserves, letting Ukrainian units dig in on the ground they had taken.
On the Lyman axis, the corps says it freed the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove and took control of Drobysheve, and that Vivaldi has kept Russia from shifting significant forces to the Kupiansk front.

IIT-Bombay faculty protest in support of Prof Doolla after deanship suspension amid student death row

articles.title: Trump said that Russia had lost diesel capacity because of the war and called on it to end the war - Zelenskyy responded
articles.body:
Trump said that Russia had lost diesel capacity because of the war and called on it to end the war - Zelenskyy responded
Kyiv • UNN
Trump said that Russia's diesel industry had suffered losses because of the war and called on it to end the war. Zelenskyy reported on the dialogue and peace ideas.
US President Donald Trump commented on Russia’s loss of control over diesel production and stressed the need to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded to his statement, emphasizing that dialogue with President Trump is ongoing and that ideas for bringing peace closer are on the table, UNN writes.
What Trump said
"Russia, unfortunately, has lost control of its diesel industry because of the war with Ukraine. A large number of their diesel refineries have been blown up and, at least temporarily, taken out of operation. This senseless and endless war with Ukraine must be ended. The entire world is suffering, while 25,000 people, mostly soldiers, are killed every month. What a shame!" the US president wrote on Truth Social on September 21.
How Zelenskyy responded
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy responded to a post by US President Donald Trump.
"Indeed, this Russian war against Ukraine and against common sense must be ended," Zelenskyy said on X.
The president noted that "from the first year of the full-scale invasion, its consequences have been far-reaching: the loss of many lives, the destruction of cities and villages, food security, energy problems, the extraordinary pace of technological development, including autonomous drones, and the rapid improvement of strike capabilities that had never existed before."
"Every new week of this war, let alone every new year, adds more and more problems. From the very first minute, Ukraine sought peace. We have already made dozens of diplomatic proposals on how to end this war with dignity, guarantee security, and prevent new Russian invasions," Zelenskyy said.
"Dialogue with President Trump and America is ongoing. There are also ideas on the table for bringing peace closer, beginning with decisive steps toward de-escalation. Ukraine’s energy sector, critical infrastructure, and our food exports must stop being targets for Russia, and this will lead to corresponding de-escalation steps on our part. Solutions are possible. We are ready to work on this, and we will discuss it with our partners on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. I thank everyone who is helping! It will no longer be the case that only the country that was attacked suffers. The nature of war is now such that the aggressor will also suffer. Technology makes this possible. The strength of countries’ leadership can—and must—ensure de-escalation, security, and peace. Thank you!" Zelenskyy emphasized.

As reported by Ukrinform, the 7th Corps of Ukraine’s Air Assault Forces announced this on Facebook.
“On the Huliaipole front, within the area of responsibility of the 7th Air Assault Corps, the Defense Forces carried out a series of airstrikes against the enemy’s logistics infrastructure,” the statement said.
According to the report, Ukrainian troops destroyed bridges near the settlement of Polohy that Russian forces used to transport personnel, heavy equipment, and ammunition to support offensive operations toward Orikhiv.
“As a result of the strikes, enemy logistics in this section of the front have been significantly disrupted. The ability of Russian units to redeploy forces and logistical supplies has been limited,” the Corps added.

articles.title: After Ukrainian Armed Forces strikes, there may be no S-300, S-400 or "Pantsir" systems left around Taganrog at all
articles.body:
After Ukrainian Armed Forces strikes, there may be no S-300, S-400 or "Pantsir" systems left around Taganrog at all
Kyiv • UNN
Specialized sources reported the possible loss of Russian air defense systems near Taganrog. Information about the destruction of S-300s, S-400s and "Pantsirs" has not been officially confirmed.
Following a series of Ukrainian long-range strikes, Russia may have lost a significant portion of its air defense around Taganrog. According to specialized sources that have not yet been officially confirmed, no S-300, S-400, or "Pantsir" systems remain near the city, Defense Express reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Taganrog is important to Russia's military infrastructure because of the facilities located there. At the same time, the latest successful attacks by the Defense Forces may have significantly weakened the city's air cover.
Over the past week, Ukrainian forces continued comprehensive long-range strikes against facilities in the Taganrog area. Among the targets attacked, Defense Express names the Beriev Aviation Scientific and Technical Complex and the Ozon logistics hub.
Air defenses around Taganrog may have been significantly weakened
According to the publication's specialized sources, following the Ukrainian attacks, no S-300 or S-400 surface-to-air missile systems, or "Pantsir" anti-aircraft missile and gun systems, allegedly remained in the area of the city.
At the same time, Defense Express emphasizes that this information has not yet been officially confirmed.
Russian military facilities are located in the Taganrog area, including enterprises in the aviation industry, so the weakening of air defenses could be significant for further Ukrainian long-range operations.

articles.title: Russia’s pro-Putin party set to win election as Ukraine exposes war’s growing reach into Moscow
articles.body:
Russia's ruling United Russia party is on track to comfortably win a tightly controlled wartime election after Ukraine launched what is thought to be the largest drone attack on the Moscow region on the last day of voting.
United Russia, which is supported by Russian President Vladimir Putin, received 57.5% of the parliamentary vote with more than 71% of the ballots counted, data from the Central Election Commission showed. It is the first election to the 450-seat State Duma, the lower house of parliament, since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
On Sunday, three people were killed in what Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin described as the "largest enemy drone attack" on Russia's capital to date. Flames and huge columns of black smoke rose from the city's outskirts, and a facility at an oil refinery was also damaged.
Russian government officials accused Ukraine, which condemned the Kremlin for having the elections include residents of regions it illegally annexed from Kyiv during the war, of trying to disrupt the election.
The results are expected to shore up the dominant United Russia, which is far ahead of its rivals, after more than four-and-a-half years of war.
All parties on the ballot have broadly pledged loyalty to Putin and his political views. The liberal Yabloko party was the only registered party to oppose the war in Ukraine, but the country's top court barred it from standing.
Elina Ribakova, senior fellow at Peterson Institute for International Economics, said the election shows that United Russia is on course to receive a much higher vote share than in 2021.
"I think it matters for the regime to show the legitimization of it, right? People have voted and just a curious fact, head of Chechen Republic [Ramzan] Kadyrov, for example, got 99.85% of the vote," Ribakova told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Monday.
"What happens after the election, that's what really matters," Ribakova said. "I think Putin himself worries the most about the participants of the war. There will be hundreds of thousands of people who will be coming back, should there be peace or a temporary ceasefire, to Russia facing stagflation: high inflation and zero growth," she continued.
"This is what Russia calls the most passionate part of the population that the regime needs to be really worried about."
Zelenskyy to meet Trump in New York
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday said he and U.S. President Donald Trump had agreed to meet in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week.
"We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelenskyy said via social media.
"There are ideas for de-escalation steps and for addressing fundamental security issues – energy security, food security, and the protection of human life. We are working together with the American team and are ready to take really serious steps," he added.
The Ukrainian president followed his post on meeting Trump by sharing an update on the situation in Zaporizhzhia, after what he called a "vicious" Russian attack overnight.
Residential buildings, a university facility and a shopping mall were among some of the infrastructure damaged in the attack, Zelenskyy said, with five people reported injured.
A separate drone strike in the Kharkiv region killed one person, with Russia striking 10 regions on Sunday evening and throughout the night, Zelenskyy said. "Russia is not backing down from its escalation and is sending many signals that it is ready to expand the war," he added.

articles.title: Why K-Pop Took Off When C-Pop Didn’t
articles.body:
It’s not often that an 18th century folk song can be said to be the inspiration for a pop concert. But those who attended the finale of BTS’ “ARIRANG” North American concert tour at Los Angeles’ giant SoFi Stadium earlier this month will long remember the tens of thousands of fans who waved South Korean flags and sang along to the traditional Korean melody.
The four-night run in LA was the finale to a tour of 31 sold-out shows, with combined attendance of approximately 1.92 million, according to figures released by the band’s agency. For comparison, Beyoncé’s 2023 Renaissance tour sold about 1.73 million tickets across 35 North American shows.
The flag-waving scenes from the SoFi capped a banner year for Korean pop, following BTS’s World Cup final halftime performance. Earlier in the year, Golden, from KPop Demon Hunters, collected a Grammy, followed by an Academy Awards performance and the Oscar for best original song.
Those performances and prizes will have brought smiles to the faces in Seoul’s foreign-policy circles, where there is a keen appreciation for the soft power that K-Pop brings South Korea. In Beijing, it will have led to much gnashing of teeth.
For more than a decade, China has looked on with undisguised envy as its Korean neighbor has accumulated soft power through cultural exports. As far back as the 2014 National People’s Congress, the Communist Party heavyweight Wang Qishan marveled at the reach of Korean culture, citing popular TV dramas like My Love for the Star and the breakout dance hit Gangnam Style by Psy, arguably the first K-Pop star to break big worldwide.
The interest went beyond public musing: Beijing resolved to learn from Seoul’s example. China’s culture ministry signed an agreement with its South Korean counterpart, providing for annual cultural-industry forums and cooperation in marketing cultural products abroad.
But it is one thing for Beijing to study Seoul’s cultural outreach, and quite another to match it. China, despite possessing a vastly larger population, an extensive diaspora, and the world’s fourth-largest recorded-music market, has failed to produce a music machine comparable to the international following of the marquee K-Pop acts. And while Taiwan’s Mandarin-language stars and Hong Kong’s Cantopop veterans have their own histories, they haven’t as yet spawned an act as ubiquitous as Blackpink or Stray Kids.
The audience Wang wondered about now extends well beyond America and Europe. Blackpink’s leading Spotify markets in 2024 included Indonesia, Mexico, the Philippines, and Brazil, spanning across the Global South, where Beijing has invested billions in the pursuit of soft power. These audiences' affection for K-pop reaches across linguistic and political boundaries, giving Seoul a welcome that its diplomats would struggle to arrange.
One obvious reason for China’s failure to produce pop stars of global reach is the sheer size of the domestic market. “A concert tour of 10 Chinese cities is probably as big as if they go around the world,” Anthony Fung, professor of journalism and communications at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, told the Financial Times. Why spend years trying to understand Brazilian teenagers when there is so much money to be made in familiar surroundings? Chinese musicians have perfectly sound commercial reasons to focus on the home market, regardless of their government’s geopolitical ambitions. Korean companies, with fewer customers at home, had more reason to take on the risks and costs of finding fans abroad.
That incentive would have achieved little without companies willing to adapt to foreign tastes. Korean agencies combined intensive training with production and promotion, recruited performers internationally, and hired foreign songwriters and choreographers. They built acts whose appeal survived the loss of the lyrics. For instance, fans didn’t need to understand Korean to dig Psy’s dance moves. The resulting music would not satisfy a purist’s definition of national, but its borrowings helped it travel: Korea’s entertainment industry learned to please people elsewhere.
Those listeners could also help find the next audience. YouTube let fans share performances without waiting for local broadcasters to discover them; viewers could join in by making videos of their own. When Gangnam Style passed a billion views in December 2012, YouTube reported that it had already drawn at least a million views in nearly 75 countries. Fourteen years later, KPop Demon Hunters shows how much further this can go. The Sony Pictures Animation film distributed by Netflix made Korean pop culture its selling point. In other words, American businesses now have their own reasons to keep the world interested in Korea.
Chinese performers, on the other hand, face greater difficulty getting that circulation started. YouTube and Instagram are blocked at home, separating their domestic following from the platforms where potential foreign fans congregate. They can release music overseas, of course. But their most enthusiastic supporters cannot pass it along as easily, so a hit on a Chinese platform has further to travel before it reaches a Mexican listener. Beijing’s determination to police what enters the country complicates its ambition to export what comes out.
The policing also reaches into the relationship between performers and fans. In 2021, China’s internet authorities abolished online rankings of entertainers and tightened supervision of fan accounts. Broadcasting regulators banned idol-development shows and demanded political correctness from entertainers, expressing special disdain for supposedly effeminate men. Some restrictions addressed legitimate concerns about children being induced to overspend. But a state that prescribes acceptable masculinity is doing much more than protecting young consumers: It is claiming jurisdiction over the tastes that pop music exists to indulge.
This is an expensive preference for a government seeking friends. Joseph Nye, the political scientist who developed the concept of soft power, wrote that “popular entertainment often contains subtle images and messages about individualism, consumer choice, and other values that have important political effects.” The messages themselves—lyrics about youthful love and angst—needn’t concern foreign policy to help a foreign minister. A country that others around the world have encountered as a source of pleasure has a better chance of receiving a sympathetic hearing when it asks for support. Seoul still needs persuasive policies, but K-pop gives it an advantage over governments whose principal introduction to foreign publics is a dispute or a threat.
China itself has supplied a demonstration of how stubborn that affection can be. Beijing’s unofficial restrictions on Korean entertainment, imposed after Seoul agreed to host an American missile-defense system, have not prevented Chinese fans of K-Pop from traveling abroad to see the performers they love.
Seoul has good reason to encourage an industry capable of sustaining such loyalties. Chinese officials might point to the Korean government’s support for entertainment companies to argue that the state has a useful role in cultural exports, but public assistance doesn’t entitle officials to supervise the relationship with the audience. Foreign listeners bring tastes no ministry can predict, and successful performers need room to accommodate them. China can afford the studios, the training, and the promotion. Its leaders must decide whether they can tolerate a pop star whose first obligation is to please the fans.
Meanwhile, back in the US, there is every expectation that K-Pop will continue to break new ground in 2027: BTS and Blackpink feature prominently in speculation about who will perform in next year’s Super Bowl halftime show. The best Chinese officials can hope for is to score tickets to the game.

articles.title: Trump prepares extensive UN schedule featuring Ukraine, UK leaders, and GCC summit
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has scheduled an intensive series of bilateral meetings with world leaders during his two-day visit to the United Nations General Assembly, including discussions with the leaders of Ukraine, the United Kingdom, among others.
Nearly 130 heads of state are convening in New York amid geopolitical strain and institutional challenges for the UN, following sharp US funding reductions across several international agencies.
Trump is expected to land in New York on Monday afternoon for political engagements at Trump Tower before addressing the General Assembly on Tuesday morning, US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz confirmed.
"The president will highlight how he has and his administration have confronted complex problems head-on around the world," Waltz said.
"He will touch on the importance of ensuring that Iran never has a nuclear weapon."
Global diplomacy
The confrontation with Iran—now spanning over six months—is set to dominate Trump's diplomatic discussions, particularly during a scheduled summit with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) leaders.
Trump will subsequently host a reception for the council, where he is set to hold his first in-person meeting with US-backed Venezuelan interim president Delcy Rodriguez.
On Tuesday, Trump is set to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who confirmed via social media that the two leaders agreed to meet during the assembly.
Trump is also scheduled for separate bilateral talks on Tuesday with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham—their first in-person meeting—and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
An additional meeting with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi is also anticipated during the summit.

articles.title: UN investigators warn Ukrainian, Russian attacks threaten civilians ahead of winter
articles.body:
Escalating attacks on infrastructure by Russia and Ukraine are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches, UN investigators have warned, raising concerns about a repeat of last winter’s suffering.
The UN’s Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine said on Monday both sides had intensified long-range strikes against civilian sites, including energy, industrial and port infrastructure, as well as ships in the Black Sea.
The commission said Russian attacks during the winter of 2025-2026 caused prolonged power and heating outages as temperatures fell to minus 20°C, leaving millions of civilians without adequate heating.
“Ukrainian authorities recorded cold-related deaths and injuries,” commission chair Erik Mose told the UN Human Rights Council.
The commission also voiced concern over reports of Ukrainian attacks on infrastructure inside Russia and Russian-controlled areas of Ukraine, saying they indicated rising civilian casualties and damage to civilian objects. It said it had been unable to investigate those reports because it lacked access.
“Continued attacks on energy infrastructure are making living conditions increasingly unbearable for civilians, and we are concerned that the coming winter will be more difficult to endure,” Mose said.
The findings came after US President Donald Trump called last week for an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, although neither side has confirmed it will participate.
Children, foreign recruits
The commission also reported on Russia’s imposition of what it described as patriotic education in occupied areas, including military training for Ukrainian children from the age of 14.
It said children were taught to handle weapons and carry out military drills.
Investigators also examined the recruitment of foreign nationals to fight for Russia, saying some had been deceived or coerced into joining the Russian armed forces.
Mose said agents and intermediaries had recruited people from various countries with promises of civilian jobs before they were allegedly compelled to sign contracts with Russia’s defence ministry.
Many recruits did not understand Russian or the contracts they signed and were subsequently sent to the front lines in Ukraine, he said.
The commission said some were killed, wounded, captured or went missing, leaving families searching for relatives from abroad.

articles.title: Ukraine builds app to cut soldiers’ paperwork. It has just saved them $40 million, mostly on fuel
articles.body:
Ukrainian soldiers have saved about $40 million through discounts built into their army app. The "Pluses" program in Army+ just signed its 40th partner, Ukraine's tactical-gear maker M-Tac, and it lets soldiers claim the deals without showing a military ID, Mstyslav Banik, a deputy defense minister, says.
Banik is the man who helps Ukraine's digital transformation. He was a part of Army+ and its companion Reserve+ development team, ran former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov's procurement reform, and kept his post after Fedorov was pushed out this summer. The new defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara, kept Banik and his team to preserve the reform's momentum.
Fuel leads the discounts
The discounts soldiers most often use, Banik says, are on fuel, pharmacy purchases, and postal services. The newest partner, M-Tac, a Ukrainian maker of military and tactical clothing and gear, becomes the ninth company in the program's "equipment" category, alongside Ukrarmor, UTactic, and Balistika.
To claim its discount, a soldier generates a code in the app and shows it at the Militarist store or enters it on M-Tac's website.
Soldiers skip the ID check
The design spares soldiers the need to prove their identity. Because only service members can access Army+ to begin with, the discounts require no military documents or status checks and therefore do not require handing over personal data, the Defense Ministry said. The ministry has also allowed soldiers to pass along offers to their families, a feature they have used more than 110,000 times.
The app started as a paperwork fix
Army+ is more than a coupon book. It was launched in 2024 to strip bureaucracy out of soldiers' lives, letting them file reports in a few clicks instead of days. Within a day of its launch, 20,000 soldiers had signed in. It has since grown to handle transfers, mobilization, the return of soldiers who were on AWOL, and services from training courses to secure chat.

France Moves to Shield Critical Defense Sites From Russian Drone and Cyberattacks
France is preparing nationwide defenses against an intensifying campaign of Russian hybrid attacks, with its intelligence services bracing for the possibility of a large-scale assault.
France Télévisions reported on September 19 that internal planning now points to autumn 2027 as an accelerated scenario, brought forward from an earlier horizon of 2030.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The threat has sharpened in recent months, according to France Télévisions, taking the form of cyberattacks against the French military and government ministries. Fabricated videos generated by artificial intelligence have also targeted candidates ahead of the presidential race, part of a wider pattern of operations striking several European countries.
In an unprecedented step, the government convened all of France's prefects in an emergency session, France Télévisions reported. Beginning next week, each department is to stand up a security and defense staff drawing together local police and military commanders, education officials, business leaders, and emergency responders.
President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged on September 18 that the security climate had shifted and that France, like its European partners, was readying itself. "I asked the government to prepare a plan to protect our critical infrastructure," Macron stated. The plan extends to the most sensitive sites of France's defense industrial and technological base, guarding against both drone and cyberattacks.
According to a confidential note reviewed by France Télévisions, the infrastructure judged at risk includes power plants and electrical grids, rail networks, telecommunications, and drinking-water distribution. Macron summoned the country's presidential candidates to the Élysée Palace's new high-security crisis room on September 18 to alert them to the danger.
France's principal airfields are already prepared against drone incursions, but the exposure runs wider, according to retired Air Force General Patrick Dutartre. "One can imagine that all sensitive sites associated with defense could be targeted," Dutartre noted.
The Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, rejected the idea that Moscow menaces Europe. "Some European leaders openly declare that they are preparing for war against Russia," Putin claimed, arguing they were merely trying to rescue "plummeting popularity ratings."
France Télévisions reported that the country's intelligence services are readying for a possible wave of massive Russian attacks, with the projected timeline steadily contracting. While planners once looked toward 2030, the reporting indicated that autumn 2027 is now the reference point.
The interference shadowing the presidential race is not new. Paris prosecutors opened an investigation in August 2026 into a campaign that circulated fabricated videos aimed at former Prime Ministers Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal. 
The falsified clips carried the branding of established French news outlets and were tied to the Russia-linked networks Storm-1516 and Matriochka. The physical threat has been just as concrete: in early August, an explosive-laden drone was discovered beside a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Germany's Leipzig airport, a plot US intelligence has linked to Russian services.

articles.title: Russia Could Use Properties in Sweden as Bases for Espionage and Sabotage
articles.body:

Russia Could Use Properties in Sweden as Bases for Espionage and Sabotage
Russian-owned properties across Sweden could potentially be used as bases for espionage and sabotage, according to politicians and security experts, as the country still lacks legislation capable of preventing such property acquisitions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to SVT on September 21, properties with Russian owners are located across Sweden, and the Swedish Security Service (Säpo) has identified foreign-owned real estate as a potential security concern.
A survey conducted by the Swedish Defense Research Agency (FOI) identified 247 properties across the country owned by Russian actors.
However, the actual number could be considerably higher. FOI researchers had to manually examine around 10,000 names of property owners registered as living abroad. Properties belonging to foreign owners who reside in Sweden do not appear in the relevant registers at all.
Swedish Defense Minister Pål Jonson said intelligence-gathering activities in Sweden have increased, while Peter Hultqvist, the Social Democrats’ defense policy spokesperson, noted that the security concerns extend beyond properties located near military facilities.
“Russia is waging a hybrid war against Sweden and other countries. This could involve properties that could be used for sabotage in Sweden, espionage, or other efforts to undermine Swedish society,” Hultqvist said.
He also criticized the pace of Sweden’s response to the issue, saying that the previous years “have not been used optimally.”
According to SVT, Sweden has spent nine years examining the issue, yet no legislation has been introduced to prevent such property purchases.
Concerns over Russian-owned real estate have already surfaced in a case involving a property near the Muskö naval base in the Stockholm Archipelago. The Swedish Armed Forces have submitted a formal request to the government to take control of the 600-square-meter property, which is owned by the family of Russian businessman Stanislav Aleshchenko.
SVT reported on August 25 that the military justified the request on national security grounds, noting that the property is the only plot bordering the strategically important naval base that remains outside military control.

articles.title: Head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence says he is satisfied with Witkoff's diplomatic work
articles.body:
Head of Ukraine's foreign intelligence says he is satisfied with Witkoff's diplomatic work
Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (FIS), has refuted claims that the Ukrainian government is dissatisfied with the work of the US President's Special Envoy Steve Witkoff in the negotiation process.
Source: Axios
Quote: "Umierov said the negotiations are under close public and media scrutiny and therefore 'it comes with criticism'.
'Nevertheless, we need to stay focused. Steve has done a great job with us. We do not waste time and stay focused on finding solutions,' he said."
Details: This was Umierov's response to a recent article by The Kyiv Independent, which claimed that the Ukrainian government is becoming increasingly frustrated with Witkoff's diplomatic work. The head of the FIS told Axios that this is not true.
Quote from Umierov: "I believe that the work of American negotiators should be assessed by people who are directly involved in the negotiation process and work closely with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner."
Details: He added that over the past year he has worked daily with Witkoff and Kushner and that they are primarily focused on finding solutions to end the war and securing guarantees of security and prosperity for the Ukrainian people.
Umierov also reported significant progress in the negotiations: "In particular, the number of stumbling blocks reduced from dozens to essentially one or two key issues that remain subject to negotiations."
Background:
- On 6 September, Donald Trump's envoys Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Kyiv for the first time, the day after visiting Moscow and holding talks with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
- Witkoff said following his visits to Moscow and Kyiv that "substantive progress" has been made, including on scheduling further trilateral talks.
- At the same time, The Kyiv Independent reported in its article that both Kyiv and Moscow are questioning Witkoff's role in the negotiation process, with only Trump reportedly unwilling to remove him.
- In particular, Ukrainian officials have allegedly expressed doubts about Witkoff's understanding of the causes of the Russia-Ukraine war and his approach to diplomacy, whilst also complaining about his lack of interest in the work, claiming he prefers spending time in restaurants instead.
- Conversely, the Kremlin is increasingly accusing Trump's envoy of failing to force Ukraine to cede territory and of not passing information to the US president in a manner that suits Moscow.
- Furthermore, the Ukrainian side is dissatisfied with Witkoff's overly accommodating approach towards Putin, whom Trump's envoy has met at least eight times, speaking warmly about these meetings on numerous occasions.
- Specifically, during their latest meeting on 5 September, Witkoff said: "After I retire, I'll look back on my meetings with Putin in the Kremlin as some of the best and most unforgettable moments of my life."
- Additionally, in 2025 Witkoff noted that he does not consider Russian ruler Vladimir Putin to be a bad person.

articles.title: Czech journalists expose Europe-based staff of Rybar, a pro-war Russian Telegram channel
articles.body:
Czech journalists expose Europe-based staff of Rybar, a pro-war Russian Telegram channel
Journalists at the Czech outlet Seznam Zprávy found that representatives of Rybar — an analytical center and one of the largest pro-war Telegram channels with ties to Russia’s Defense Ministry — work in Europe and regularly interview politicians, journalists, and experts.
Seznam Zprávy exposed Rybar staff by drawing them to a meeting under the pretext of an interview with Bohumil Kartous, an expert on media literacy and disinformation. Rybar representatives had contacted Kartous first: a producer who introduced himself as Boris reached out and said Rybar was preparing a “documentary series on the current sociopolitical and economic situation in Europe.”
According to Seznam Zprávy, Rybar representatives planned shoots not only in the Czech Republic but also in Slovakia, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Austria, Hungary, Belgium, France, and Russia.
The Czech journalists identified the producer of the Kartous interview as Boris Dvorkin, a Russian citizen who had not previously been linked to Rybar. They also found that one of his projects was funded by Russia’s History of the Fatherland Foundation, which Russian President Vladimir Putin set up by decree.
Two Rybar staff members who introduced themselves as Vitaly and Igor came to Prague to meet the journalists. Seznam Zprávy identifies them as Vitaly Chashchukhin and cameraman Igor Dolmatov. Both men have EU residence permits. The journalists also noted that Chashchukhin had worked with Izvestia, Channel Five, and REN TV, all of which are subject to sanctions. When the Seznam Zprávy journalists revealed who they were, the Rybar staff members left.
Rybar’s Telegram channel was founded by Mikhail Zvinchuk, a former employee of the Russian Defense Ministry’s press service, and his colleague Denis Shchukin. According to The Bell, Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin helped fund the channel.

articles.title: Unelected EU official fumes over Russian election
articles.body:
Unelected EU official fumes over Russian election
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has lashed out at the results of Russia’s parliamentary election, dismissing it as a “veneer of democracy.” The senior EU official, a noted Russia hawk who was appointed, not elected, to her post in 2024, made no mention of the 1,600 drones Ukraine launched into Russia during the vote.
Her claims of democratic dysfunction did not include Ukraine’s own indefinitely suspended elections, but stuck to a vote whereby some 60 million people cast ballots across 11 time zones.
In a post on X on Monday, Kallas targeted the three-day elections in which the ruling United Russia party retained a commanding parliamentary majority with nearly 58% of the party-list vote, well ahead of its rivals, according to preliminary results. Turnout exceeded 59% from 51.7% in 2021, according to Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova.
Kallas claimed that “the so-called Duma elections marked another major setback for Russian democracy,” adding that “their outcome was never in doubt.” She further accused Moscow of silencing its critics, stressing that “the veneer of democracy is all that remains in Russia.”
Kallas also claimed to have “proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories.” The EU said separately that it would never recognize voting held in Crimea, Donetsk, Lugansk, Zaporozhye, and Kherson regions – all of which voted to join Russia in public referendums in 2014 and 2022.
Australia, Canada, New Zealand, Norway, and the UK issued a joint statement likewise describing the voting in those territories as a “sham.”
However, neither Kallas nor other Kiev’s backers made mention of a huge Ukrainian drone raid on Moscow amid the election. The attack – which Russian officials said involved more than 1,600 drones and was aimed at derailing the vote – killed two civilians in the capital suburbs and damaged an oil refinery, residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure. Ukrainian strikes in frontline regions also damaged dozens of buildings housing election commissions, according to local officials.
Kallas was ridiculed by social media users over the fact that she herself was not elected by EU voters to the position, having taken office as the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy in December 2024 after serving as Estonian prime minister and a member of the European Parliament.
Kallas and Kiev’s Western backers have consistently refrained from calling on Ukraine to hold its own presidential election, after Vladimir Zelensky’s term expired more than two years ago and he refused to call a new vote, citing martial law. Russia has since declared him “illegitimate,” arguing that Zelensky’s dubious status complicates any eventual peace settlement.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova responded to the election criticism by mocking Kallas’s earlier call for EU states not to recognize the Russian results, saying that “EU countries had stopped recognizing Kallas herself a long time ago.”

articles.title: France vows response after Iran closes language centre in Tehran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
France vows response after Iran closes language centre in Tehran
France will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities sealed a French language centre affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.
"This new attack against France's cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and unacceptable," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement.
Ties between the two countries have been strained for years over Iran's nuclear programme and Tehran detaining several French nationals.
Although the relationship had improved after their release and Paris distanced itself from the US war on Iran, the situation worsened over the summer after two of its diplomats were arrested and subsequently expelled. France reciprocated.
Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported earlier on Sunday that authorities had closed the French language centre following a judicial order from the Tehran prosecutor's office.
Iran cites security concerns
The centre operated for years under the cover of foreign-language teaching despite repeated warnings to obtain a licence, authorities said, accusing it of activities against Iranian culture and national security, including identifying and building networks as well as facilitating the departure of skilled Iranians from the country.
France has previously dismissed such allegations, saying there had been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as Paris sought to increase its support for, and contacts with, Iran's civil society following a crackdown on protests at the start of this year.
Diplomats said Iran has also been irked by a recent social media post from France's foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, to mark the fourth anniversary of the death of Mahsa Amini, which triggered protests across the country.
In response on Friday, Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araqchi, called the post "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of slaughtering 1.5 million Algerians during the war of independence.
"Your silence when the US massacred our schoolkids said it all," he said, referring to a strike in Iran that Tehran believes the US was responsible for.
The two ministers are set to meet on Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations.

articles.title: European intelligence services expect Russian provocations to intensify
articles.body:
European intelligence services expect Russian provocations to intensify
Representatives of the intelligence services of Czechia, Latvia and Sweden expect an increase in Russian sabotage operations in Europe, whilst assessing the likelihood of an invasion of NATO countries differently.
Source: representatives from European intelligence services in an interview with The Guardian
Details: In separate interviews conducted over the past week in various locations, three heads of European intelligence services shared their perspectives on the potential threat posed by Moscow.
Michal Koudelka, Head of the Czech Security Information Service (BIS), believes that Russia could resort to a small-scale invasion of NATO countries or false-flag provocations within the coming months, rather than years.
Koudelka noted that, in addition to increased drone activity, small-scale invasions into the territory of NATO countries bordering Russia could form part of the Kremlin's plans.
"It's possible. It could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, a massive influence campaign," he said in an interview at the BIS headquarters in Prague.
Koudelka noted that this scenario could play out within "months, not years", but added that "a lot of people are doing everything they can to make sure this doesn't happen".
"We don't see indications of an imminent attack," stated Normunds Mežviets, Head of the Latvian State Security Service (VDD), in an interview at the agency's headquarters in Riga. He acknowledged that there are indications Moscow is preparing for more decisive actions in Europe but noted it remains unclear whether these plans are simply part of a destabilisation strategy.
"It's still an open question if they have direct and concrete plans or if it's just within the context of their overall attempts to spread fear and uncertainty in western society," he said.
As reported by The Guardian, Baltic politicians, who for many years have criticised western Europe for its soft stance on Russia, now find themselves in the unusual position of having to urge some western leaders to show restraint in their public statements, fearing that talk of an imminent invasion could harm their societies and economies.
Mežviets noted that, overall, it is positive that western Europe has woken up to the threat posed by Russia.
Koudelka said the Kremlin seeks to exploit vulnerabilities in western societies in order to undermine their support for Ukraine's war effort.
Thomas Nilsson, Head of the Swedish Military Intelligence and Security Service, noted that he sees no signs of Moscow's readiness for genuine negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.
All three intelligence chiefs stated that, regardless of how events unfold, Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe is likely to intensify in the coming months.
Nilsson called the recent incident involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig Airport, which German authorities have linked to Russian intelligence, a "gamechanger". According to Nilsson, behind the recent escalation in Russian sabotage activity lie several goals: to diminish support for Ukraine, sow division within NATO and intimidate the European populace.
Mežviets noted that Russia is transitioning from chaotic acts of sabotage and arson aimed at spreading panic to targeted attacks on specific facilities linked to western support for Ukraine.
Koudelka noted that another consequence of the sabotage campaign is the overstretching of intelligence services' resources, as doubts frequently remain even when incidents are caused by other factors.

articles.title: Swiss lawmakers  grill defence minister over botched F-35 deal
articles.body:
Swiss lawmakers grill defence minister over botched F-35 deal
Swiss defence minister Martin Pfister was bombarded with questions about the procurement of F-35 fighter jets, two weeks after the publication of a damning report.
Pfister faced 19 questions by parliamentarians who wanted to know who was responsible for the scandal and whether there would be any criminal consequences.
“The Federal Council will set out its position in due course,” he replied on numerous occasions. The government is due to give its official position in December on the report by auditors.
More
F-35 jets: fixed-price scandal will have no immediate consequences
A September 8 report revealed serious shortcomings in negotiations with the United States during the procurement of F-35 aircraft. No fixed price was agreed, contrary to earlier statements by former defence minister, Viola Amherd, and military procurement unit armasuisse.
“Standard practice”
The report also highlighted issues with external consultancy, Homburger, which was commissioned to assist armasuisse in the contract negotiations.
This centered on a conflict of interest within Homburger when deciding on the fixed price. Several lawmakers have questioned the legality of this practice.
“Enlisting the help of an external consultancy is standard practice,” said Pfister, adding that the report “found no unlawful conduct or financial loss within the meaning of liability law.”
“Within the rules”
At the time, the government had planned to purchase 36 fighter aircraft. It has since scaled back its plans in light of the higher prices demanded by the US.
Switzerland will ultimately purchase only 30 aircraft. The government has asked for CHF394 million to cover extra costs.
By the end of June, Switzerland had paid out nearly $2 billion for the fighter jets. The total budget earmarked is CHF6.4 billion.
Pfister said operating costs are “on track” to meet budget.

articles.title: Ukraine Sets New Hospital Rules Amid New Two-Level Air Raid Alert System
articles.body:
Led by Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi, Ukraine’s government has ordered hospitals to continue life-saving procedures – such as surgery, resuscitation and intensive care – even during a red-level air threat, when patients and medical personnel must otherwise move to shelters immediately.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced the new rules on Monday, Sept. 10, building on the two-level air threat system unveiled earlier this month.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Emergency medical services will operate without interruption. Patients with urgent conditions will be admitted regardless of the threat level,” Koretskyi said.
Hospitals to operate under both yellow and red air alerts
The new system was imposed due to Russia’s increasingly changing attack tactics, designed to provide the public with more clarity over the level of danger while allowing parts of the economy to keep operating during less severe threats.
The yellow alert is primarily used for incoming drone strikes, while the red alert signals ballistic and other missile threats, alongside mass attacks.
The new measures announced by Koretskyi require hospitals to provide medical care, dispense medications and accommodate patients inside shelters or other designated safe areas.
Under a yellow-level alert, medical facilities will continue operating, but must provide employees, patients and visitors with unrestricted access to shelters.
Medical personnel and patients must immediately move to shelters under a red-level alert. However, procedures that cannot be safely interrupted will continue, and patients who cannot be relocated will be provided with treatment in the safest available areas of the facility.
Russian Attack Destroys Pet Retailer Warehouse in Kyiv Region
Emergency dispatch centers will continue to accept calls and ambulance crews will respond to patients regardless of the threat level, Koretskyi said.
The government also instructed authorities to strengthen protections around operating rooms, intensive care units, maternity wards and admissions departments.
The measure additionally covers rooms containing backup power supplies and critical medical equipment.
Metro running through drone alerts as well
Beyond the hospitals, the government recommended earlier in September that Kyiv keep its metro operating normally during yellow-level alerts.
The capital should also increase surface public transportation when necessary, allowing people to reach workplaces, metro stations and hospitals despite ongoing drone threats.
Kyiv shortens night curfew
Kyiv authorities have adopted a new curfew as well, shortening the restriction by one hour.
The curfew now runs from 1 a.m. to 5 a.m., instead of starting at midnight.
Since taking office amid a broader cabinet reshuffle on July 16, Koretskyi introduced measures aimed at reinforcing Ukraine’s resilience, including a winter preparedness plan centered on energy systems, fuel reserves and physical protection for critical infrastructure.
Ahead of the Sept. 1 school reopening, the government also introduced new security measures requiring local authorities to protect children by limiting large ceremonies in high-risk areas and ensuring rapid access to shelters.

articles.title: Trump considering ‘blowing up’ Iran – Fox News
articles.body:
Trump considering ‘blowing up’ Iran – Fox News
US President Donald Trump is weighing several options regarding Iran, including blowing the “entire nation up,” Fox News has reported. At the same time, Trump has reportedly signaled that he is open to talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
The US and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February, killing senior officials and commanders, including longtime Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. A June 17 memorandum intended to halt the fighting expired in mid-August without a lasting agreement. Maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted, pushing up global energy prices.
On Sunday, Fox News correspondent Trey Yingst reported that Trump had told him he was in “deciding mode” and teased “very big things… happening in the not-so-distant future.” Trump is considering “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal,” according to Yingst.
The president also reportedly indicated that he is “open” to meeting Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week.
Trump has repeatedly threatened Tehran in recent months. In April, he warned that Iran’s “whole civilization will die” unless it accepted Washington’s demands. The US nevertheless suspended its latest wave of strikes in late July amid reports of ammunition shortages, which the White House denied.
Washington shifted toward greater economic pressure last month, announcing a “crushing economic operation” aimed at isolating Iran and penalizing countries that continue trading with it.
Meanwhile, Tehran has warned that any renewed US attack would trigger retaliation against American bases and interests across the Middle East.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said over the weekend that Tehran had conveyed seven conditions to Washington for the start of negotiations. He later told Al Jazeera that they include an end to the war on all fronts, the release of frozen Iranian funds, and an end to the US naval blockade. Qatar has been acting as an intermediary.
“Trump’s threats will not achieve any results. We are prepared for a decisive war,” Rezaei said.
Against this backdrop, US diplomatic missions across the Middle East issued security alerts over the weekend, urging Americans to exercise heightened vigilance amid the risk of further escalation. The warnings also cited renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis.

articles.title: German auto workers protest historic job cuts
articles.body:
German auto workers protest historic job cuts
Tens of thousands of auto workers across Germany have staged protests demanding protection for employment and factories after Volkswagen announced plans to cut 100,000 jobs.
Employees at Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Audi, Porsche, and major suppliers are taking part in more than 280 actions nationwide on Monday. Germany’s largest industrial union, IG Metall, has warned that the country’s automotive industry “faces the risk of total collapse” as it grapples with high energy costs following reduced imports of Russian oil and gas, US tariffs, and growing competition from China.
”We expect corporate leaders and management teams to take responsibility for Germany as an automotive nation, for employees and for jobs,” IG Metall chief Christiane Benner told workers at Volkswagen’s headquarters in Wolfsburg.
Volkswagen’s planned reductions include some 50,000 previously announced cuts across its brands and another 50,000 under a new agreement. The company also slashed its 2026 operating-margin forecast on Friday to no more than 1%, citing weakness in China, restructuring costs, and problems at Porsche.
Other German carmakers are also scaling back. BMW is cutting about 8,000 jobs, while Mercedes-Benz is reducing production at home and expanding capacity in lower-cost Hungary.
The industrial contraction extends beyond layoffs. Volkswagen ended car production at its Dresden plant last December, marking the first closure of a German car factory in the company’s 90-year history.
The automaker has also dropped out of the Euro Stoxx 50 for the first time in 15 years, with its shares down more than 75% from their 2021 peak. By contrast, shares in German defense giant Rheinmetall have soared over 1,100% since the start of 2022 as Berlin boosts military spending.
Parts of the automotive sector are also turning to defense. Volkswagen’s Osnabrück plant, where car production is due to end next year, is set to shift toward military manufacturing, with Israeli arms maker Rafael lined up to produce air-defense systems and components. Mercedes-Benz has also explored opportunities in the sector.
Germany has budgeted €108.2 billion ($124 billion) for defense this year, with spending set to rise further under Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s drive to build what he has called Europe’s strongest conventional army.
Moscow has criticized the buildup. Russian President Vladimir Putin said in June that NATO had moved beyond supporting Ukraine and was now “openly” discussing preparations for war with Russia while increasing military budgets.

articles.title: Trump says U.S. is working on ‘major deal’ to replace Canadian potash with Belarusian supplies, but President Alexander Lukashenko says Minsk has none to spare
articles.body:
Trump says U.S. is working on ‘major deal’ to replace Canadian potash with Belarusian supplies, but President Alexander Lukashenko says Minsk has none to spare
President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the U.S. is working on “a massive Deal” to buy potash fertilizer from Belarus.
Trump, who is currently waging another trade war with Canada, said, “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”
Just hours before Trump’s post, however, Alexander Lukashenko said that even if Belarus regained full access to Western markets for its potash fertilizer, it still could not supply them because all its potash was already under contract:
“As far as I know… We’ve managed to shift our exports eastward. Our negotiations with the Americans are proof of that. A lot of people here are making a fuss about potash. Even if we wanted to supply other markets — Western markets — we simply don’t have the volume. It’s all under contract.”
The U.S. relies on imports for nearly all its potash fertilizer. Canada supplies almost 80% of those imports and Russia another 12%.
Belarus is one of the world’s largest potash fertilizer producers, alongside Canada, Russia, and China. But sanctions have restricted its access to Western markets. The sanctions were imposed over the brutal crackdown on Belarus’s 2020 protests and the Lukashenko regime’s complicity in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
After Trump was reelected to a second term, the U.S. began improving relations with Lukashenko and, among other steps, lifted sanctions on Belarus’s potash industry. The EU, however, has kept its sanctions on Belarusian potash imports in place.

articles.title: Exclusive: Iraq PM to ask Trump for more time to disarm militias
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraqi PM to ask Trump for more time to disarm militias
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is expected to ask US President Donald Trump for more time to disarm pro-Iran militias when the two meet next week, an Iraqi government source told The New Arab.
The meeting comes as a 30 September deadline set by Baghdad to bring weapons held by militias under state control approaches.
The source said al-Zaidi intends to provide fresh assurances over his government's commitment to the disarmament process and ensuring that the Iraqi state retains a monopoly over the use of force.
However, he is also expected to raise the challenges facing the process and argue that more time is needed to implement it.
"Al-Zaidi will ask the US president not to impose financial or economic sanctions on Iraq," the source said.
They added that parties within Iraq's ruling Coordination Framework coalition were "pressuring al-Zaidi on this issue and are attempting to secure additional time for the process".
The source said resolving the issue by the end of September was no longer possible.
Al-Zaidi is scheduled to meet Trump on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this week.
The Iraqi government now appears to be seeking to manage the deadline rather than conclude the disarmament process by 30 September, potentially giving armed factions opposed to surrendering their weapons more time to reassess their positions.
"The committee established by the government to oversee the process of bringing weapons under state control is continuing its work, and pressure is building to turn the deadline from an endpoint into the starting point of a longer process," the source added.
Al-Zaidi had committed to Trump during a visit to Washington in July to resolve the issue of militia weapons by 30 September.
However, the government has struggled to make progress, with major armed factions refusing to surrender their weapons and allied political groups in parliament backing their position.
Iraqi armed groups have fired missiles at US-linked sites in Iraq amid the ongoing US-Israeli war on Iran.
Washington has shown no sign of easing its commitment to the 30 September deadline, raising fears that the US could resume strikes on militia sites in Iraq.

articles.title: Russian strikes halted 90% of Ukraine's steel production – FT
articles.body:
Russian strikes halted 90% of Ukraine's steel production – FT
Three plants that produced 90% of Ukraine's steel have halted operations following Russian strikes.
Source: Financial Times
Details: In early September, Russian ballistic missile strikes knocked out Ukraine's three remaining major steel plants, located in the industrial centres of Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
"As of today, [Ukraine] doesn't have a steel industry any more," Oleksandr Vodoviz, head of the chief executive's office at Metinvest, an international mining and steel group headquartered in Ukraine, told the FT.
Quote: "They [the Russians] knew everything about the plant, they knew exactly where to hit."
More details: The ballistic missiles targeted the blast furnaces of three plants, including two Metinvest plants and the ArcelorMittal plant in Kryvyi Rih.
The companies said these plants, which accounted for 90% of Ukraine's steel production, had to be shut down.
"Right now we do not understand how long it will take to make the repairs, days, weeks, months or years," said Vodoviz.
He said the shutdown of the plants, which together employ more than 15,000 workers, could have a significant impact on tax revenue for Ukraine's budget.
Background:
- On the morning of 17 September, Russia attacked the shut-down Zaporizhstal (Zaporizhzhia Steelworks), a major iron and steel manufacturing plant in the city of Zaporizhzhia, with two ballistic missiles. One employee has been taken to hospital. Production equipment and railway infrastructure have been significantly damaged. This was the fourth attack on Zaporizhstal since August.
- Following a Russian ballistic missile strike on 11 August, Zaporizhstal completely shut down operations. In late August, Metinvest said that it was not yet possible to determine when the steelworks could resume operations.
